Might academics and academies alike be ignoring these essential queries right now and yet again, as they have done for more than twenty years?

Conveniently for us all, there are no academics at work in hobgoblology today. None of us need suddenly realize, “Oh! That’s my job!” But any of us may be skeptical of Edwards’ reasoning in “Paragons,” because logic is (or ought to be) a general, not a special, attribute among us.

Edwards’ purpose in “Paragons” is to show that “the unique psychology of hobgoblins, on both the individual and the societal level, fills a special niche within the monstrous world.” Understanding their psychology leads to the conclusion that “Unlike their chaotic humanoid cousins, hobgoblins maintain a highly organized social order that operates with military efficiency. Because of the hobgoblins’ military bent tactics are an important part of any encounter with them. It is necessary to know the tactics that hobgoblins commonly use as we make plans to contain the hobgoblin threat.” In Edwards’ view, our past ignorance of hobgoblin psychology explains our past military failures, and our new knowledge offers hope for future success. It is an enticing message with major implications for the foreign policy decisions that Furyondy is making right now.

Unfortunately, there are major errors in the royal decree’s reasoning. Edwards represents hobgoblin psychology as a social construction based on “the life metaphor of the personal perimeter, which young hobgoblins are taught as soon as they are old enough to understand spoken words.” The life metaphor embodies the central philosophy that will determine hobgoblin behavior; its principles influence all aspects of a hobgoblin’s life.

Each hobgoblin learns early to establish a personal perimeter of defense. This perimeter represents not the chaotic creature’s need for personal space but a highly lawful creature’s portion of the greater tribal perimeter. In the hobgoblin mindset, one hobgoblin controls his own immediate area, two control still more, and so forth. Thus, a whole tribe jointly controls a significant area that it claims for its own use. The methods used to achieve this mental condition are harsh, to say the least. Abuse, both physical and mental, is common. Combat training is the only emotional outlet allowed to hobgoblins, and learning to defend a space is the most integral part of maintaining a personal perimeter. Years of such extreme programming yield an unquestioningly loyal soldier who desires nothing more than to serve the tribe.

The block quote makes clear that a personal perimeter consigns “all aspects of a hobgoblin’s life” to service in training a consummate soldier. The price for such training is everything that is decent in commensurate society.

Mercy and compassion can only weaken the perimeter and cloud thinking. Individual freedom is meaningless and has no place in hobgoblin society. Marriage and monogamous relationships are unheard of in hobgoblin culture since the emotion evoked by such close ties would weaken the personal perimeter. Hobgoblins reproduce through a selective breeding program in the hopes of producing superior offspring. Peers generally arrange couplings during religious holidays or post-victory feasts. Although parents maintain roles of authority in their children’s lives, hobgoblins are raised in a communal environment. Their only true family is the tribe.

Could anything be less commensurate and more totalitarian? Of course not—unless it be the perfectly incommensurate suspicion that “Paragons of War” is nothing but Ministry of War propaganda.

Might I be allowed to suggest that hobgoblins live in acknowledgment of the following precepts: That the emotions aroused by monogamy and marriage may be conducive, not injurious, to fighting for your tribe and so may parental and filial bonds; that men and women will fight beside one another for the sake of their children rather than for a chance to further abuse them; that suppressing natural emotions except during combat training will not, after all, lead to heightened combat discipline; that a life metaphor based upon defending themselves does not explain their success in attack; that a hobgoblin nation capable of kicking our butts for a decade has more to commend it than masochism, sadism, mutilation, and perversion; and that academics—right now and yet again—are failing to expose these pseudo-academic absurdities, because they receive funds from a government that publishes royal decrees in service to a kingdom preternaturally determined to wage yet another war.

When might we hope that enough will be enough?

Reviewer: Daesnar Braden, Professor of Philosophical Enquiry, University of the Duchy of the Palatinate, Leukish, Duchy of Urnst.

§

SCENARIO THREE—VOLL AND THE VALE OF LUNA

§

Chapter 11: The Crook of Rao and the salvation of Voll

~The shepherds' challenge

I have mentioned that only two copies of my manuscript exist—yours (dear readers) and mine. Why do you suppose that is?

Really—I'm asking.

It was part of the contract I signed on my commission. And while knowing the manuscript will not be published gives me a liberty I will envy subsequently, it all seems a bit mysterious, don't you think? Not a mundane mystery you want to figure out, but one you don't look into unless you're tired of living. Which I'm not, especially.

But life is finite and so is its value. All things are worth considering, and it is only human to hope that venturing a mystery will bring a reward: wealth, acclaim, gaiety. An assassin's sudden dispatch.

Readers, behold! the mysterious Crook of Rao, boasting an impressive array of features. It is historical although eternal, sacred although profane, celebrated although secret, peaceful unless belligerent, and an artifact of Rao, the god of Reason, Peace, and Serenity.

He seems nice, right?

Except, no. Not for years have I believed it. If only Countess Osgold did not always burn in my mind! Her hair, which was long and wild when Piecus lighted it, was the first thing set aflame. The priests dripped paraffin on her head, neck, and shoulders to kindle her brains. I watched as her face slackened, fluxions of skin exposing the boiling blood beneath. Her eyes, unpurposed, swayed in pools of former flesh before falling from their sockets into the soot that stopped her mouth.

My neighbor spat on me when I wept. Am I supposed to forgive it? The countess had epitomized eloquence and science, now reduced to a soily mound, a grease, a pudding pitted with blackened bone. Her lipless teeth showed gumless in the ashes. And now, as whenever this vision intrudes on me, my tears well up, blotting the page I write on. (Nevermind, readers, I will send you a fair copy.) Countess! Of course the rascals burned you headfirst; they despised what would depose their deluded creeds.

No use crying, spilt milk, horses fled the coop. Doh!—I meant barn. I thought it right to bear her witness. Those around me bayed and cheered. I cannot stop hating them for it! I did not think the sight would be so indelibly tattooed on me. Pierce the skin, and the blood runs through.

Countess! Insanity's sweet victim. In my mind, your sufferings do not cease. If mine end, do yours? A bargain, if it's the going rate.

At any rate, my ready students, be advised: what you read now contains enmity. My argument is sound (as you may judge), but priests of Rao stood with Pio Nono when he set reason aflame. Clerics of reason martyring its embodiment! A sin for which their god will damn them.

But first, I get my turn.

You may prefer that my argument were not vengeful. Fine. I ought to put spite aside. But my enmity has a purpose—to convince you, my heroic few, that pious good shepherds are lost in deceit no less than we. You may point to one that is humbly serving. So what? The bulk of them fleece the herd, and over time, their influence grows. They beat their shears into swords, their swords into scythes, their scythes into crooks. War is their justice; casuistry is their reason; kings sanction their sermons and errors.

Am I wrong? Let's put me to the test.

So that the good pastors may prove my sin and their righteousness, let them choose a champion against me. You will agree that this is more than fair. The finest of shepherds, robed in glory, versus me, the befuddled Bifurcati, scribbling on a page blotted by unmanly lamentation. Wouldn't I do just as well to jump directly into the pit of constant cudgeling that St Cuthbert the Zealot, the most eager of divinities, is preparing for me?

So be it.

Their choice is obvious. There can be only one Shepherd's Champion: The Canon of Veluna, king of Your Graces, versus Bifurcati, a professor of tears.

The conclusion is foregone, surely. Yet I issue the challenge—with relish.

§

~The legendary Crook of Rao

May I introduce my opponent? No one on oerth is more revered than Hazen, Canon of Veluna, His Venerable Reverence and Shepherd of the Faithful, pastor of Rao's flock and of much of the Flanaess, which holds Hazen to be a light to the world. Five million people at this moment will swear they know grace because they know Hazen, monarch of Veluna, ruler of Reason, rector of Peace, and soul of Serenity.

What a pity he does not resemble the hyperbole. This turbulent priest has led us into so much delusion, war, and fear that I doubt his salvation. He lost his faith six centuries ago and has not thought to recover it. He is apostate; we will get to that.

A simple shepherd carries a crook; a magnificent one, the Crook of Rao. Simplicity befits the simple; magnificence will be entrusted to the magnificent. Except, Hazen was not entrusted.

He bought the damn thing from the evil undead. It is widely known. Before Hazen worked the heroic Flight of Fiends by its power, the crook had belonged to Drax the Invulnerable, the undead Lord Protector of Rel Astra, who had commissioned a fiend-sage to experiment on the artifact before selling it to the canon.

Could that be significant?

The crook had a checkered past from long before Drax offered it to Hazen on terms an appraiser would find suspicious. It had belonged to the Flan people of the Vale of Luna from a time before history, which means that a preliterate migratory tribe remembered having a crook they lost long ago and that turned up again when Veluna and the Church of Rao most needed it. Or something like that, as legends may hap.

I may add—because helpful facts should be noted at first—that "Veluna" is a cognate of the "Vale of Luna," and the nation of Veluna was formerly known as Voll. Two hundred and fifty years before Veluna was so called, it began in the Vale of Luna as the nation of Voll. So, if you, my young scouts, grasp in your minds that Luna, her vale, Voll, and Veluna are related but not identical; that they succeeded one another rather than coexisted; and that they meant different things at different times; very well, then, we are prepared to adventure.

Luna's vale opens to our eyes as it once did to the Vollar, a migrant tribe of Oeridian barbarians fleeing the Twin Cataclysms in search of the destiny they were foretold by their shamans—and by me, too, in the previous scenario.

§

~Reason and Serenity in the Vale of Luna

Five centuries before the start (called the first day of Needfest, 1cy) of the Common Years dating system, a tribe of Oeridian refugees from the western wars passed through the Fals Gap and settled in the Vale of Luna, where they lived peacefully among the native Flan. The two folk integrated over the centuries until "the culture of the valley was as one."

One, but not equal. The new people called themselves the Voll, a cognate of the Oeridian Vollar, while the name of the Flan folk was forgotten. Denominally and predominantly, the culture of the Voll was Oeridian, not Flan.

About the Flan little is known, although they did contribute to Voll's religion. According to Raoan scripture—written in Oeridian—the natives had been worshipping Rao, the Lord of Peace, when the Vollar arrived in Luna's vale. This requires two comments.

One, the Flan folk were preliterate when the first book of Raoan scripture, Word of Incarum, was written. Incarum was complete before the Flan had learned to read and write, and therefore its depiction of the Flan is suspect. I do not mean that Voll religion overwrote the Raoan faith while retaining the god's name. But literary criticism maintains as a rule that scripture is written in the interest of its writers, which are often markedly different from its audience. In the Vale of Luna, the writers were Oeridian clerics; the audience was the ordinary folk of Voll, Oeridian and Flan.

Two, Incarum interprets the Flan Lord of Peace as the god of Reason, Peace, and Serenity. The Church of Rao does not dispute this, although the interpretation was freer than is implied by the retention of the Flan honorific. Reason was not a specified attribute of the ancient Lord of Peace, and a personification of reason would have been challenging to a preliterate people. The Flan would learn rationality in the same way they learned literacy, from their Oeridian friends. Moreover, a second divine attribute, serenity, was joined to reason and was said to follow from it. For the Voll, Raoan faith began with reason and ended in serenity. Peace became conducive. "Reason is the greatest gift. It leads to discourse, which leads to peace, which leads to serenity." The Flan had not thought of that.

§

~The Crook of Rao and Mitrik

Five hundred years after the Vollar encountered the Flan in Luna's vale,

Oeridian divination magic was mixed with Flan legend to locate the legendary Crook of Rao. The place of discovery was called Mitrik, or 'salvation,' and a new nation was formed on the spot.

The source of this excerpt—we may call it ◒Voll◓—fits "legend" and "legendary" into only five words, enveloping "to locate the," so that . . .

Professor? Aren't they fitted into only three words? I mean, if you unify the infinitive and omit the article?

Why, yes, young lady, they are! How amazing you are, and correct. Very well, the source fits legend and legendary into three words so that we perfectly understand: the legends authenticate the crook, and the crook, the legends. Should we believe it?

Divination magic—despite a widespread fear and reverence of it—is debatable. We wonder at diviners and often ask them Is you is, or is you ain't, a secret cabal in pursuit of a dubious agenda? We ask because we know they are. We commonly ignore them and, apart from the perfect Cassandra, doomed princess of Troy, with good reason. They are commonly wrong. And so, I ask you, my unlearned scholars, has the aforementioned sister of Hector ever prophesied in the Flanaess?

No?

Then let us hear no more of diviners and turn our attention to the legends. They're pretty cool, right?

Legends are stories about unforgettable although not necessarily true things; their informational value is limited. Written legends commonly begin as oral ones, and oral legends, when they are written down, are selected from many that aren't. The science of literary historical criticism attempts to make sense of this process and its outcomes but doesn't have much luck.

In our case, oral Flan legend was mixed with Oeridian divination magic to find a lost artifact used in assimilating the Flan Lord of Peace to the Oeridian god of Reason, Peace, and Serenity. Coincidentally and coextensively—same time, same place—a predominantly Oeridian nation (Voll) was assimilating an anonymous Flan tribe (unknown) in the Vale of Luna. So, I ask you, my highly select yet lowly educated literacists, what do you think? Might anyone in the Vale of Luna be suspected of having a vested interest in the interpretation of an Oeridian divination of Flan legend? Might clerics of Rao be among the suspected?

Yes?

To me, this is very disconcerting. It saddens me when historical science pertains to eternal faith, and I fear that I—a man of constant sorrow—may unduly influence my young accreditors. But,

Believe me, if all the endearing young minds,
Which I gaze on so fondly today,
Were to change by tomorrow, their credence resigned
And their innocence faded away

I would not think less of you for it. Which is to say (in the parlance of our times) that historiography is a cynical science that puts an end to youth and faith. But as I always say, with wisdom comes experience, and since I have been instructing you for a while now, you are probably only a little amazed at how things are turning out.

I conclude that the nation of Voll and its established religion are not only coupled but are the same thing, wedded from the beginning by the Crook of Rao. To this day, the happy fortuity of marrying religion to nationalism via a crooked device▽That is, a sacred artifact. (Eds) is lauded across the Flanaess. The blessed union of Veluna—nation and church—is owed to its Oeridian founders: the diviners, scriptural scholars, and wedding planners of Rao.

§

~The Soteriological Controversy

The Canon of Veluna is my subject, and you, my incredulitibles, may want to know whether he played a part in divining the Crook of Rao, proclaiming the nation of Voll, and establishing the Raoan church. Regrettably, ◒Voll◓—our historical source—is rather dull about this. It says nothing at all.

In my possession, however, I have a private account from a dwarf (she wishes to remain anonymous) that happened to be there. Her antiquity testifies to its plausibility, and her sex forbids impugning her honesty; she is credibility itself. Although, I find her wording and syntax a little slack, and regrettably, she confounds the man she describes both at once as the "canon" and "high canon" of Mitrik: progenitor of all the Canons of Veluna. thus, she introduces rather than resolves doubts I have over how the Canonry per se came to be.

She begins in medias res, and straightaway, arrives at what is known today as the soteriological heresy and controversy. At the time, of course—in 9cy—no one said there were heretics involved, and so, as encouragement to your improvement in the historian's cynical arts, I allow you, my apprentices in such inquisition, to guess which party to the soteriological controversy hid future heretics in its closet. Don't be dismayed; it may be easier than you think.

I am a student of heresy in a small way and have footnoted something concerning what my fair dwarven friend has said. You should also be told, as a hint of context, that following its divination the Crook of Rao was discovered in a pasture two hundred yards east of the Fals River at the site today of the city of Mitrik. In that pasture the leaders of Voll and a throng of its common people gathered to celebrate the birth of their nation.

After they had proclaimed the spot where they stood "Mitrik" (an Oeridian word meaning "salvation")—engendering a sectarian debate on "whether they had saved the spot or the spot had saved them"▽This celebrated controversy came to a head centuries later, in 241-249cy, when Voll was becoming Veluna. Supporters of the canon's increasing authority maintained that he had saved the spot but spoke against the belief when accused of it. Their opponents believed that the spot had saved the canon, were likewise accused, and argued against it. In Raoan theology ever since, soteriologists subscribing to canonical salvation are known as spotists, while adherents of spotific salvation are known as canonists. This led to the popular doggerel of the day:
"The Canonists say that the canon is /
A spot on anti-Canonist. /
The Spotists gainsay /
Surely, 'tis nay; /
the canon's a sure-fire-v-Spotist"
which you may even today see scribbled on the bathroom wall at the sign of The Cask and Scholar in Veluna City in a faint, third-century scrip. (AB) —the outstanding men of Voll declared a new high canon in residence at Mitrik according to the dignity of the spot and those men. Having established an office superior to themselves, like dukes creating a kingdom and then looking for a king, they found the right man nearby, a rich shepherd named Old Pietro. As he had been behind in leading before, they offered to let him lead them a mitre further. Visibly, he is humbled by the honor. Mildly, he accepts his ceremonial garb—conveniently fetched from behind the altar—of robes, surplices, stoles, cincture, mitre, rings, medallions, the Heart of Rao, and the socks and slippers he was wearing because changing socks in public is humiliating. With humble ostentation he is handed the implement discovered for the occasion, the Crook of Rao, whose stumpy wooden staff had been fitted with an extensive crook of white gold, which Old Pietro raised to nearly the tip of the pointy hat on his head. Thus invested, installed, and crooked, the first canon of Mitrik performed his first act of grace, ordaining a holy nation to popular rejoicing.

My dwarf's account presents a conundrum. Raoan episcopal ecclesiology dictates that bishops appoint canons to their cathedral staff; the Canon of Veluna is the only exception, a canon anointed, not appointed, to office by the bishops. A "high canon," too, is ordinarily not at the head of bishops but of a chapter of lower-order canons and is appointed to the office.

We may ask, therefore, whether our dwarven friend's analogy of canon to king is true. Were the "outstanding men" of Voll analogous to dukes crowning a king, or to bishops appointing cathedral staff? I have asked her, but my dwarf's memory is not that far certain. The problem of understanding the high canon of Mitrik's real authority confronts us here.

The high canon of Mitrik is the Canon of Veluna's forefather; understanding his place in relation to the "outstanding men" of Voll is a notable problem: Had the High Canon of Mitrik in 9cy been anointed or appointed to an superior or inferior office? When he wielded the Crook of Rao, was he also the leader of Voll? Or something more like a prophet, speaking on behalf of the leaders and people of Voll?

I told you, young heroes, how much it saddens me when historical doubts are pertinent to matters of faith. Imagine my sorrow at finding, so early in my combat over grievances with the shepherd of Veluna, that his holiest armor against me—his divine rulership— may appear to be flawed at its forging. Perhaps it required reforging in the furnaces of subsequent history. We will see.

Turning the plain wooden rod into a golden, longer, and crooked one is an interesting detail. Gold crooks, of course, are meaningless except where shepherds are important in a society. Did the Flan of the ancient Vale of Luna have shepherds like that? I cannot be sure, but I call bullshit. At Mitrik, the shepherds getting their staff extended were only religious ones. Real shepherds don't need an extension like that. And if Rao had had church shepherds in mind, he could have bent the shaft himself.

§

Chapter 12: The High Canon of Rao is not the Canon of Veluna

 

For five and a half centuries after founding Voll, the Crook of Rao did nothing but symbolize the young nation and its established church. Nonetheless, the Voll people since nearly their beginning in the Vale of Luna had been led in part by prominent Raoan clerics. The origninally seven Raoan bishops, for example, had been religious, social, and political leaders for centuries prior to Voll's existence as a nation, when Rao's worshippers had been citizens of seven semiautonomous regions (variously called duchies, counties, and baronies) ruled by seven noble families.▽An eighth region, the Citizenry (and the Archdiocese) of Veluna City, would be established at the Extraordinary Episcopal Council, in the Eademer Battistero, in Mitrik, in 446cy. (Eds)

In those days, a bishop's authority was restricted to the domain of a noble lord. The appointment of a high canon in 9cy, commemorating Voll's national foundation and "salvation," was the conclusion a long and piecemal process by which the seven dioceses were gathered into a cross-regional church that was collectively ("collegially") headed by its bishops. The seven noble houses likewise were gradually formed into a national federation. Throughout its existece as a nation, from 9-254cy, no monarch whether political or religious ruled Voll. Political rule was by noble peerage; religious rule was by episcopal fellowship.

Although, we have only my dwarf's word for parts of this. Apart from her testimony, there is no direct evidence for an installed high canon prior to the events of 109cy (which we will soon consider). And even if there were, there would be no reason to identify the High Canon of Mitrik with a monarchical ruler such as the later Canon of Veluna. When official titles change, it generally brings a corresponding change of status, authority, and responsibility.The titular difference between the High Canon of Rao (or of Mitrik, or of Voll) and the Canon of Veluna is especially important in this respect.

Had there ever been a theocratic monarch in the Vale of Luna prior to the middle of the third century, when Voll became the Archclericy of Veluna? An affirmative reply is ordinary to most historians but not to me. On whose authority, I ask, will we elide the obvious re-denomination and equate Voll's High Canon of Rao to the later Canon of Veluna? On the authority of the canon's later church? Which has, indeed, a lot of evidence, all of it suspected (we will examine an instance) of being postdated, predated, interpolated, and fabricated?

Although we know too little about it, Voll was "already a burgeoning culture" by the end of the first century, and historians stand to learn something of it by not regarding Voll at that time as merely Veluna by another name. The "leading men" at Voll's founding ceremony are still unidentified by historians, and to characterize the high canon as their leader is an unwarranted license. The people of Voll may not have lived in a theocracy but under the rule of local nobility. To be convinced either way, we must lift the Velunar lid from the Vollar cauldron to see what brewed within.

§

~The Overking of Ahlissa and the peace of Rao

In 109cy, the nation of Voll, one hundred years removed from its founding, was confronted by the Viceroyalty of Furyondy, a political and military superpower recently delegated to the central Flanaess by the overking of the imperial Great Kingdom of Ahlissa, far to the east. Faced by this crisis, the high canon of Rao was decisive in averting a military conquest of his nation and negotiating a favorable vassalage to the overking. One hundred forty-five years later, the vassal would prove crucial to the viceroy's successful rebellion against the Great Kingdom, when Voll would forswear vassalage and also became an independent state. The relation of the sovereign Kingdom of Furyondy to the sovereign Archclericy of Veluna has been the foremost foreign policy concern of both nations from that time.

The Archclericy of Veluna is imponderable without knowledge of Voll's earlier homage to the overking. What we know of the vassal state opens a window for historians to look out onto the culture of Voll. There would be little to say aside from it, and to identify the High Canon of Rao with the Canon of Veluna blinds that window rather thoroughly. The High Canon of Rao was not the Canon of Veluna, and the rulers of Voll, I will maintain, were not theocratic but secular.

Your task, my wide-open eyes on the lookout, is to observe and maintain such distinctions. I will welcome to the task, at the appropriate time, the contribution of an old friend that has much to say on the subject, all of it unsolicited.

We begin with the Great Kingdom of Ahlissa. ◒Voll◓—our historical source—tells us that "When the Great Kingdom's soldiers surged from Furyondy in a drive to spread the empire further west, they came upon the people of Veluna, already a burgeoning culture." That was in 109cy , and you, my sprouts out of the soil of historical study, must understand that the thought of soldiers at the border spooks me even more than the truly monstrous horrors I have encountered over the years in my pursuit of sholarship.

It's true, I tell you. Although I am a coward, I have survived enough horrors to surfeit a fiend hunter. My professional predilection is to retrieve and archive lost artifacts of the anient Flanaess (it pays my salary at the museum),▽As noted under the monograph's opening subhead. (Eds) and when I do, denizens of darkness are often lurking nearby. I never offer to slay them (do you think I'm crazy?), and after several famously dialectical encounters were ended to our mutual satisfaction, the denizens and I began to jointly refine the proceedings. I have talked my way out of a torturous death so many times that, by now, I am celebrated among the evils that haunt ruins. Most horrors I meet are so transported by adulation that I must talk them down for their own safety. I get letters occasionally offering an artifact if I would go to a layer of the abyss and fetch it, which is a tricky call. If I go, it's likely to be a heinous trap. If not, I've disappointed a fan.

I'm OK with horrors. But I don't like armies; they're unreasonable and usually mean business. Cajoling soldiers is pointless because they exercise no autonomy. They're doers, not thinkers. When the army of the Great Kingdom appeared on Voll's border, I imagine it was terrible to see: bigger than belief, arrogant about its chances, and filled with savage platoons recruited from distant places in tribute to the overking and his haughty Court of Essences.

Therefore, I find it quite astounding that according to ◒Voll◓:

The High Canon of Rao met with representatives of the Great Kingdom and explained to them the goals of his peaceful land. Mindful of the vast host looming on his borders, the canon wisely agreed to support the empire. So it was that the Archclericy of Voll entered vassalage to the Viceroyalty of Furyondy under a banner of peace and great religious expectations.

That was brave of him. Very assured; very commanding; unremarkably intelligent. But wise? Oh, please.

Students, you see already that ◒Voll◓ is an unreliable narrative. Wise? I didn't know that standards of sagacity could dip like that. Your strategy, High Canon, as I understand it, was to greet the overking's representative and say, "Yo, bro'! Peace out. I just scored some dank weed." That could work. Wisdom is oftentimes obvious. And what choice did you have, "Put 'em up"? But really, my illicitly High Canon—let's be frank—was explaining your peaceful land even true? You expounded it, yes—but was it true?

Were the goals of your land so peaceful that they could passively disarm the Great Kingdom's army? How peaceful was that? I admit that, among the historical folk I know about, the people of Voll are among my favorites. But gods show mercy! they were human beings, not angels. Angels, mind you, may be so peaceful that it is actually imposing, but are there any humans like that? Was your wisdom actually real, or is it legendary by now, like Arthur at Camelot? I beg you, Almighty High Expositor of Peaceful Intents, be as precise as you can: What was it about your nation's goals that made them beter than anyone else's? I mean, was your neighbor the Viscount of Verbobonc so bad? What was there about you? In all honesty, High C-, the wisest thing you could have done in your situation was to lie about Voll values. I mean, right?

The Great Kingdom of Ahlissa did not aspire to peace! It aspired to the possession of Voll. And Voll "wisely agreed" to vassalage, not to expounding lofty goals. If the viceroy of Furyondy had wanted a shepherd to guide him to green pastures, why did he send an army to say hello? Couldn't he have been more neighborly?

◒Voll◓ says that vassalage to the overking was accepted "under a banner of peace and great religious expectations." May I ask, whose? In Voll, peace was sacred to Rao. In Rauxes, peace was obedience to the overking. Rauxes bestowed peace on a business model, in exchange for monetary gain and military service. None dared beseech the Great Kingdom's spiritual improvement, and none besides the Great Kingdom was threatening the peace of Voll. Honestly, vassalage was a protection racket—you enjoy peace while you pay me homage for it. Negotiations for vassalage were on the overking's terms; you may rely on it.

The notion that Voll's vassalage was a religious expectation begs an explanation. I submit, that when the High Canon of Rao explained the goals of his peaceful land to the Viceroy of Furyondy, they perfectly understood one another; vassalage was a security guarantee to be accepted on persuasively renewable terms.

§

~Great expectations

What were the high canon's negotiating points? According to ◒Voll◓,

The canon saw in the easterlings a passion for progress and innovation that could be tempered by conversion to the holy tenets of Rao.

The canon was in a tight spot, but he had temperance in his pocket and he knew it. He understood the Malachite Throne's perpetual dilemma, the overking's soft underbelly. The easterlings were passionate about progress, but not everyone equally looked forward to it. Plenty of people wanted more or less progress than they got, and the disgruntlement was general, maybe universal. Who, asked the canon, could placate these grievances if not Rao, Lord of Peace? Who could persuade the people to be reasonable if not Rao, god of Reason? If Rao's church could sanctify progress as a service to the overking and in exchange for the freedom of Voll, that would be vassalge worthy of a liege's indulgence. The overking would hear when the high canon proffered that.

There was subtlety to it. The banner of peace meant a protection racket, but the religious expectations were sophisticated. "Tempering progress and innovation" meant winning the hearts and minds of subjugated people, two or three million of them in the Viceroyalty of Furyondy, each one disgruntled because imperial innovation was so plainly less progressive than inevitable. But progress may always be represented as an opportunity, and rationalizing progress' inevitable benefits to millions of subjugated people was a service to the empire that the Raoan church could well provide for a price. As the High Canon said to the viceroy of Furyondy at the time, "If Voll did not exist, the Great Kingdom would have to invent it." And so, a religious apology for progress and innovation became the charter for Voll's vassalage to the overking of Ahlissa. A nation's homage and the imperial church's one foundation were settled by the high canon of Rao.

Over the next one hundred and fifty years, the political and economic benefits of vassalage reaped by Voll and the Church of Rao may hardly be exaggerated. Raoan clerics were appointed to the viceregal court in Dyvers (the capital, the City of Sails, at the mouth of the Velverdyva River) to positions of increasing significance. Roads and ferries connecting Voll to elsewhere in the Great Kingdom were built and improved. The Viscounty of Verbobonc —an independent and wealthy incorporated into the empire—was granted to Voll to rule as a vassal, and Voll's mercantile economy grew as rapidly as Furyondy could help it.

Excelling that, the Raoan churches obtained something truly extraordinary: the power to exculpate the sins of an empire. Progress, innovation, and the holy tenets of Rao became an unrenunciable trinity for instilling reason and exacting peace across the Ahlissan territories. Raoan churches were built throughout the viceroyalty and beyond, largely at imperial expense and attended by all the right people. The church's prestige extended to nonbelievers in the viceregal court and even in the Ahlissan Court of Essences, because when a religion is grafted onto a society the rulers, too, must exhibit themselves adherent.

But this marvelous windfall did not drop freely or effortlessly. All the citizens of Voll, not just the high canon, integrated into the Great Kingdom and its great expectations. Were they all as willing as he? Was everyone happy when the high canon pledged Rao in support of the overking and the viceroy of Furyondy?

§

Chapter 13: The secular rulers of Voll

I confide to you, my scantily allotted readers, that in most ways historians are unlike the gods. For one thing, we are very many (and obliged to our students for it) while they are only seventy-one (counting the acknowledged ones) and obliged to no one. It has been said that prudent mortals sacrifice to the unknown gods, whose obeisance is forgotten until one of them plucks—with long, jealous, immaterial fingers—a soul from life's unhappy tree. Perhaps, my students, you—fate’s chosen novitiates into the mysterious ways of the deities—believe it would be better if you could trust the gods. But that’s life! Although, because the gods are unable to tell whether they are being flattered, I will say this much about them out loud: they are the kings and queens of caprice. Regarding their limitlessness, however, I may only whisper this in writing: the divine host is officially seventy-one and therefore not omniscient on the bare assumption that they keep secrets from one another. (Yes, my innocents—they do.)

Historians are a little like that. We have secrets too. We don't always tell everyone whatever we know, and sometimes, we don’t tell them anything at all! So, you may see the wisdom of my immaterial (as I believe it was) commissioner when it specified legally that my manuscript is never to be published. thus, I am thus enabled to do as contracted: speak freely to you. I may as well then admit to you, my enumerable angels dancing on a pinhead, what you will discover soon enough for yourselves, that I, Annalo Bifurcati, am a private person no less than a coward. I cling to the harboring embrace of anonymity like a suckling to the teat. And I fully intend to remain in the arms of my unnaming, unfailing, obscurant lover—so inconspicuous, so fair! She has favored me so far. Why not stick by her? Why not follow her to the ends of the oerth?

Since I write this with anonymity’s blessing, I will defend outright the statement implied by the head of this chapter. I take my defense from preparations I made for a lecture I gave to an undergraduate class at Olde Maurian College on 5th Flocktime, 590cy . The lecture scathed me like a tub of hot water, as you will see, but recompenses me now. It went like this:

It is never acknowledged but true nonetheless that Voll had secular, not theocratic, rulers until the establishment of the Archclericy of Veluna, in 254cy. Near the turn of the second century, the Great Kingdom of Ahlissa subdivided into four viceroyalties, the last of which was the Viceroyalty of Furyondy. But government by feudal vassalage was unique to Furyondy, instituted because attempts to employ religious authority had resulted in unstable government elsewhere, in Medegia, Almor, and The Pale, for example. Vassalage in Furyondy was intended to preclude theocratic government there, and it is only in ignorance of this that historians have mistaken the secular nature of Voll’s homage to the overking in Rauxes. The evidence that Voll’s homage was paid by the High Canon of Rao turns out on examination to be spurious, and because vassalge was intended by Rauxes to preclude theocracy, we ought to presume, if the evidence allows, that Voll’s homage was due from a secular ruler. The idea that a religious figure pledged allegiance ought to be considered incredible without considerable evidence of it, and the least credible claim would be that the overking established a religion in his viceroyalty on the homage of a theocratic leader of a theocratic nation. Kings and emperors are not so whimsical in their commands and decrees.

My reasoning is sound but, as I said, nowhere acknowledged. It would be nice to believe (as you, my ingenuous young friends, undoubtedly did and may still) that this is because other historians have not yet thought of it. But historians keep secrets, as I said, and I tell you, my confidants in anonymity's assurances, that in my possession I have an explicit rejection of the idea of secular rule in Voll. It was conveyed to me by a private letter from my friend and nemesis Roger Moore, the author of the history “The Great Northern Crusade” I reported on earlier.▽See Chapter 3: The nature and origin of monstrosity. (Eds) The letter was received four months ago and runs like this:

Birfucati you bastard –

I have it from an actual scholar that you are at it again. In the name of divine reason—which you never hear—you must desist from this perversity! Will the college whose sewers you suck never scrub its drains of your scum? By the weary gods, man, spare your sudents! Do they ever recover from a semester spent with you? If they do, Olde Mauraian has a remarkable infirmary.

I must advise you again that the longer truth abides the more vulnerable it becomes to poisonous pens like yours. Bifurcati! People must have their ancient truths. Every qualified academic is bound to stop your raving by any means at hand.

I think you will acknowledge the authority of the following text: "On behalf of the people of Veluna, the High Canon of Rao met with representatives of the Overking and wisely agreed to support the Malachite Throne, seeing that it could be tempered by conversion to the holy tenets of Rao. So it was that the Archclericy of Voll entered vassalage to the Viceroyalty of Furyondy."

Sweet heavens! Bifurcati, even you can see that Voll and Veluna are interchangeable in this passage. Veluna is said to have existed prior to vassalage and so is Voll. The High Canon of Rao is the monarchical leader of Voll, having authority to explain things and, magisterially, agree and enter into vassalage. The Archclericy of Voll existed back then and could have been called the Archclericy of Veluna just as well. And Bifurcati—prithee, be not a churl—allow that the head of an archclericy leads the sacred church and the secular state alike. Thus, the High Canon of Rao is head of the Church of Rao and the nation of Voll (also called Veluna) too. In short, the only difference between the first century system and the one of today is that the Canon of Veluna was, back then, sometimes styled the High Canon of Rao. My good fellow, all this is not only obvious, it is orthodoxy! You must submit!

—Moore

PS. Old friend, I am calmer now and regret resorting to profanity. I do not worry, because I know you will see reason. I have labored in patience but not in vain.—Moore.

Actually, his labors are in vain like witches scrying mirrors for Sleeping Beauty. Isn’t that pretty? Moore is witches, and I am Sleeping Beauty! I like it. And if you, my awaited first-kissers, ever think you want to know whether I keep secrets from you, remember how this turned out. I haven't endured such language since my hobgoblin friends were in good humor (may Merikka restore their company to me one day).

I showed you Moore’s letter so that you may see: scholarly consensus is not always consensual. Often it results from a determination to force divergent views underground. The “actual scholar” Moore mentioned was an Olde Maurian student that attended my lecture after being schooled outside class in the art of monitoring his mentor. Treacherous knave.

§

~Refutation of an addendum

Let me refute Moore with the whittled brevity of a professed colleague. Screwed to his tightest, Moore will insist that the Archclericy of Veluna existed before the Viceroyalty of Furyondy. He notes that the Archclericy "of Voll" swore fealty to the overking, proving the theocracy’s existence and authority. But Moore overlooks many things.

I have already noted the overking’s intention to have secular vassals serve him in Furyondy. The imperial policy meant subordinating religious authorities in vassal states to the secular system, and the first vassal to pledge was the one in Voll. The High Canon of Rao's authority was religious and unacceptable on that ground. Would the overking have set aside his purpose at the first attempt to implement it?

Before we consider the question, let us first ask, "Why would he?" Rejecting the possibility was not only consistent with the emperor's purpose, it was his purpose. The claim that the overking set aside his policy in admiration of the peaceful tenets of Rao is unconvincing. And would the high canon, either, have been willing to pledge his god to the service of a foreign empire, a service that extended to preaching the gospel of inevitable progress in Voll and misrepresenting the Raoan faith to millions more people? I would hope that a leader of the Church of Rao would say, no. Yet Moore has asked me to acknowledge, upon the authority of an old manuscript (◒Voll◓) that had originated in the canonical library in Mitrik as a copy of a lost autograph written much earlier, that on the High Canon’s authority “the Archclericy of Voll entered vassalage to the Viceroyalty of Furyondy.”

Why would I do it? Moore had been informed by his spy that I found ◒Voll◓ unreliable, and then without addressing my concern, demanded I acknowledge it anyway. And on this point specifically, in its consideration of the Archclericy of Voll, ◒Voll◓’s narrative becomes markedly more rhetorical and less informative than on perhaps any other. It notes, for example, that the High Canon “supported” the idea of Voll’s vassalage, but what was at stake was not being supportive but pledging homage. Similarly, ◒Voll◓ does not state that the overking and the viceroy were considering conversion to the tenets of Rao but that the High Canon was considering it on their behalf. In fact, ◒Voll◓ looks more like the expression of not the overking’s views but the views of unspecified Raoan clerics.

The passage cited by Moore is the only evidence historians have of an archclericy in Voll prior to 254cy, and it is unacceptable. In fact, if the High Canon of Rao were presumed to be not a theocratic monarch but a representative of Voll's noble houses to negotiations with representatives of the overking—which is more natural to the text—then ◒Voll◓ contains no evidence of a theocracy other than the concluding remark that “the Archclericy of” Voll entered vassalage. Omit those words, and ◒Voll◓ relates in clear prose how a secular nation negotiated terms of vassalage to its benefit by emphasizing the potential service of Raoan doctrine to the Great Kingdom. The High Canon of Rao was pivotal to the negotiation, but that proves him a partisan, a politician, and a theologian, not a theocratic monarch nor, necessarily, a spiritual man.

It is, therefore, on the authority of a singular three-word phrase— “the Archclericy of”—that the Archclericy of Voll is said to exist. Moreover, the phrase is a change of subject, which would otherwise be the nation, not the archclericy, of Voll. Once isolated and exposed, these three words assert an apparent anachronism dating the archclericy to the wrong historical epoch. They are, in all likelihood, an interpolation added to ◒Voll◓ one hundred years after the lost original autograph and at about the same time that the Archclericy of Veluna was being established.

On the strength of the interpolation, two subsequent and consequential claims have been affirmed by historians: that the Archclericy of Voll became the Archclericy of Veluna, and that the High Canon of Rao became the Canon of Veluna. Both gloss genuine doubts about how the archclericy and the canon became what they are.

If the High Canon of Rao was not the Canon of Veluna, and if there once had been a secular ruler of Voll, then it cannot have been the good shepherd's leadership that brought Veluna out of Voll. What, then, may have done it? This is a consequential doubt, and all that Hazen, Canon of Veluna, Shepherd of the Faithful, and chosen avatar for good shepherds everywhere must do to resolve it is open his archives and permit the inspection of a manuscript possibly interpolated, allowing an exmination of what it has to say.

I have made these points to Moore in private, which may account for his tetchy salutation. At any rate, an historian's secret is now out for your consideration, my alarmed readers.

§

Chapter 14: The Vale of Luna

 

The library in my rooms at Olde Maurian has a classification system that has occasionally been impugned as haphazard. On the contrary, it is organized on an intelligible principle; the older items are at the bottom of each pile and things ascend from there in the order they were received. Could that be by chance? Any child will tell you, no, and what's more, I recall passably well which piles were raised first and when I acquired the documents that lie in the top foot or so. Everything is mostly retrievable, and what's more, my PISS (Physical Information Storage System) is an inducement to keeping current on publications that may supercede buried ones, which is a virtue in a scholar.

Like pressed flowers, the piles will preserve their contents more or less eternally. As a case in point, take this little postcard, printed in Greyhawk in 564cy. It isn't really a postcard but is printed to look like one in a cursive font that links its letters in a semblance of handwriting. It was published by GoThereGuides.com, whose name is stretched all along the bottom as—for some reason— onelongword. Styled after the prose of an endearing, popular, and obsessed thirteen years old girl on tour in a foreign land and worried that her friends at home think absence makes her boring, the card gushes over totally tight boys and literally lesser attractions in “Ye Olde Vale of Luna.” The postcard declares that the tour takes in all the major attractions, although the printed itinerary actually sticks closely to the Great Western Road and the Velverdyva River, where the hotels are grand and just as encouragingly proximate.

I am gluing the card here: 

                                                                             
⸢                                              ⸣

                                  

⸤                                              ⸥

Although, I'm noticing that the glue doesn't look too good.

And speaking of looking good, the brochure’s illustrations are true to life, as though GoThereGuides accidentally employed an artist. See, there is the Velverbridge, Concordance Stack, Yasgur’s Farm in Woodstock, the Devarnish Market, Greatblister Abbey, the Eademer Battistero, the Fals River Palaces, and soothing Temton Water. Some of them are places we have been to or will go to soon, and for the sake of the pictures I forward the guide. There are elven elders living now in Fellreev Forest that lived long ago in Ye Olde Vale, before the press of humanity sent them away. They remember the old days and might share their memories should you show them the postcard; may it guide you in dark places, when other guides mislead.

Historians are like guides, too, sort of. We show you what we want you to see, and when we take you to Veluna, we generally provide a hagiography of sorts, like the biography of a sainted land. I'll give you a few examples. The first of the Velunar hagios was written by Gygax, and it says,

"the Archclericy of Veluna has long been a shining example of the better side of humankind in the Flanaess. It has treated fairly and justly with its neighbors and championed the cause of righteousness everywhere."

A generous depiction. “Shining" and "everywhere" could have been omitted without harming reputations. A more recent hagio—written by Gary Hoolian after the Greyhawk Wars had reached the height of the central Flanaess' dependence on the wealth of Veluna to continue its foreverwar against Iuz—goes further, abandoning all restraint to attain obsequiousness:

The folks of Veluna have long represented the best aspects of humankind. Here, humans and elves live in harmony, farming arable land and working together to build a common culture, founded on peace, reason, and serenity. The influence of the Church of Rao is everywhere in Veluna, gently enforcing the administration of their doctrine through fair, firm (but not overly harsh) laws.

That is sycophancy to flatter an aged canon whose mind has been addled, it appears, by the Flight of Fiends. It is an exhibition of flattery enlisting even the elves to the service of Raoan values. Hoolian did show mettle when his topic was law enforcement, though. He began "gently" and pushed past "fair" to "firm" before settling on “not overly harsh,” pegging Veluna’s mercy back three notches in only half a sentence, a race well run to come from behind a pack of lies and finish near the truth.

The histories of Veluna and its canon are connected. Their reputations amount to a cumulative argument against me, and the argument benefits mightily from the hagiographic ghosts of canons past. The holy honorific His Venerable Reverence, Shepherd of the Faithful links to a long, clanking chain of spectral ancestors. I do not know how many Venerable Reverences precede Hazen, the procession is in none of my references, and though it exists (carved in marble) in Mitrik, I do not care to go there, because sanctity gets in my nose somehow. But Hazen’s chain drags for 582 years, and if your heart greatly desires (as some do) a long succession of His Graces (but I remind you, if you hope for a Her Grace in the list, of what little Alice said through the looking glass: One CAN'T believe impossible things), then you may as well begin in the year 9cy, on the spot of Salvation, in the nation of Voll, in Ye Olde Vale of –

§

~Celene and Luna are granted for guidance

Hang on. The Vale of Luna. That's right!

The vale is old, even without the emphatic “e.” Along side it, "Veluna" is nought but modernism and contraction. The Vale of Luna, spelled out proper, is archaic, a name so old that we do not know how old it is. We read it in what may be the most primitive writing in the Flanaess, the first chapter of Word of Incarum, the first and most sacred book in the scripture of Rao, god of Reason, Peace, and Serenity.

Incarum may be the oldest book that is original to the Flanaess. Every rival to its antiquity is written in Suel and has origins in what is now (but then wasn’t) the Sea of Dust. But Incarum is written in Oeridian, and its inception was Flan. How much of the Flan is identifiable today is a matter of scholarly debate, although the general answer will be: not much. Flan was an unwritten language, with no unbreachable defense against Oeridian reformulation.

But Incarum would have been read to the Flan, and they could have challenged its accuracy or meaning. The most primitive passage, for example, depicts the Flan natives greeting the migrant Vollar tribe and welcoming their “new brothers to the 'Vale of Luna, most sacred of all lands protected by Rao.’” The single quotes contain a transliteration in Oeridian characters of words the Voll collectively recited in Flan, so, the Flan self-identify as the people of the Vale of Luna, a sacred land protected by Rao. Raoans in Voll, from as far back as we can see, have taken this to mean that the vale was sacred to Rao. But the proper denotation is “protected by.” So, we may ask: Could the vale have been protected by Rao and sacred to Luna? Who—besides a plain moon—was Luna?

In Raoan faith, Incarum settles the issue by stating, "the Lord of Peace granted the humans of Oerth the moons Celene and Luna, that they might gain guidance from tyranny and darkness." Stated that way, Luna appears to be a plain moon, a gift from Rao and sacred for that reason. And although this is Oeridian language, not transliterated Flan, we know it reflects Flan belief, because it was being read to the Flan alongside the transliterated text. It contains a reference to the aquamarine moon, Celene, who is singularly insignificant to Raoan theology. It is remarkable, then, that in the most primitive Raoan scripture and in the Oeridian language Celene is given syntactical precedence over Luna in Luna’s own vale. Similarly, in Oeridian, Luna’s dominion is properly delimited: her vale is one of untold lands protected by Rao, although this wider provenance is, once again, otherwise unimportant in Raoan theology. Evidently, then, the primitive Raoans in the Vale of Luna knew of a separate tradition in which the moons were bestowed by Rao for guidance to the Flan in all lands under Rao's protection, not only to the people of Voll.

This creates tension within the scriptural narrative. Incarum intends the Vale of Luna to be sacred to Rao, but its most primitive words go against the intent by giving precedence to Celene and describing the vale as protected, not sacred, to Rao. When texts preserve discrepancies that beg to be overwritten, it must be because the discrepant phrasing was too firmly settled in the writers’ minds to suggest either alteration or omission: the scribes simply and uncritically wrote down what was being said and repeated. The fact that the ancient scripture contains an Oeridian transliteration of Flan words confirms this understanding. The words of Incarum literally betray tensions embedded in the Flan origins of Raoan scripture.

So, we may wonder: What had the primitive Flan been doing when, before the Vollar arrived, they honored Rao for bestowing the moons and protecting their vale while looking to Luna, not Rao, for guidance from tyranny and darkness?

§

~Luna the moon, Rao the god

Gaining guidance from a moon may be done in two ways: by charting its motions and appearances against a zodiac, giving it a rational, predictable, and mechanical aspect; or by praying to it, ascribing to the moon a personality. Luna may be a celestial object, rationally charted and observed, or a celestial person, a divinity. You may think, why not both? And you may be right, to an extent. But holding rationality and personality together is not easy. A moon rationally charted is a machine; ancient scholars drew celestial gears. Something personal is always different: animate, intentional, even spiritual. How can we determine whether the moon Luna was mechanical or personal to the Flan, a preliterate people, one thousand years ago?

Answering the question is disappointingly easy. But let me first assure you, my dear friends, that it is not untoward to personify a god, whether the Lord of Peace, Our Lady of Reason, Our Lamp in the Heavenly Darkness, or the Celestial Abacus of Our Insight. The fact that human personalities waver does not mean that divine ones do. What response would you have Lady Reasoning give to our human ineptitude besides her incomprehensibly feminine disdain? What right have we to accuse the moon of inconstancy and variability? She constantly reminds us of it, so we ought to admire the higher constancy in her, her personality, matched to ours. A human personality cannot comprehend the gods, but it is the most inclusive idea we possess, the one that omits nothing from our experience.

Luna’s guidance was personally beseeched by the Flan of the valley—one person, beseeched by many—which we know to be true, because Rao had not yet been rationalized by the Voll. The Flan Lord of Peace was not yet the Oeridian God of Reason when the Vollar arrived in the Vale of Luna. Raoan scripture agrees, saying, “Over time the Vollar settlers worshipped the primitive Flan god Rao, whom they interpreted as a power of reason and serenity.” How had Rao been worshipped before growing rational and serene? In Word of Incarum, the only identifiable reference to the primituve god is the Flan honorific “Lord of Peace.” Rao’s peaceful aspect is more primitive than rationality and serenity, and it is distinctively Flan. It identifies the Flan god and tells us something about what it meant to say that "the Lord of Peace granted the moons Celene and Luna, that humans might gain guidance from tyranny and darkness.” To the Flan of the valley, the moons had been light-bearers in service to peace when rationality was as yet unheard of.

Luna, then, was a personal moon bringing guidance, light, and peace in association with her celestial embodiment. We ought to think of her, then, as a supra- or spiritual personality. The Flan made no categorical distinctions between mortal, natural, spiritual, and divine persons. They coexisted in a spectrum reaching from valleys to mountains, forests, streams, plants, animals, humans, spirits, and divinities. Divinites could appear as creatures and vice versa.

Today, we think of the moons as natural luminaries. But it was different for the Flan, to whom the moons were supernal. Luna, whether spiritual or divine, was not a part of nature because she literally was not sublunar. She dispensed guidance, light, and peace from above, not life, death, and rebirth from below. As a heavenly being, Luna was a peer to other deities there, including Rao. We may be sure of this admitting no objection from the later, rationalized Raoan church. Whatever the primitive Flan had meant when they said that the moons were granted by Rao, they could not have been thinking of a gift or an exchange of property. Gods do not have the power to give other divinities away, and especially, not to humans.

The Raoan interpretation of the the moons as Rao's gift is entirely wrong. "The Lord of Peace granted the humans of Oerth the moons" is the best translatation of the Oeridian words, but it is wrongly interpreted to mean "gifted" or "bestowed." Gifting and bestowing are unilateral acts; there is no grant that is not an allowance or a consent. What cannot be refused is no grant.

The question is: Who consented to Luna as goddess and guide to the Flan of the Vale? But we cannot readily answer the question. We do not know the relationships that pertained to the four concerned parties, the Flan (in general), the Flan of Luna's vale (in particular), Luna, and Rao. Although three remain culturally prominent today, there is no significance to Luna (the goddess, not the orbiter) anymore apart from the inferences we may draw from Word of Incarum. Even in antiquity, worshiping Luna was probably restricted to the culture of the valley. But in that place, Luna cannot be understood as a plain moon for the reasons I have given. There is no objection without showing I am wrong.

Although we cannot be sure of the precise arrangement, we can say that the granted request was consensual. Without evidence, it is unwarranted to think that Rao, the Flan’s Lord of Peace, would have imposed Luna on the valley’s people or vice versa. More likely, a mutual request was misconstrued as a god’s unilateral gift by a faith that no longer understood Luna personally. When gifted or bestowed, Luna ceased to be a goddess and became a plain moon; her volition was constrained, her personality was denied, by mechanical principles. This is true not only according to my argument but because it is what happened. For the past thousand years, Rao has been worshipped not as the Lord of Peace but as the god of Reason, while Luna has become a plain moon and the Vale of Luna has become Veluna, a Raoan theocracy.

Word of Incarum states that Luna was granted by Rao to the people of her valley. The statement preserves older beliefs that predate the arrival of the Oeridians, the rationalization of Rao, and the depersonification of the goddess of the valley. History has saved Luna’s appearance by concealing it within Oeridian Raoan scripture, and if history is the will of the gods, her reappearance must be adored.

§

~Romeo and Juliet

Lady, by that yonder blessed moon I vow—

O, swear not by the moon, th’ inconstant moon, that monthly changes in her circled orb, lest that thy love prove likewise variable.

My constant students, it was not my intent to stray from my subject and insert these pages on a luminous moon. But to know Veluna, you must know Rao, and to know Rao, you must know Luna. And because I wanted to send you the postcard from Ye Olde Vale—did you get that, BTW?—I found myself in consultation with my library, delving into six cubic yards of my own PISS, occasionally skipping a cubic foot but regretting it and going back, until I found my treasure at last, clasped it to my heart, glued it to your autograph, examined its depictions, and had the happy thought: Why not write about Luna?

It used to be that thinking about Luna made me sad. Do deities die? Yes. No. The loveliest ones, I think not. They become faint from human neglect. Most nights, I watch Luna, still luminous in her chosen orb, chosen freely before Rao granted her request to be our light and guide in the darkness. Out of love for us, she orbits still her erstwhile adorers, who have forgotten her. Why should she continue? For one thing, she was not abandoned. Her failing worshippers succumbed to insidious friends, and she may well weep for us. Perhaps, for our sake, she stays true.

The inconstant moon? O treacherous Will! You must be joking, and despite you, I will swear by her. By Luna, I swear to remember all that I can of the passed and wonderful ideas harshly overwritten by men. Sometimes, historiographers may do more than decipher clues and return past probabilities. Occasionally, we enliven something, or revivify it. When I look at Luna now, I fancy she is not quite so sad as before. Because I love her. I think it makes a difference, even if I am the only one. I love her as the epitome of everything the world has been granted and discarded. Mostly, though, I love her as the goddess of a simple, vanished people, the preliterate Flan of her own vale.

May I possibly become one of them? May I? Despite my decades of devotion to literacy and my long life full of Oeridian ideas, may I?

Friends, I am an historian. I do more than read. And I tell you that, someday soon, I will earnestly try.

§

Interlude: At Grey College Chapel

(Gods’day, 11th Fireseek 592cy )

Did you see that? The way it swooped? I had to duck under the lectern. You saw nothing? It came from the shadows. The ceiling of the chapel is cavernous at night, and all day, I felt like I was being watched. Does something harrass us at this troublesome hour?

Apologies. Let me begin again. Dean Wiseword, thank you for that kind introduction. Allow me to commence.

Ladies and gentlemen: these are the times that try men’s souls. A great man, a preeminent church and government, and a foremost nation have been called into doubt by a book written by someone that no one outside his profession knows anything of. I am of that profession; I know the man and am attacked in the book. And I am not no one. I sit, as you know, on the Historical Board of the Church of Rao, which I proudly serve. And the church, the board, the college, and all of you have invited me here to answer one question: Is any of it true?

No, it isn’t. The Canon of Veluna—apostate? The God of Reason and Serenity—impersonal and usurping? The Archclericy of Veluna—not ancient but modern and obsessed with power? These are preposterous things. They are dangerous things. They are erroneous things.

Let me dispose of the least consequential error first. I am libeled by Professor Bifurcati—the unhappy author of The Veil of Lunacy and a man I believed was my friend until he informed me otherwise—libeled, I say, as a man “in no danger of drowning in depths of logic he never swims,” practicing “strange human logic,” and not “entirely serious” when I wrote, on two separate occasions and at length, on the history of the Oeridian conquest. The conquest was happily concluded a millenium ago and has been regarded ever since as a triumph of goodness. I was perfectly serious when I wrote the histories, and today they are widely referenced by hundreds colleagues as the definitive studies on the subject.

Obviously, Prof Bifurcati does not think highly of my colleagues and me. Some people find it easier to be brash than respectful. I am not the lone authority on Flanaessian political history, and no one person is. But together, reputable scholars instruct and correct one another. Whatever our disagreements and failings, we speak plainly about what must be true. We protect the foundations of knowledge from superficial attack. And we tell you, unanimously, that there are no authorities who think like Prof Bifucati does. Having misconstrued, in tremendous detail, many points that remain quite settled, it is very difficult now to contain the overflow and publicity of his errors. That is why we attempt to dissuade historians from writing long books we know nothing about until they are published on spurious presses. Nlessie’s Old Books? In Molag? I have warned Prof Bifurcati about this sort of thing in person and on several occasions. He is incorrigible.

His arguments depend on two suppositions. First, that hobgoblins are not monstrous, and second, that Oeridians are. I do not know where all the Oerth’s hobgoblins came from. I do know that they initially attacked the first Oeridian settlers everywhere in the Flanaess and without provocation. We came. They attacked. They died. The historical and moral simplicity of the tale is its finest proof.

Are Oeridians monsters? We are not perfect. We come here, for example, to the Chapel of Truth and Reason in Grey College to humble ourselves before Rao and renew our dedication. Examine this chapel. It is dark and in shadow this night, but in the morning light will come, and it will be itself again. I know this well from the hundreds of times I have worshipped here over the past fifty years. And tomorrow, it will be lighted, open, well proportioned, sturdy, and enduring. Truth endures. How can it be what gets knocked down?

Are Oeridians monsters? Is it merely by a false comparison to hobgoblins that we have an apparent glory? I do not believe that any of the the men and women here tonight will be able to convince themselves of that, try as they may. We are not perfect. We are subject to error, vanity, flattery, and greed. But we know that we must stand before the gods of knowledge, truth, and goodness at last, and that we will submit (and always have submitted) to their judgement for our benefit and correction. If we doubt that, we doubt the gods themselves.

It comes to this. The Canon of Veluna has done us the services of a saint, so, we know him to be one. In a devilish world, it is not easy to stand up for truth and give it proper standing. Prof Bifurcati is of the world. He is its excellent representative. In such a world, how will goodness and truth prevail? The purity of our saints may be compromised, and no doubt, it too often has been. But they work miracles for our sakes; it is unavoidable and necessary that it be so. Shepherds do not stay peaceful while they fend off wolves; it is folly then to let the wolves speak their opinion of our shepherds.

We do not venerate our saints for their perfection. We venerate them for contesting against the forces of evil, triumphing on our behalf, and remaining in grace. They do not suffer corruption from doing what would corrupt us. Hazen, Canon of Veluna, has contested with evil. He has grasped it, wrestled with it, suffered for it, and triumphed over it. He is triumphing over it even now, in a renewed and eternal war against Iuz. He secures our churches, our borders, our kingdoms, cities, and farms. He leads us to pastures of peace and keeps the dire wolves at bay. We must thank him for it, and I know we will.

It is our turn now to act as shepherds; an enemy tempts us to abandon our strength and our redeemer. But Prof Bifurcati and his book are not immediately important. We must attend dirctly to our true enemy, Iuz! We are at war! We must not be confused. We will not be confused.

May Rao keep you and bless you. Good night.

(Ducks and exits)

§

Monologue: A party to the contract

I would fear for your nerves at this juncture, my "Heroes heroes burning bright in the forest of the night," except I know how risible that would be. I should fear for you? Ha! I burned my thumb last night while snuffing my candle and had an uncomfortable night of it, the gravest injury I have suffered, or am like to suffer, on this adventure. You have breached the Fellreev Forest this sightless midnight—hell hounds to the left of you, hell hounds to the right—fighting for reasons that are good and intelligent and brave, while I was induced by a generous fee to compose loose thoughts I only half admit having, even to myself. I pray Nerull hath no scythe for you tonight; I pray I submit your copy of my next installment on time.

I am not altogether confident about it; I have forebodings. What, I ask, is the usual consequence of failing in a public debate? A phial of humiliation ingested at the urging of your colleagues, who will no doubt make a meal of it. My particular debate, moreover, is conducted here, in the unpublished pages of The Veil of Lunacy, to be read by no one but you, who know not the prepartion of a phial of that kind. So, it's all good, right?

The great difficulty—the awful fear—is this: I am no longer convinced that my little joust with Canon Hazen is confined to the rhetorical tilt. The doubt drains me—like a baby spider sucking its first victim—that Hazen is gaining an insubstantial reality, and I am in actual danger!

Oh, why did I sign that contract! Nine awful lawyers plus nine august scholars on the side of the angels opposite me at table and one unapparent lurker among us, stayng hidden in the legal proceedings, unremarked in the legal writ, inhabiting the spaces between, and occupying the coughing, the hemming, the hawing, the silences, the punctuations, the cross-outs, the blotted illegibilities. Oh, my gods! That I, a scholar of my skeptical kind, should have forgotten that there is meaning in such things and put my signature to it!

To this contract, I happen to be “Party B.” I'm reading it right now, and it says: “Party A shall provide Party B's coindemnification," etc. Egads! What the hell are those cross outs? Did I sign that? I don't THINK so! This contract lives! It evolves! It is the unnatural selection of deliberate variation!

My situation is dire. You, my peers newly seated at the roundable of historical dilemma, have no doubt foreseen my error. I have put off discussing until our next (and fourth) scenario a point on which the three completed ones depend: Who is the Canon of Veluna? When will he strut the stage? He was not the High Canon of Rao; he did not participate in the Oeridian conquest; he did not extinguish the hogboblin nations; he did not lead the Flan nor rule the Voll. How, then, can any of it matter? How will Hazen be found guilty of doing what he did not and saying what he said not?

My forebodings rise. Where is my strength and my salvation? If my contract be against me, who can be for me?

Calm yourselves, my hero adventurers. The great personalities in this historical drama have ever been on stage and are so even now. Only their names have been changed to protect the innocent. All is, if I have grace to use it so, as ever in my great indemnifier's eye.

It is past time I should provide you with a list of characters. I do it now. Some of the actors will be found playing more than one part. You will learn who and why by the bye.

SCENARIO FOUR—VELUNA

§

Chapter 15: The Advent of Veluna

~Laudine

The village of Laudine no longer exists. When the swamps southeast of Bolsover Town broadened and deepened three centuries ago and then just as unexpectedly subsided a century after that, a swamp sickness beset the village and the opulent monastery it served, emptying their populations. The monastery’s monumental stones sank two feet into the flat, grassy soil; its wooden ceilings and floors were dissolved; and the superb vaults of the library and the church fell into the ruins that feature in Lord Gordyn’s poem “Velunar Bards and Dissenting Preachers.” The village was lost. It did not resurface from its dip in the swamp, and no one alive knows where it was.

Laudine had always been remotely situated, and today its remant lies in the interior swamp, twenty miles from nowhere. No one goes there except on St Hermiod's Eve, when the fishermen’s wharves at Bolsover Town, ten miles up the Voll River’s underwater stream and perched five inches above it, are crowded with pilgrims boating to the moonlighted festival of St Hermiod, the “Celebration among the Ruins.”

St Hermiod is the two-headed mythical beast that provides the occasion for Gordyn's poem. It was once a mortal man, Hermiod of Laudine, elected the monastery’s abbot in 230-, the High Canon of Rao in 243-, and the first Canon of Veluna in 254cy. Including the beast in The Veil of Lunacy was a problematic decision; everyone regrets historicizing a romantic creature. But Hermiod (the man) is a pivotal figure in our history and of necessary concern. His life and works comprise much of what we know about the initial establishment (there was a second, centuries later) of the Archclericy of Veluna.

Opinions will vary on the significance of fantastical beasts. You—my pride of adventuring lions persuing a dark path to the antipode of paradise—may think no more of a thousand fantastical beasts than of one fell knock at the gate of the city without counterpart in the whole world: when a moment will knell the woe of years; noise will be everywhere, the toll increasing like a bell; and Dauntless the slughorn to your lips you will set and blow, “We few to the Dark Tower came!”

Perhaps you find the latest sentence too effusive and lacking in context. It's not the fault of their author, and I, too, have an excuse: I am awestruck! I gasp at the risks my impetuous cubs undertake at the wager of their hell-bound lives.

But from now on, as they have no bearing on my history, I exclude mythical beasts from consideration and leave you, my brave and endangered species, to grapple the real ones. You may begrudge this as selfish and unfair because it reserves the lion’s share of salutary outcomes to me. But bear in mind that I did not labor for lo! these twenty years for tenure at Olde Maurian for no reason; my writing's sanction and the encumbant shelter from its consequences were on my mind; better safe than sorry. Besides—if I were to die, who would finish my book? Where would that leave you? Did you ever think of that?

My thinking drifts to this: The year 254cy, in addition to promoting the former High Canon of Rao and abbot of Laudine into the original Canon of Veluna, determined much of the subsequent history of the Flanaess; it was the year of Furyondy’s rebellion from the Great Kingdom, when the empire covered two-thirds of the continent, taxed most of its people, ruled its farthest seas, and had not lost a war in four hundred years. The doubt was how the overking of Ahlissa would treat the Furyondian rebels. What would be their fate?

At about the same time, "as Furyondy was born, in 254cy, Voll (now officially recognized as Veluna), too, declared sovereignty," an even more problematic event. Voll stood pledged in fealty to the overking and in practical service to the viceroy of Furyondy. When Furyondy broke troth with the overking, neither the fealty nor the service were ended for Voll.

Whom did it serve? The overking, in troth, but more presumably Furyondy, its good neighbor, not the remote and licentious Malachite Throne. Yet after delaying for six months Voll (as Veluna) declared its emancipation without specifying which of its lords it had emancipated from. The armies of its two lords were opposed by then near the fortress of Eastgate, east of Dyvers; war was at hand, and the wide world wondered at Veluna's ambivalence.
