Whom did it serve? The doubt may be expressed this way: When the Canon of Veluna declared independence, had he broken troth once, or twice?

§

~The break from the kingdom

After three and a half centuries, the answer remains elusive. The King of Furyondy today formally retains his claim as the legitimate ruler of Veluna, which the archclericy does not acknowledge. No treaty agrees their coexistence; the alliance of Furyondy and Veluna does not offically exist and never has, not even over the past decade of forever war against Iuz.

Nonetheless, the assumption (somewhat begrudged by Furyondy) that the alliance is deep and abiding runs through every historical study of the two nations. For example, one Velunar historian has written that

In the years before the establishment of the archclericy, Voll had acted as a sort of moral compass for Furyondy as a whole. Key adherents of Rao gained major positions in the court of the viceroy. It was only after gaining the council and support of Canon Hermiod of Laudine that the man who became ThrommelⅠinitiated the plan to declare independence from the Great Kingdom. As Furyondy was born, Voll (now officially recognized as Veluna), too, declared sovereignty, although the two states remained close.

Is that how it happened? It’s debatable, at least by me. But whether or no, there is no mention of a formal alliance, because there wasn’t one. The only official recognition of Veluna's independence was Veluna's. And Furyondian historians tell the story diffrerently, as in this example:

In 254cy, the heir to Viceroy Stinvri was crowned in Dyvers as ThrommelⅠ: King of Furyondy, Prince of Veluna, Provost of the Northern Reaches, Warden General of the Vesve Forest, Marshal of the Shield Lands, Lord of Dyvers, etc. The adjunctive states were soon lost, but the central core of the kingdom was sound and viable and has persisted.

ThrommelⅠ, first King of Furyondy, was publicly crowned as the ruler of each of the former videroyalty's vassal states; foremostly, ass Prince of Veluna. In Furyondy’s view, the former overking’s vassals became subjects of the new king. We may understand, then, why Thrommel did not congratulate Hermiod on Veluna's independence; we may even ask whether—had he not been confronting an army sent by Rauxes—Thrommel might have viewed Furyondy's independence as a rebellion.

General historical studies—that is, studies of no particular nation—hold points of view that resemble Furyondian historiography more than Velunar:

In the mid-third century, the outer dependencies of the Great Kingdom began declaring their independence. The Viceroyalty of Furyondy led the way, becoming the Kingdom of Furyondy. Other regions also broke from the ineffectual government of the overking over time, creating their own governments after achieving success in their wars of rebellion.

 

The civilized states of the central Flanaess fought with the Great Kingdom of Ahlissa for their independence. Perranders, Velunars, Furyondians, and The Pale achieved success, establishing independent status one after another in a series of minor but bloody wars.

These views gloss the truth that breaking from "the Great Kingdom" meant breaking from Furyondy, too; King ThrommelⅠof Furyondy had been crowned as the ruler of each of them. But they acknowledge that independence was realized in different ways and at different times for the different nations. Perranland claimed sovereignty in the early fourth century in the names of “mountain and lowland tribesmen that had long served in Furyondy’s military and had gained the experience and discipline necessary to mount a successful rebellion.” Shield Landers remained “loyal to the ideal of the Great Kingdom but wholly opposed to the regime in Rauxes, never declaring complete independence and existing somewhere between autonomy and their status as vassals.” The High Folk quietly drifted from the Furyondian throne by behaving more independently each passing year until real independence was a fait accompli. Dyvers did not secede from Furyondy until the sixth century.

Each newly sovereign state had its own reasons for declaring independence. Perrenlanders felt they had never been incorporated into the Great Kingdom but only occupied by the viceroy’s soldiers. Shield Landers took exception to the “decadence” of Rauxes. Furyondy rebelled against the “extremely difficult lives led by the majority of the viceroyalty under incompetent overkings,” viewing the Great Kingdom as the one to break troth by governing badly. Veluna considered independence a just desert for its history of benevolent influence on the Ahlissan empire. There was no agreement on the purpose, timing, or means to these emancipations. Each sovereign nation acted realistically: as it saw fit, when it saw fit, and in its own interests.

Velunar historians nonetheless tend to interpret the different rebellions as aspects of a common, progressive movement (sometimes called “the Furyondian movement”) toward liberty realized under the auspices of the beneficent King ThrommelⅠand his enlightened advisor Canon Hermiod. They stand alone in taking this point of view. Other historians do not oppose it explicitly but say discrepant things; they view the King of Furyondy, for example, not as benevolenth but as jealous of his monarchical authority. They are surely correct.

Kings are not crowned by public ceremony unless they intend to rule. To be crowned and fail to govern is humiliating, and accordingly, the King of Furyondy never freely acknowledged the sovereignty of his former vassals. At one extreme, Perrenland had to fight a war of independence, while at the other, High Folk gained recognition of sovereignty as part of a trade agreement after two hundred years in limbo.

The question, then, is not whether Veluna is correct in its understanding—it evidently is not—but comes to this: Why do Velunars see things so singularly, and why do the others gloss their dissent by so much apparent agreement?

§

Chapter 16: The Moral Compass

(At the verge of the Fellreev Forest)

Professor, do we have to climb this stupid hill? I'm weary, and Doraka'a is that way!

We're almost at the top! If any young lady starts to fade, a young gentleman may assist her.

Assist her? If she fades, why can't I!

What manner of chivalry is that? We will reach the summit together unfaded. Stand back, now! Don't approach the fog bank that lies over this high ridge.

What's in the fog?

Nothing. I warn you against what lies beyond. The fog is a veil or curtain.

So—what's beyond the veil?

A mystery! I have something that pertains to it in the pocket of my gown.

(Produces a compass, fabulous in appearance, needle unmoving)

Oooh! What's that?

A magical artifact, a regulating compass of moral direction—or of moral deception, as is sometimes said by the sardonically inclined—for the mechanical regulation of moral behavior.

Can it be?

It's impossible!

It's improbable. . .

Is it dangerous?

Is it dangerous, possibly?

Oh, yes. Possibly, very dangerous. It is one of several hundred regulators built four hundred years ago on the alternative plane of existence known as Mechanus, the Clockwork Nirvana, by a modron septon named Cogitamus Idemus. The modrons gifted the compasses to the theocrats of the The Pale, who worship Pholtus, god of Absolute Law and Order. The modrons had hoped to increase order on oerth by automatically regulating The Pale, but Cogitamus misunderstood his instructions. The works of his compass presumed users whose morality was based on consistent ethical principles. The Pholtans, however, had no principles but only thousands of precepts that they rigorously enforced. The compasses fluctuated wildy; the Pholtans followed their directions; chaos ensued!

Wow. Can I see it?

Certainly. The housing contains hundreds of gears, each with its own gear-spirit. When the regulator is activated, the gear-spirits detect a moral conumdrum and configure their gears accordingly. Whiz, whirl, grind—the needle spins and points to a direction! The face of the compass shows four directions on two axes, analogous to north-south and east-west. On a moral regulator, however, north-south is "admonish-rebuke," and east-west is "strongly-mildly." Since the compass presumes users with consistent ethics and precise moral precepts, it indicates no specific action but only a general direction to a certain degree. Pholtus' priests were left to their own devices in determining which of their precepts was best to follow while the regulators' needles spun wildly between stongly-mildly and admonish-rebuke. A social catastrophe!

(With frightened eyes) What happened?

The Pholtan theocrats had been assigned to rule The Pale on behalf of the Great Kingdom of Ahlissa decades before the creation of Furyondy and the other viceroyalties. The Ahlissan Court of Essences thought lawful theocrats would make excellent leaders, but unhappily, the Pholtan clerics were quite irrational despite being lawful. Even so, the modrons believed that the Pholtan priests were more orderly than the chaotic Ahlissans, so they tried to help out by giving them the moral compasses. When the extent of Cogitamus' mistake was realized, a modron court ruled that it had been the result of a broken contract (because Cogitamus had mistaken his instructions) and sent hordes of inevitables—which are something like self-guiding attack drone—to find the compasses and destroy them all. The regulator I now hold was dropped into the Nyr Dyv for some reason and escaped detection. It was given to me ten years ago by a spirit naga who lured me to the bottom of the lake in hopes of exchanging the compass for my autograph on an indellible scroll she was hording. The naga claimed she was the reincarnate spirit of the dead Cogitamus, who had turned renegade out of spite and been drowned by the inevitables. But who knows? Perhaps she only wanted to appear special in my eyes.

Cool! Can I keep it?

Oh, dear me, no. (Disappointment and disgruntlement) That's to be avoided above anything. A regulating compass goes awry when it is operated by someone with unprincipled morals, and from what I have learned of your circumstances, you were chosen for this adventure because of how remarkably unprincipled you are. Besides, the activating gear-spirit is missing, so the device no longer works. But if the modrons hear of it, they will send the inevitables anyway. Best you should return it to me.

But look here, Professor. Why did you show it to us? What has it got to do with climbing this hill?

It has everything to do with it. The regulating compasses were almost all destroyed in the first half of the third century. At the same time, the Pholtan theocracy in The Pale was being replaced by theocrats of Zilchus, the god of Money, while in Voll, the Raoan theocrats were readying the new Velunar government. Although most gods (especially the lawful ones) do not get along well with the pedantically legalistic Pholtus, Rao has the knack for getting along with anyone. He is amenable to Pholtus, and he is an ally to Zilchus and Rao. It is quite plausible, then, that a number of Pholtan theocrats would have fled after their expulsion from The Pale to Furyondy and Veluna using their regulating moral compasses as an inducement to take them in.

The truth is less important than the plausibility of this view, which suffices as an illustration of the gulf between administrating the Ahlissan Imperial Church and establishing a national government in Veluna. There is little evidence that, in Voll or Furyondy either, the Raoan church administration was seen to be preparing an independent Velunar government. The apparently spontaneous generation of a functional theocracy shocked everyone and disrupted everything, and indeed, the best evidence for mistakingly identifying the High Canon of Rao with the Canon of Veluna is that Hermiod of Laudine had been serving as the former when he was translated instantly into the latter. But that continuity may be accounted for in many ways having little to do with honoring a traditional lineage. What mattered was signalling to the empire that certain leading actors in Voll were still in control of Veluna following what amounted—as I will argue—not to the restoration of a tradition of spiritual shepherding but to a political and ecclesiastical palace coup.

Blurring the distinction of what was new in Veluna and what was old in Voll mattered immensely; the new theocracy's national, political, and religious legitmacy was at stake. The Church of Rao had existed in Voll long ago, but the Archclericy of Veluna had not. Raoan clerics had never before been responsible for governing Voll. Could the novelty of a theocratic government be papered over? Could the Canon of Veluna in his person disguise a political revolution as the restoration of a spiritual tradition?

All this and more will be revealed. Behold!

(Waving his arms to sunder the curtain of fog and reveal an impossible thing)

§

Chapter 17: The nativity of Veluna

~The concave illusion

A fast wind whistling like Erythnul’s stoneheaded mace rends the veil and reveals the wide world around. The adventurers are stranded on a slender stone column rising miles above the bottom of a vast, semispherical concavity infinitely deep and broad and burning and flaming in black, orange, and red beneath a dark and empty sky, like hell.

Bwahahahaha! wails the evil professor.

My contract, he said, stipulates that I am allowed one high-budget magical effect on our adventure, which I have put in right here. It has no reality. You could jump off this precipice into the yawning abyss and no harm would come to you. Would anyone like to try?

Oh! Oh! I would!

Very well, young lady. But I caution you. It will take 25.62 seconds for you to hit bottom, at which time you will reappear here. During that time, I will continue my lecture and you will be missing out. So be sure . . .

(She jumps. Laughter, cheering, and screaming)

Hmm. My word. Scholars, surrounding us is an immense section of the Oerth’s convex surface that has been inverted to the concave; sunk down like the surface of a death star where the planet-killing super-laser’s dish is set, or like the inside of a porcelain bowl decorated and fired with scenes from Hades. But as you may see (a second wave of the arms illuminates the sky and soothes the distant flames), the surface below is neither metallic nor porcelain but is the Oerth’s natural topography sunken in. Since we are standing near the bottom center of the fantastic scene on a rocky needle that rises only three miles from the surface, the far horizon sweeps up and away from us for a thousand miles in all directions without vanishing as shortly as the horizon of the sea when we see it drop off from the top of a volcanic island’s peak.

(The jumper reappears, prone, stunned, shaken, and recovering quickly)

Woooooo! Holy smokes, I wonder if I want to do that again!

Impermissible, I’m afraid. One departure only, per the terms of the contract. As you can see, the entire magical concavity is visible from here, from the Icy Sea to the Gearnat and from the Rakers Mountains to the Yatils.▽Viewers that dislike illusions may want to consult a map. (Eds) (zooms nearer) The Nyr Dyv is south of us halfway up the concavity’s side, and almost every oerthly place mentioned in this monograph so far is visible to us. The most recently mentioned (the illusion spins until the heroes face the east) is the Theocracy of The Pale, where the modrons distributed their moral regulators once upon a time.

(Extending an arm with his palm upturned, the professor wiggles his fingers and The Pale zooms in)

Please, if you will, follow the progress of the ship that is sailing the long, slow bends of the Artonsamay River toward the Nyr Dyv. It goes along the lake’s northern shore and passes the craggy Rift Canyon, the steaming White Plume Mountain, and the verdant meadows of the Shield Lands; billows south to the mouth of the Veng River and then west past the coast of Furyondy to reach the far southwestern point of the lake; where lies Dyvers, the City of Sails (zooms closer) with its famous, eventful royal palace (closes again, shifting the scene until the scholars’ point of view is on the ship’s prow, looking southwest as the vessel moves into the mouth of the Velverdyva River). We move up river going west, with Furyondy on the northern and Verbobonc on the southern banks, until we reach Veluna and the river’s great northern bend to Iron Wood, Daple Wood, Tempton Water, and the four-hundred-mile stretch straight to Fals Palaces, the Carnalion Mountains, and the mouth of the Fals River Gorge; where we leave the river (and the ship) to go south to Mitrik, then east into Veluna and onto the Lortmil Mountains; east further to Celene (the forest realm of the fey Queen Yolande) and then to the city of Greyhawk, Gem of the Flanaess; reaching, at last, the Duchy of Urnst on the southern coast of the Nyr Dyv; where we find the city of Nyrstran, the arboreal campus of Old Maurian College, and even the little tower in which I live and, right there, if we maximize the zoom, the window to my rooms where I am casting this illusion and . . . hmmm . . . why can’t I find me?

Because you’re here, Professor.

Don’t be silly. I know where I am.

But Professor, if we turn around and look behind us to the north, why is everything and everywhere still black and burning like hell?

That’s the way to Doraka’a, my boy, the path you are actually on. In that direction, the illusion displays what’s in store, not what you would see. Don’t get upset. Nothing I can do. Terms of the contract. Although, in a happier manner, I may show you something more encouraging. Directly southeast of here, only five miles away, the Ritensa River flows out of the Fellreev Forest: that’s the way you came to get where you are now. By backtracking the river going south (zooms in), we retake your journey, racing through the hobgoblin plains to Law’s Forge, your home; where, as you see, everything is quite normal, everyone is quite safe, and they are only wondering what has happened to you.

(Hugs, tears, and mutual encouragement among the scholars)

As you can see, my dears, it is an easy trip by sailing ship from The Pale to Dyvers and then to Veluna via the Nyr Dyv and the Artonsamay River, the same route that (as I propose) once transported an untold number of regulating moral compasses from the abolished Pholtan theocracy in the east to the adventing Raoan theocracy in the west. This could explain how my compass came to be horded by a spirit-naga in the Nyr Dyv’s depths: someone sailing this way might have dropped it in. Too, it casts in an intriguing light the blockquote I am inserting into our book right now, which is excerpted from ◒Voll◓, the historical source that, as we know, contains interpolations made by Raoan scholars at around the time that the Archclericy of Veluna was founded and the Pholtan theocrats were exiled from The Pale. Here it is, I copy it for you:

In the years following the establishment of the viceroyalty, Veluna acted as a sort of moral compass for Furyondy as a whole. Key adherents of Rao gained major positions in the court of the viceroy.

A moral compass, did it say? Although the modrons’ regulators had worked disastrously in the hands of the Pholtans of The Pale, in the possession of the Raoans of Veluna they might have worked very well. Raoan theology is highly principled, philosophical, ethical, rational, and systematic; Raoan clerics were imbedded within the imperial politics of the viceroyalty and the Great Kingdom of Ahlissa, from both of which they hoped to extricate themselves conspiratorially while creating a theocratic government of their own. The great difficulty of hatching an independent government from within the empire is what we must attempt to explain, and if the Raoans’ surreptitiously but admirably rational, orderly, and lawful powers might receive a magical boost of moral direction, what might they have achieved?

Frankly, it boggles the mind. When understood as ◒Voll◓ would like it in the blockquote—as a metaphor for counsel given to the king and court of Furyondy—the moral compass seems sturdy, sensical, and plain. But the author of ◒Voll◓ (perhaps) had a sense of humor. We know that the empire was not dismantled by only morality; the breakup was both plotted and dangerous. Before its proclamation the archclericy had not been in prospect. Voll was ruled by secular princes, theocracy was prohibited by the overking, and national fealty had been pledged to the empire in great religious expectations that were not shared by the overking and the viceroy. The immanent clerical assumption of government was unlikely foreseen even by Voll's own nobility; Furyondy's Thrommel Ⅰ had been crowned as Prince of Veluna, a careful and courteous title acknowledging that he was not a noble of Voll and would cause no disruption to its political order.▽Voll had been a federation of counts, dukes, and barons. Thrommel I's coronation as Prince of Veluna acknowledged the title's lack of precedent in Voll while also asserting a degree of sovereignty over the commensurate populations elsewhere in Luna's vale. The Canon of Veluna would echo the Prince of Veluna in assuming this dignity. (AB) Nothing of this indicates that Hermiod, the High Canon of Rao, was seen as anything more than a political advisor to the King of Furyondy on behalf of the Imperial Raoan Church. Officials of that church would appear, then, to have presided at a ceremony that legitmately crowned their king, whom they would disavow within half a year.

Seen in this context, I ask: Was Veluna’s moral compass only a metaphor for the advice and counsel given by Raoan clerics to their foreign liege? Or might it have been a euphemism for something not metaphorical but magical and real? Had the modrons’ regulating compasses of moral direction been used to help bring about political events leading to Veluna’s independence? Were the regulators used to mask the intents of the Raoan clerics from the Furyondian king and court while manipulating history in preparationm for the independence of Voll?

The bare possibility, my adventurers perched on a rock betwixt heaven and hell, sounds incredible and conspiratorial; you are rightly incredulous. Even so, it will not do to dismiss the thought without first understanding how remarkable Veluna’s surreptitious achievement actually was, because remarkable events require remarkable explanations.

Let’s see.

§

~The Furyondian wars of independence

Sending an illusory thread of gold into the hellish darkness of the burning forest below, the professor retrieves a great firewood for the adventurers to camp beside atop the stone extrusion, conjuring (from behind a scholar’s ear) marshmallows, chocolates, and grahams that the campers begin eagerly gluing together. (The concave illusion darkens everywhere although flaming grimly in the northwest)

Voll was a nation, the professor told the bunch, that held a deep and abiding faith in the god Rao and the Raoan church, but politically it was ruled by a federation or collaboration of seven noble families heading seven distinct territories that had each its own bishop. The federation's nominal ruler, probably known as the plar, did not serve as a monarch but to pledge homage to the overking and ensure that the pledge was redeemed. In addition to the Church of Rao and the nobility, there was a Raoan mission (as the church at first considered it) from Voll to the Great Kingdom of Ahlissa and known as the Imperial Raoan Church, dedicated to providing a divine sanction for the rule of imperial realms west of the Viceroyalty of Nyrond (come to glow faintly).

It is unfortunate, he told the bunch, that I may tell no tales of heroic battles fought to win Furyondy’s freedom from the Great Kingdom. Although they loom large in expectation, and there were kings, counselors, armies, generals, officers, soldiers, and heroes enough, yet the great battles never took place. North of the Nyr Dyv (comes to glow dimly) the territories that would soon unite and become the Shield Lands were already skirmishing over loyalties divided between the one king, rising in Dyvers, and the other, sinking in Rauxes. Rauxes sent an army to assist its supporters (zoom to soldiers crossing the Artonsamay), escalating the skirmishing into a civil war (comes to glow brightly) in which thousands died but that, even so, remained a civil war in the Shield Lands not a broader war for freedom. Furyondy took no real part in it.

Rauxes also sent an expeditionary army to Greyhawk that was intended to cross the Selintan River and march on Dyvers (they come to glow dimly), but the attack never happened. The Great Kingdom’s army remained camped near Greyhawk for five incredible years (bedraggled soldiers, flickering fire, dead of winter) bivouacked in inertia. For all that time a supplemental army was supposed to arrive from Urnst, but it never did, because barbarian raiders—so remote in the east that they are under the concavity’s horizon—were threatening the borders of the empire’s North Province, and Rauxes required a third army to contain them. Rauxes soon withdrew its soldiers from the Shield Lands to send against the barbarians, too, allowing the civil war to peter out (fades to glow dimly) in favor of Furyondy. The Flanaess watched in astonishment as the invincible Great Kingdom’s war of reclamation against Furyondy (comes to glow dimly) dispersed in 260cy like investors reckoning a failed corporation. The Malachite Throne in Rauxes was incapable of raising armies to fight on multiple fronts.

The failure was attributed throughout the empire to the overking’s waning hold on his viceroys, vassals, and allies (zoom to the Malachite throne, in Rauxes, where the Raxian overking sits alone and in shadow). And speaking generally, historians today understand Furyondy’s rebellion as the result of a broad “resentment” over the “decadence and incompetence of Rauxes,” not as an exercise of political ambition. “The viceroy had ruled fairly from Dyvers while Rauxes had created extremely difficult lives for the majority of Furyondians,” one historian wrote, and another remarked that “Furyondy bore the brunt of attacks by foreign raiders from the north while the Overking did little to protect his western lands.” Twice, as a consequence, in 252- and 253cy, Viceroy Stinvri withheld tithes due to Rauxes and redistributed them in Furyondy, claiming that the viceregal court in Dyvers was too benign and efficient to obey an unjustifiable imperial mandate (zoom to poor folk receiving alms from the viceroy). But should we accept this explanation at face value?

The incompetence of Rauxes was real, but historians have failed to point out that withholding the tithes also served to test whether the overking was capable of enforcing imperialism. When Rauxes responded only by protest and threat, the viceroyalty’s declaration of independence became effectively inevitable (Stinvri grins greedily when the poor aren’t looking). The idea that the viceroy hoped to resume the overking’s service if dutifulness were restored in Rauxes is incredible. There is no evidence for it, and certainly Stinvri’s timing had been politically calculated and had risked the Great Kingdom's wrath. Would the overking have overlooked that bid for autonomy had defeated Furyondy in war? The answer must be, no.

The limits of Stinvri’s benignity are further indicated by the reaction of his former vassals to their new king’s coronation. The determinative factor in choosing the day was Stinvri’s illness and premature death in 254cy. Crowning his son and heir as King Thrommel Ⅰ of Furyondy, not as viceroy of the Great Kingdom (people cheering, nobles applauding, and Raoan priests hallowing), happened as quickly as Furyondy’s vassals could be summoned to participate. When the gaudy ceremony “loudly announced Thrommel as King of Furyondy, Prince of Veluna, Marshall of the Shield Lands, Warden General of the Vesve Forest, and more,” the volume of the announcement was due to the ignorant overking's need to hear it from fifteen hundred miles away, in Rauxes (the doubtful emperor cups hand to ear). Had the vassals been slow to assemble, the overking may have had time to arrive in Dyvers and change Thrommel's coronation into an imperial homage. But as things went, the new era rang in smoothly, although the new king’s rule over his former vassals (now his sovereign subjects) remained unsettled in many ways (Furyondy comes to glow).

At the time, the Shield Lands as we know it now did not exist; there were a number of petty “nobles on the Nyr Dyv's north shore,” many of whom “refused to acknowledge the new king, remaining loyal to the ideal of ancient Aerdy although wholly opposed to the decadent regime in Rauxes.” The many that supported the new king were those nearest to Furyondy’s border, furthest from the Great Kingdom’s Viceroyalty of Nyrond. This geographical and political divide (zoom to petty nobles hurling insults across a ditch) was evident at Thrommel's coronation, which was imperfectly attended and threw the squabbling nobles into civil war (they take up swords). "The Shield Lands" was originally an alliance in support of the new king (comes the ditch to glow brighter on one side). Thrommel acknowledged the alliance by crowning himself “Marshall of the Shield Lands,” but his opponents did not admit the Shield until after Nyrond, too, had rebelled against Rauxes.

Similarly, the title Warden General of the Vesve Forest signified Thrommel’s importance as a defender and protector, not a ruler. Like the Shield Lands, the High Folk (comes to glow) of the Vesve was then not yet a political unit. The relation of the humans of the town to the elves of the forest was (and remains) customary: they had no common government, a borderland existed between them, and Thrommel’s rule reached no further than his promise of military protection against monsters and forest raiders in exchange for open trade with Furyondy. The title “Warden General” was Thrommel's accomodation to the High Folk, as "Prince of Veluna" had accomodated Voll, and "Marshall," the Shield Lands. The new king had somewhat more authority among the humans of the High Folk than among the elves, but not by much.

(Waves off the concave illusion)

None of the foreign lands that Thrommel claimed to rule sovereignly were asked to renew their feudal allegiances; they were to be subjects, not vassals. Furyondy’s independence was in this way a turn from feudalism toward limited monarchy and modernity; the powers of a prince, a marshall, and a warden are not those of a king, even when a king holds the titles. The accomodations indicate Furyondy’s vulnerability in bidding for independence. Having broken troth with the overking and expecting a retaliatory war, Thrommel appealed to the loyalty of prospective subjects, not the obligations of vassals, and allowed his subjects degrees of freedom suitable to them. Thrommel meant to be king of a modern, international empire based on constitutional liberties, although a monarchy even so.

How was the offer received by Voll? To the nobility it must have seemed natural that the plar, a noble elected to pay homage to a foreign ruler, would be subordinate to an hereditary prince serving a complementary purpose and making no great difference to government in the Vale of Luna. But the feudal allegiance of Voll had been pledged not only in secular terms but also in the great religious expectations of the nation and, in particular, of imperial Raoan clerics that had long served Furyondy's viceroy, not the King of Furyondy, not the Prince of Veluna—and not the plar, nobility, people, or national Church of Rao in Voll either. What would be the status of Rao's imperial clerics when the feudal oath to the empire was broken, the medieval viceroy became a modern king, the nation of Voll became the secular Principality of Veluna, and the Imperial Raoan Church fell under the rule of modern nations whose memories of imperial vassalage were not fond?

The answer to these questions must have seemed as dark and frightening to the Imperial Raoans as to your eyes, my adventuring captive audience, seems this grimly glowing and even hellishly burning concavity, whose horizon reaches to the moonless heavens encircling all around and beyond.

If into this darkness there had fallen the light of a magical regulator, might you have been tempted to let such a guide—not purely Raoan, not thoroughly religious, not at all spiritual, but quite possibly effective—show you the way? My answer to the question will take us to the Canon of Veluna’s introduction into the pages of our fantastical history. The birthday of Veluna is nigh.

(The concave illusion is restored)

§

~The nativity of Veluna

As we huddle around our campfire, making our sweet s’mores, much of the Oerth in front of us and the whole of hell behind; imagine—

You live three hundred and fifty years ago as a ranking cleric of the Imperial Raoan Church, a religious establishment of the Great Kingdom of Ahlissa, and have great expectations of the government you serve. But imagine, there is another Church of Rao established by another government based not in Dyvers but in Veluna City, the capital of Voll, your homeland. Voll is governed by seven noble families and seven diocesan bishops (there is no archbishop yet) united by a secular ruler, known as the plar, that is elected by the nobility. But you are not the plar or a noble or a bishop; you serve not the people and parishioners of Voll but the Viceroy of Furyondy, and you owe fealty to the overking, in Rauxes. Although a citizen of Voll and ordained to its church by its bishops, your political authority derives from the overking, your clerical authority, from the High Canon of Rao, resident in Mitrik far to the west on the Fals River south of Carnalion Gorge.

That’s how things are meant to be. Preserving the independence of Voll inside its borders is the purpose of pledging vassalage to Rauxes, and distinguishing between the Church of Rao and the Imperial Raoan Church is suited to all parties. In Dyvers, the Basilica of Serenity (the illusion zooms in) rises but a mile from Longroods, the viceroyal palace; in Veluna City (zooms there), deep in the midst of the Vale of Luna, Greatblister Abby (where the Church of Rao will bar Poet’s Corner against the misfit Lord Gordyn one day) solely dominates the town, where there is no royal palace to complement the abbey, because in Voll there is no royal family only the plar, a noble elected for life on purpose to pledge fealty to the overking. You, a Raoan advisor to the viceroy, indeed reside in a royal palace, but your rooms are in Dyvers, not Veluna City, and the other palatial estates (images in rotating vista) that you frequent—the Fals Palaces in Castle Sepher and, in Mitrik, the Canonical Court, the Eademer Battistero, and the surpassing High Chapter—belong to the Imperial Church in Veluna's distant northwest, south of Carnalion Gorge.

There are historical reasons for the separation of the Velunar from the imperial Raoan establishments. The lords and bishops of Voll traditionally met in Veluna City when on government businesss. But in 109cy, the imperial army sent by the viceroy of Furyondy to threaten Voll had marched from the far west, from Crockport, not from Dyvers, and had arrived at Voll near Whitehale. The viceroyalty’s territories lay almost all west of Dyvers, and it served the empire to keep an army stationed there. For similar reasons it also served to base the imperial church out west, where more people needed the gospel of peace to be preached than nearer Dyvers. Mitrik at the time was a politically insignificant settlement but the spiritual home of Voll (you may liken it to Valley Forge in mythical Pennsylvania) and, too, the seat of the High Canon of Rao, chief negotiator on Voll's behalf to the empire. Imperial vassalage, the Imperial Church of Rao, and the newly-imperial High Canon of Rao were all to reside in Mitrik together.

Governing the imperial Raoan establishment was more profitably done from Mitrik than anywhere else in the viceroyalty. The location co-opted Raoan heritage and was easily accessible to the imperial army, and yet it respected the independence of the Voll government in Veluna City. Nearly half way along the new Royal Highway, the Fals River Palaces (zoom east through the Carnalion Gorge) became in essence an unofficial Raoan imperial court (look in a palace window, where cigar-smoking men seated in armchairs are fetched crystal tumblers of Azure Sea Pirates rum set out on silver trays). Furyondian officials occupied the palaces on the south bank of the Fals River, while the canon’s theocrats built theirs on the north. Although Rao's advisors to the viceroy's court, in Dyvers, were appointed technically from Veluna City, they were practically chosen in the Fals River Palaces by deliberations that the bishops and lords of Veluna City did not need to attend.

(The zoom is dismissed and the concavity’s true and inverted perspective returns with the Flanaess bathed in daylight—except in the north)

Now, I ask you, my campsite academics on fantastical adventure: Given the historical, geographical, and political divides within Voll, the viceroyalty, and the empire, what are the odds that in Mitrik, in 254cy, when the (formerly High) Canon of (formerly Rao) Veluna declared independence from Furyondy and sovereignty for the archclericy that did not exist, what are the odds that he acted in the best interests of the overking in Rauxes, the king in Dyvers, the disputedly independent former vassal states, the Great Kingdom, the Kingdom of Furyondy, the plar of Voll, the nobility of Voll, the nation of Voll, the bishops of Voll, the Church of Rao, and the Vale of Luna?

(One hand is raised)

Yes, my boy?

None, sir?

Wonderful! Well done. And yet, in his official capacities, Canon Hermiod of Luadine, prior to proclaiming the Archclericy and declaring the independence of Veluna, had no interests other than those I mentioned. His service to the viceroy was done in fealty to the overking; his ordination to the priesthood was an oath of obedience to his bishops; his native duty as a citizen was to serve the plar's government and the nobility of Voll; while within the viceroyalty he administered a cadre of theocrats and court advisors (something like a sacred civil service) in the imperial promulgation of Raoan doctrine to the worshipful masses of subjected peoples. He was not a bishop, was not a prince, and could not ordain clerics or legislate policy. He was in every way subordinate, had no interest of his own—and what was true of its leader was true of each cleric within the Imperial Church, all of them citizens of Voll, civil servants to the Viceroy of Furyondy, pledged in fealty to the Overking of the Great Kingdom of Ahlissa, and ordained to the oversight of the Raoan bishops. None of them had an authority of their own.

Since the theocrats that would form the Archclericy of Veluna were without constituency or self-interest, how might the government be made? How could its leader, the Canon of Veluna, appear so suddenly in glory? Why are the only historical records of its past authority suspected of interpolation? Why have historians said (why do they still say) nothing of the situation, glossed it, misrepresented it, and even tampered with the evidence? What power could intimidate so many, so well, and exact such deference? How on Oerth did the Archclericy’s sanction become the one and holy explanation for everything? What was (is) the awful obfuscation? Who were (are) these inimitable men? What kind of moral compasses do they wield?

It is probably unfair to tell ghost stories at a campfire lighted deep in the darkness of hell, but it is remarkable that such questions bring us to the essentially moral doubt that sits at the bottom of everything: Was it only a cadre of Raoan clerics, or was it some awful heart of darkness that devised the nativity of the Archclericy of Veluna, so unnatural to its time and so thriving today?

The gap between what seemed possible and has since transpired is scary. The Archclericy's creation seems, more than anything, like a staggering Frankenstein's monster, invented in Mitrik, laboratoried in Rauxes, and stalking its master in Dyvers. “The influence of the Church of Rao is said to be everywhere in Veluna” today, and for a long time has been. But from whence did it come? The Raoan faith in the Vale of Luna had not always been a theocracy or even an organized religion; it had been at first a decentralized aspect of a Flan tribe's nomadic life. The origin of Voll's religious establishment, organized into bishoprics and dioceses, depended on writing Word of Incarum, recovering the Crook of Rao, ordaining a Good Shepherd and a nation, wedding the nation to its religion, and escaping its captivity through imperial treachery.

If you are going to credit all this to one man, what kind of weird would he be?

But not every weird is bad; some are a delight to see. And before we chase our canon further into the darkness, perhaps I ought to show you what may seem a light at the end of the tunnel, a fable not only of doubt but of romance, of hope, and of love at last.

§

INTERREGNUM

§

Chapter 18: The Unified Kingdom

Few lovers influence history. You may propose Dido and Aeneas or Cleopatra and Antony; but Aeneas abandoned his Carthaginian queen, too proud of his destiny to defy it, and Cleopatra—whose luxurious bed was a ploy to liberate Egypt—went to war beside her Roman husband but never swooned for him. They died as they had loved—not inseparable, not far apart.

Love makes trouble. Of the seventy-one gods that have failed to bless me, thrice-kissed Myrhiss would be chief were it not for two kindnesses. One was the story of Thrommel and Jolene, the fabulous romance of our time. I did not know them and, even today, know little of them more than what everyone knows. Their marriage, which would have changed so much, never happened. Why, then, do they feature in my history?

In part because the adoring people of Furyondy and Veluna are right—Thrommel and Jolene are a constant midsummer’s dream, flowers entwined, enduring, and unfading. Only in real life are they locked forever in winter and ice.

Rumors of Prince Thrommel's reappearance are still heard upon occasion. After eighteen years, if he had opportunity, would he approach his mistress again? Time must have changed them. Could he believe that his apparition would abate her sorrow? Or would he choose to remain obscure now, forsaking a kingdom that needs him to preserve the tranquility of her grief? The wide world knows that despair would have killed Jolene had it not become her. Could Thrommel’s return restore her to joy? Or, without so intending, would it denounce her for once having loved?

The Supreme Mistress of Samprastadar lives and, in some ways, prospers. I may not speak for her. But for Thrommel, a man middle-aged if he breathes and bereft of hope and love, a man much like me, for him I venture this consolation:

Joey kissed me when we met,

Jumping from the chair she sat in;

Time, you thief, who love to get

Sweets into your list, put that in!

Say I'm weary, say I'm sad,

Say that health and wealth have miss'd me,

Say I'm growing old, but add

Joey kissed me.

Myrhiss' other kindness sent to me I will not tell you.

⚜

Ferrica Aposnos' book, Mistress and Prince: The Romance of Jolene of Samprastadar and Prince Thrommel Ⅳ, was the literary sensation of the 570s. It is possible that all other books published that decade (one or two were mine) combined to sell fewer copies. It had everything—politics, nobility, scandal, mystery, murder, war, fairy tale, and love, love, love—and it was written by a known and intimate friend of Jolene's. Since the Supreme Mistress said nothing against the book—from ten days after Thrommel's disappearance she said nothing in public at all—Jolene's sentimental confessions (as the book styled them) to Ferrica seemed confirmed. It was not so easy, though, to credit Aposnos’ equally intimate knowledge of Thrommel's feelings, or that the famously colloquial prince had expressed himself with the allusive flair of Mistress and Prince. But Ferrica had a friend at court who was Thrommel's confidant, and there was nothing implausible about that.

When the romance’s author was sensationally discovered to be not Ferrica Aposnos but the Honorable Edmore Wunsay, third child of the Baroness of Littleberg, everything was tossed about. Wunsay had been privy counselor to Thrommel for ten years and was well known to be in love with him. So, the intimate revelations about Thrommel became indubitable, and the ones about Jolene were suspect. Had Wunsay fabricated her confessions? Or had Ferrica Aposnos been Wunsay's source? The story’s principle characters still living—Jolene, Wunsay, and Aposnos—had nothing to say on such matters. They retreated from public view and have been content there ever since.

Mistress and Prince begins on the day Jolene and Thrommel first met, in Castle Estival, west of Verbobonc Town, Flocktime 25th, 569cy. An evil cult buoyed by an army of monsters had assembled nearby, threatening Verbobonc’s possession of Welkwood Forest and the nearby mountains and hills. To combat the threat, armies had been sent against the castle from each of the six nations, pledged to the command of Prince Regent Thrommel Ⅳ, Marshal of the Furyondian Army.

But in a manner characteristic of the commensurate races, the prospect of making war against a common enemy had divided the evenses into separate camps seeking political advantage. The prince and marshal was tasked with overruling the persistent racial and nationalist divides and commanding the assembled Six Nation Army.▽No reference to Jack White, because I do not like that song. (AB)

Thrommel dismounted outside the castle gates unnecessarily; he could have ridden to his destination within. But the path to the marshal's quarters went through several courtyards and the prince would greet every diplomat that hurried to be in his way.

From a tower window my lady and I watched him trod among the serpents, each poised to bite his heel. They distressed him not at all. To the contrary, he spoke benevolently as to worms he would elevate to humanity, and so poised that I partly believed he could work the change. I was young, ignorant of court, and entirely mistaken. There was no hope of transforming those snakes that measured their worth by the length of their fangs. Thrommel and Jolene, throughout their time together, defended themselves by keeping the cobras uncoiled. It was their gravest misjudgment. Uncoiled snakes will resort to assassins.

It took three weeks to exact the political toll of the Six Nation Alliance. In the interval, the six armies garrisoned at Castle Estival might have been reduced to eating their horses without a diplomat to care. The intriguers had no concern but themselves. Similar calculations, in unabridged form, would later deny the mistress and prince their wedding day.

At Castle Estival, however, the prince would have his way. Everyone understood that an agreement would be reached to place the Six Nation Army under his command, and in consequence, the hope of uniting Veluna and Furyondy by the wedding of mistress and prince wedding grew daunting.

Wunsay wrote everything that need be said about the politics at Estival in the first pages of his book and then said no more. Bickerers! If you will listen you may hear magic gathering! In Wunsay’s romantic prose, the castle’s old stones harbored not diplomatic deceits but a fey garden luxuriant under the unsetting sun. Storms broke hourly on the castle’s walls, only to drop the rains of heaven upon the invariant love within.

I have seen Castle Estival; it is a functional old fort, two or three nice buildings and one fine garden attached to the marshal's quarters. There, Thrommel awaited Jolene at breakfast—and she, him, at dinner. That they talked only of love was impossible. "What do you think Thrommel's politics will be tomorrow?" woofed Urthgan the Eldest of Tulvar while dining with the castle’s contingent of gnomes that evening. The elder did not care and enjoyed the discomfiture of the humans whose ambitions depended on the answer.

At Estival, Prince Thrommel was a political neutral, presumably. The Plar of Veluna's second daughter was not. Yet, although Lady Jolene must have influenced him, it was difficult to see when or how. Her father’s agenda was not visibly furthered, or anyone else’s for that matter, beyond the need for a limited political agreement. But Thrommel gained from Jolene solutions to fractious problems that were not meant to be solved. "Truth be told," the Duke of the Reach said resignedly after the Treaty of Estival was signed, "most of what's in there came out of Thrommel's garden."

Literary critics have said that Mistress and Prince lacks realism. They were not embarrassed to say that realism is not among the talents of Edmore Wunsay—the man that wrote much of the Treaty of Estival—which to me seems like a derangement of mind. Wunsay cupped politics in one hand and love in the other like pollution and rainwater, and after filling your hands that way you cannot clasp them again and still hold rain. Wunsay’s romantic portrayal of Jolene and Thrommel spilled the admixture and retained the love, and it did so with exceptional fluency, because Wunsay was not in love with only Thrommel. Mistress and Prince is inconceivable without the attachments that bound Thrommel, Jolene, Wunsay, and Aposnos to each other. I do not speak of togetherness, closeness, or intimacy but of active participation, which is not ungainly because participation is always a gain (although the knack of it is not often found in people).

⚜

As marshal of the principal army and prince of the largest nation, Thrommel was inevitably the commander of the assembled Six Nation Army and the arbiter of the treaty for the Six Nation Alliance. The day of his arrival at Estival occasioned a ceremonial procession down the castle’s great hall, a formality with a routine meaning. Thrommel was expert on such occasions and knew the cardinal rule: do not acknowledge by a look or a bow anyone on the sidelines that you do not intend to favor.

He had no intention of favoring the Plar of Veluna when he glanced on the plar's second daughter and then, in an move that would change the world, glanced again.

§

~Mistress and Prince

Everyone talks about the prince and Jolene! Right now my friend has written me a letter, Jolene is engaged with her father, and I think I have time before she returns to copy it out:

My dearest Ferrica,

I write this hastily. It is important news, and who knows when I will again have time again. This morning as is my custom I went down to breakfast twenty minutes ahead of the prince; if there were troubles brewing I wanted time to cool them. I found one simmering on the fire or, rather, set at table where an extra place had been prepared among the dignitaries. The placement card read, "Lady Jolene of Samprastadar." I thought about it. There should be no one at table whose name, title, and face I did not recognize, yet, this Lady Jolene was nobody to me.

Then again it was all too obvious. The only nobody in the castle coming to mind was the plar of Veluna's second daughter. She had turned the prince's head last night, everyone saw. The impression made on him must have been deeper than gossip had dared speculate. I could think of no one else it might be. It must be her! I could only hope that she would not be at breakfast directly from Thrommel's bedchamber.

Yet, surely, it was not that lady! If Thrommel were to invite her, then her father and elder sister must be included. Courtesy and protocol required it. Besides, if Lady Jolene had arrowed Thrommel's heart, why would he seat her defenseless at a table with twenty sharpened knives? Since she was Count Lorrish's second child, would Thrommel insult the plar and the heiress by neglecting their invitations while granting one to a girl they called, what, "dear little Jolie?"

Actually, Thrommel risked insulting every ranking person at table and their relatives back home with this invitation. Did he believe that the Archbishop of Veluna City would not notice the plar's daughter unaccountably seated one place below him at breakfast? Come to that, why was this lady seated halfway up? The second child of a Velunar count? Unavoidably, this would insult the table's lower portion. Was Thrommel really risking our hopes of the Six Nation Army to talk to a girl?

When I got to that last bit, Ferrica, a terrible, mistaken judgment imposed itself on me. Yes, I thought. Risk an army, risk a war for that girl, if that is what your heart commands. When it comes to that, what else may a man do? People want wars and always get them. Love, though, leaves the unready in losing situations. I suddenly felt like a coward compared to my prince and to all men worthy of a lover's claims, from Troilus down to hopeless Jude Fawley. I will not go so far as to say that I admitted this folly: I allowed myself a moment's confusion.

While engaged by these thoughts I began looking for the castle steward. My idea was to reverse the aberrant decision that, almost certainly, the prince had made himself. The table could be reset without Jolene's place, and the lady prevented from arriving. Actually, she was probably hoping for that relief, which would spare her confrontation with such a street dog as Branditon, the police commandant, whose place was opposite. Thrommel would be enraged if I intervened, but he would hear reason. He might even be brought to see things as I did, as a relief to the lady's sentiments.

But by the time the steward was found, my ideas had drooped to their pliable utmost. I am so tired of war games, Ferrica! You cannot imagine how dreary and incessant they are. Especially this one, which no doubt shall be recorded as a legendary alliance although it is only a new occasion for political squabbling and political gains. Occasionally, I sink to believing that the gods themselves view such aspirations as virtuous.

In this mood, when I found the steward I only inquired whether anyone had been charged with escorting the singular Lady Jolene to a place at table and offered my services to that end. Unnecessary, she assured me. Prince Thrommel had charged one of his captains with that duty. She confirmed what I was by then perfectly convinced of, that Lady Jolene of Samprastadar was the second daughter of Count Lorrish, Plar of Veluna. If it were possible to groan, giggle, and cry all at once, that is what I did.

I returned to the table and exchanged my placement card with that of someone set a little lower, thus sitting nearer the woman in question. I wanted to watch her closely and observe the effect of the prince's conversation on her. I had decided that, whatever weaknesses she exhibited during this exposure to society's unkindest elements, I would run a rapier through the rhetorical spleen of anyone who exploited them. I could well do it, they each one knew.

The seated table waited five minutes for her arrival. This was so obviously arranged that the prince winked at me when I raised my eyebrow. When the girl arrived at last—I say, "girl," because only the prince and I were within a decade of her youth, and most of the assembly were thirty years her senior—and when Captain Hansleath was seating her, I rose from my place and slightly bowed. By this antique custom—which I was alone in observing—I sought to signal to everyone, not least herself, that this lady was not without an ally having a station high enough to be reckoned with yet low enough to redeemably commit a discourtesy. I knew that no one at table (excepting the prince and the young lady) had not fallen previously to my talent for the final tilt in a joust.

It was all worry for nothing. Lady Jolene's etiquette was perfect. No, it was more than perfect. Perfection requires only practice. The lady's manners were purposed, directed, targeted, intelligent. I do not believe she initiated a conversation that hour. But after Prince Thrommel had addressed her, everyone at table was obliged to replicate the courtesy. Watching the nobles and high clerics composing their cranberried expressions into sweetness before addressing "Lady Jolene" cured my ill humor. They may not know who she was, but in following the prince, they must acknowledge her person. Every remark that passed their pursed lips was carefully crafted to sabotage, to deceive her into a reply that could be calculated or smirked at. Her responses remained poignantly meaningless, as placid and fathomless as a lily pond on a quiet night. The prince was more and more in good humor, as his Lady of Surprise vaulted airily over every attempt to pit a weaker wit against hers. That dog Branditon dared not speak; it is dangerous to engage someone who has ten times one's mind.

I found the Lady of Samprastadar more wonderful every minute. Were I not already in love, my heart might have been in jeopardy. Lady Jolene is pretty, Ferrica, and I have always found that to be sufficient in explaining love. But it is hardly adequate to the case in hand. Loving someone takes fifteen minutes to sink in. Thrommel had found the plar's daughter captivating at a glimpse, enthralling at a glance.

He seems aware that he has discovered a treasure, and I hope to hear him try an explanation sometime. He will fail. The lady's figure is good, but neither voluptuous nor refined enough for singling out from a line of personages in one passing, angled look. Her face has expressions that most fail to convey, and her eyes, once you know them, are powers beyond measure. But everything that is excellent about Lady Jolene requires knowing her a little to see, and Thrommel had not had that occasion. Nothing that she was would have singled her out among the ladies lining last night's procession.

Will you believe that, upon occasion, the existence of one person is something magical to another? No, of course you won't. I appreciate your acquaintance, Ferrica, and you lead me again to hope that someone will understand this idea of mine. I am not speaking of love at first sight (although, it is that, too), which is likely a physical attraction that diminishes, often enough, in a short while. The magic I speak of is an impossible insight, a knowledge won at one look that should take days or weeks or months to come as a surprise; that you love the other, that your personality has bent to theirs, that you may be absent from them only to discover that you never were. I am half persuaded that your Lady Jolene is, to Thrommel, a magic girl. She does not and probably cannot deceive him in this. He knows her in a way that transgresses the rules of acquaintance and defies the pitfalls of infatuation.

As for the lady, she is intelligent and kind enough to do his mind and feelings no reduction. Whether there is in her something reciprocal to what has befallen him, I dare not say. My first duty is to deter Thrommel from such stray thoughts. But I have seen Jolene, spoken with her a little, and I cannot say that I will acquit my duty too well. In fact, I have already encouraged him the other way.

Clever Ferrica, I will tell you something that I do not want you to include in your diary. Although I denied it, there was one brief conversation that Lady Jolene initiated at breakfast. When the guests had momentarily left her alone, she raised her eyes and addressed me as "Sir Edmore," making a polite inquiry about me.

"Lady, do you know me?"

"I know that you are kind where it matters and deserve more than you get in that way."

I stared at her. I hope I did not fall into a frown. Was she playing me? Was she sincere? I do not think that, in my entire life, anyone had silenced me before by an introduction. This lady, this incredible girl, had put me in a muddle that I could not define and could not escape.

"My Lady," I replied, with a noncommittal nod.

"No," she said, "you must call me Jolene."

My mind flashed in recognition of the truth. None of this was by accident. The prince had surely met this lady last night and seen that there was no reason to shelter her from enemies. Let her draw her sword, and she will slay what comes her way. I cannot tell whether I have been slain or counted a friend, but there will be time to find out. Probably, Thrommel had told her about me, and if she will favor the prince, then her favor toward me may be presumed.

I leaned back into my chair, assuming a relaxed posture. I glanced left and right to see who was watching, and satisfied that there were enough to commence rumor and scandal, I returned to her an absurdly broad smile.

"Oh, yes. And I would never forgive you if you named me anything but Ed." Until that moment, only the prince and my family had ever called me by that name. But you see, sweet Ferrica, that is the whole question. That is essentially the problem of Jolene. You see her, know her a little, and you either believe, or you don't. I am more than halfway to believing.

In confidence,

You Know Who

⚜

(Three weeks later.)

Ferrica,

We march before dawn, going east to Hommlet. Thrommel has chosen Greenway Valley, which terminates in a narrow pass the enemy will be watching. He wants to gain a position to the north that is favorable.

I accompany him as a political aide or spy. Our generals each have ambitions to be checked, so, I watch for self-aggrandizing tricks. If everyone behaves, I have nothing to do.

Dearest Ferrica—I address you by the superlative endearment consciously—you must not worry. On the morning of a war, friends become dearer and remain so. Think on that, not on worse things.

You are never dismayed but too often expect the worst. Thrommel tells me that your lady, though she acts like a lion, hides a mouse inside. Our war is an unworthy trap set for her and the prince, so, if the mouse runs, go with her; find a place to hide; alcohol works a treat for me.

Wait for our return.

Your dearest Wunsay.▽Aposnos’ stay at Castle Estival had been awkward in the beginning. She had accompanied the plar, Count Lorrish, Jolene’s father, on assignment; pretend to be his mistress to gain insight into the negotiations by gossiping with servants and staff. It was a big ask of a provincial farmer's daughter confounded by the role and unused to the artifices of court. But Ferrica had been Jolene’s childhood friend and was loyal to the politics of the Lorrish family. The count trusted her. Too modest for the play, Aposnos’ best success (although a noble) was Wunsay, who gossiped with her freely while convinced she was a double agent. His reputation as a vindictive courtier gave her good reason to fear the consequences of this arrangement, but by the time the truth came out, they were genuine friends. (Eds)

⚜

Leen woke me two hours before dawn. What? I asked. Her urgency was not a proper answer. We dressed quickly and basically—our hair stayed uncombed. We walked out the castle gate to the road the soldiers would take from their camp. It was nearly midsummer, but the atmosphere was damp and cold. We held burning torches to enlighten our faces and watched our wild hair grow nested with dew. When Prince Thrommel saw us, he halted the marching column, galloped to us, dismounted, and gave my Leen a long, sweet, declarative kiss. "Huzzah! Huzzah!" shouted the troops, brandishing their halberds and swords in the moonlight.

Everyone gained motive for the fight. Somehow, these two lovers always know what to do.

⚜

Thrommel is not the soldier to marshal his troops from the rear. He stays near the front, riding into the greatest confusion and standing his horse on the highest ground to sort it out. He grieves for the soldiers who have died protecting him that way. "Were I not a prince," he says, "a hundred others could do better."

I put this to Captain Hansleath, expecting him to exclaim the unique miraculousness of Marshal Thrommel. But he said, with the honesty of someone who could be dead in two weeks and is a commoner speaking to one, that "the prince knows the worth of his troops. We die for him because princes always lead, and this one, at least, fights as well as we. When he gives an order, we can see its logic or, at least, soon catch up to it. That is our motivation."

Jolene will not go see Thrommel fight the Horde of Elemental Evil. "I will not watch him die from too far away to be at his side." If he falls she hopes they might get the body home—but monsters are not nice with bodies.

Jolene cries too often. "Ferrica," she said, "I'm afraid I love him very much." That was the first time she confessed it to me. She had known him a month! Others have done more in less time, but Thrommel and Jolene have not been conventionally in love. They were instantly together, one locket discovering double miniatures within. Both know it is an inauspicious match, because Jolene's standing as the plar's second daughter gains Thrommel nothing but trouble. Doubting it would be permissable to love her, he had waited, she admitted, to kiss her the first time on the evening before he led the army away. It was strange that the first kiss should seem sad. Then, he told her that he loved her.

He said, "I have no right to say it. I should wait for a safe return. But I could not say goodbye without confessing what you already know. How can saying one plus one is two do any harm? If I didn't say it, you might think I'm too stupid to add it up."

I waited awhile for her to tell me that she, too, had confessed. She didn't, and I have heard her regret his soldiering before. Had she kept a tether to her heart until this war should be over? She had kissed him for the second time the next morning before dawn, in front of ten thousand soldiers. Had that been a panicked confession of what had not been said and an admission that love is mortal, that it often dies unspoken?

"Yes, Rica, my angel," she said, with that part of her she calls the mouse. Then, glancing out our tower window looking east, "It was something very like that."

⚜

Impossible! Gods, no! Edmore himself comes with news. He rides hard into the castle and directly to our tower door, stopping for no one, up two flights two steps at a time by my counting. At the chamber door he stops. Stops. Waits. We can hear his breathing become slow, quiet, until we hear it no more. Jolene, her father, the servants, and I are waiting. Does he not know we wait? He has brought news personally and with dispatch—apparently determined that we should hear it from no other source—and now hesitates to tell us what he is determined to say. Every expression in the room has sunk to an identical recognition: the news will be bad. It will be terrible! Only Jolene looks differently from us; she looks already dead.

The knock comes at last. The doorman is lucky; courtesy dictates that he lower his eyes when he admits Edmore to our rooms. The rest of us face him in tears. The plar steps forward and Edmore bows. "For the sake of the gods, Wunsay, have you nothing more to show than a display of courtesy!" The count moved to take the arm of his second daughter, and I feel keenly that that was where I ought to be. But protocol insists.

Edmore looked up and took things in. "My goodness, such faces! Apologies. The prince is safe and sound. All the news is good. I suspect you will not believe how good it is. Anyone with a friend in the army should have every hope. The Horde has been irrevocably routed, and our losses are a tenth of our least fears. Everyone should hope."

Jolene was in her father's and her sister's arms, hysterical with relief. The servants were hugging each other. I was alone, and no one was left but Edmore.

"Oh, hoh!" said Thrommel's perpetually jilted lover, accepting my arms around him and holding them there. "This is what I came for." I burst into tears that fell on the arms that held me.

I had always thought that "safe and sound" was a redundant phrase saying the same thing twice, like "hale and hardy." It is not so. Hearing Edmore say it made this immediately clear. Thrommel is safe, and he is sound; two different, wonderful things. I ran to Leen to share this insight. "Safe AND sound, Jolene." We sang it together: "Safe and sound! Safe and sound!"

When emotions had subsided to within grasp of normalcy, the servants brought tea. Wunsay had barely eaten that day and had need for the time being to avoid any company beyond our rooms. He must stay with us! The military messenger dispatched with news of the battle, whom Edmore had ordered to start no sooner than twelve hours later, would deliver Thrommel's official report. What Wunsay had to say was for friends.

And lover.

⚜

I remember Edmore's description of the battle, the dangerous march through Greenway Valley, the perilous path through Gnarley Forest, and the final advance on the High Road to arrive at the awful Temple of Elemental Evil. But this is not a war story. Thrommel's victory was owed to a simple stratagem; arriving at the deserted village of Nulb he divided his army, sending more than half directly at the temple and the remainder two miles farther east behind a rocky escarpment that extended along Imeryd's Run into the Fens of Tor that have given the battle its name (Tor Fens). The Horde thought to trap the advancing commensurate army against the confluence of the rocks, the river, and the walls of the fortified temple. But one mile to the north the escarpment had hidden Thrommel's foot soldiers, which then crossed the river on rafts that they had carried disassembled. Their attack came from behind and by surprise in a coordinated maneuver that forced the fleeing monsters to run a deadly gauntlet to the east, where the survivors were chased into Emridy's Run to drown or be slaughtered.

Tor Fens was the most important and thorough military victory since the Hateful Wars, and it made Prince Thrommel a hero. The strategem was owed to his characteristic, even pedestrian ingenuity: when the threat of the Horde had caused the villagers in Nulb to flee their homes, Thrommel had thought to consult them on the local terrain.

The prince had the wind in his sails; the public was calling him a hero; a hero may have what he wants; this one wanted to marry Lady Jolene of Samprastadar, the Plar of Veluna's second daughter.

⚜

Something was pelting our window. The first hit, you do not hear. The second, awakens you. The third, you think you won't get up. The fourth, you do.

"Come down, farmer girl."

"Oh, thank gods. It's for you."

"Go back to sleep, Leen. I must go and see what's wrong with him."

"You know what's wrong, Rica. But you must go. There are things I cannot do."

"Don't sound regretful. It is what it is. You should be happy all the time, and it annoys me that you aren't."

"I always knew that I was an annoyance. Don't stay out till dawn. People won't be happy."

"People aren't happy, Leen. Only you are."

"Hmmmph."

⚜

After Tor Fens, Castle Estival should have emptied. The treaty was signed, the battle was won, and the princes and clerics should have departed to toast the vintage of political victory or bemoan the vinegar of defeat. The gnomes, dwarves, and elves did go, but the humans would not leave before Jolene of Samprastadar did.

It was obvious that Thrommel would marry her. The only hope, for those holding out, was that a consideration of the political consequences would cause Thrommel to back out. The couple's enemies believed that Jolene had come to Castle Estival at her father's behest on purpose to marry the Prince Regent and Marshal. That was untrue. Although the plar was an intimidating political agent and his second daughter was his choicest asset, it was not because she would catch the prince's fancy.

Jolene of Samprastadar had been raised not to be a dowry but to dismantle the theocracy of Veluna and restore its government to secular form. As a child of eight years, she had dazzled from among the children of the Velunar nobility that were her peers. She led them, invented their games, harmonized their friendships, soothed their disagreements, and thought circles around them. The plar, realizing a big gun had been born to his house, did what he could. He sent this daughter to a place of his devising to train a political mastermind, a weapon to deploy when he chose. Jolene was his second child and not entitled to inherit, but her father carved from Lorrish County a holding for her in the upper Capstor River valley, twenty-five miles north of Lorrish Town, and he called it Samprastadar. The income from the property was modest, but it was hers to use for any reason.

For this young woman the Six Nation Treaty was intended as an introduction, an opportunity to observe and be seen at political negotiations for the first time. Stay modest and quiet. Don't be noticed. Jolene was trained for it. But the plar had not anticipated that, despite everything, she was Jolene, and standing in a ceremonial line where the Prince of Furyondy could see her was a trigger that fired everything.

The invitation the plar received that night to a late supper with Prince Thrommel included also his eldest daughter, Sulda, heir to Lorrish County, and Lady Jolene of Samprastadar. The prince had learned the name of the plar's younger daughter and invited her to supper. For ten minutes, Lorrish was perplexed. The prince's attraction to Jolene was undoubtedly good news, but it could easily go wrong. He resolved that only one person was qualified to deal with these intricacies, and that was the woman in question, Jolene. He informed the prince half-way through the evening that he and his eldest must excuse themselves, as they had an early engagement tomorrow. Jolene did not come home for three hours, at two a.m., the last decent hour.

Her father did not care about decency but cared very much to learn that the prince did. He first enquired after, and then insisted on, knowing the details of their conversation, but his daughter was too well trained to be bullied by him. She would not tell him what had been discussed. The plar grew fierce with anger, but the ferocity was simulated; his talent was calculation, and if Jolene would not betray the prince, then the two were already together. Every further calculation was premised on the theorem.

⚜

"I am happy for them, Ferrie." He called me "Ferrie" now, because he needed an endearment and "Rica" had been taken by Jolene. "I know how happy I would have been if he had loved me."

He was drunk. Not enough to miss my window with his pebbles, but he held a bottle and had been nursing it since.

"You should leave here, Ed, and come to Samprastadar with me. My father owns a cottage where you can stay. You could see me every day, and not see them."

"That would be abandoning Thrommel in his need. I won't do it. They must marry. And I don't want you to call me 'Ed.' I want 'Eddie.' No one calls me that, especially not them."

"Ed . . ."

"Eddie."

"Whichever, you're not making sense. The prince has lots of counselors. And from where I sit, you're killing yourself. You should quit it."

He started to cry. Soon he was beyond it and on to sobbing. Nothing stops such tears; I was beaten. Edmore Wunsay's grief, which had been preparing for seven or eight years, was now something only time could heal. Time, and distance. I tried again.

"We could leave before dawn. Jolene will kiss you goodbye. Not Thrommel, though. I won't allow it."

"I don't want to go, Ferrie. I want to be privy counselor. What am I, if not that?"

"My friend, Ed."

"I said, Eddie."

"You're stupid. You've never seen Samprastadar. There are lots of places you haven't seen. We should go there."

"Where? Lots of places?"

"Yes."

"Ferrie, I'm in love with you. Platonically, you know; which means not at all, really. I'm very sorry, because I know I should be. I've always thought so." He was talking nonsense.

"I used to be afraid of you, Ed. Most people are. You shouldn't be privy counselor if it makes you ridiculous."

"Ed? What's wrong with Eddie?"

"Ed, come with me to Samprastadar. You're bleeding, and I have bandages there."

"If I don't, will you stay? You are a bandage, and you know it. I want to kick the canon out of Veluna. I'm ridiculous and want to do it."

"Well, that bit's actually not so bad."

"So, will you?"

"Gods, you are drunk. No, Sir Edmore. I'm going to abandon you in your need."

"Sir Edmore? I should quit before I'm Honorable."

"Nothing could make you honorable."

"At least I've got that."

⚜

My father loves trips, and I have seen the whole region. Samprastadar is typical of the northern Lorrish Valley, quiet and bucolic in ways that many places duplicate. And if you want landscapes that are invariably gentle and agrarian, then I may recommend it. The peak of civilization, my father says, is not an urban accomplishment or the verge of a wilderness but a countryside of cultivated meadows and, where the land is fit for trees but too stony or wet for cultivation, interspered woods. Samprastadar is about equally accommodating to meadow and stand. In all seasons, it has charms. In summer, it is a cure for sickness and moral woe.

Our cottage, Binsvale, is well situated a half mile from our farm, hidden in a wood, and open to the southeast from whence it gathers the sun. There we put Edmore and his servant, Rie Flandspout, whom, he said, "Could do everything and cook a little too. Soup, you know, he's very good at." Dear Eddie! I am so glad you are here.

My father had nothing in common with him but liked him immediately. Both found the other's life amazing. Life at court—which my father despised—was "amazing" when it included Edmore Wunsay. And farm life, which Eddie had never known except as told by a steward, was "amazing" when my father explained its possibility. Edmore dined with us each evening; each night he looked a little more like someone I suspected but had not known—a happy Ed Wunsay. During the days, he sat in the shade and walked the rural lanes. Sometimes, I went with him.

He had come to Samprastadar less than half by choice. Prince Thrommel, after defeating the Horde, had spent a further week in camp with the Six Nation Army. The reason, I could surmise, was partly to assess the defenses of the Horde's remnant inside the temple fortress. He would not leave without assurance that eradicating the monsters would be a straightforward siege deferrable to his generals. And although, this time, the enemy was few, Thrommel never left a battlefield before his dead had been buried and he could adequately assess their number. A fortnight after Wunsay had brought the news of Tor Fens, Thrommel returned to Castle Estival.

He sent word for Jolene from two miles out and waited for her. Without congratulating him, she said, "I'm sorry for all of it!" He kissed her, their third kiss. What else was there to say?

"Joey, you draw this from me now. It was supposed to be later and more romantic. But I can think of nothing else." He claimed the best ring from his grimy hands and offered it to her. "You are too excellent. Marry me despite it?" His face was upturned as he knelt, and tears were gathered in its crevices.

Jolene nearly collapsed. Slipping her finger through the ring where he held it, she said, "I think, my heart, that I already have."

⚜
