Readers, it was a bit unnerving to read how easily Wilna Dastabrail had understood my mood—"desperate," "worry-ragged." As you are increasingly aware, the circumstances of writing this autograph are unpleasant, even ominous. A darkness is at its margins that will not be enlightened; a monstrous intent touches every page. Even Dastagirl had edged on a threat of violence.

Of course, since these pages will be read by a number of people that would just about comprise a small seminar at an obscure college, I run no risk of fouling D-girl's injunction against publicity and controversy. I am only sorry to hear that Edmore Wunsay, who once took on the world, now needs castle walls to shelter from it. You may call that weakness. No doubt, he is vulnerable. But hearts are vulnerable things; and perhaps he retains his, despite the efforts of many. I am almost able to say the same.

After Thrommel's disappearance—no one wants to call it his demise—the world got on as it could, as my history must too. Yet, in many ways, you, my companions in the picaresque, never got to see Thrommel Ⅳ in a life-sized portrait. Tor Fens, yes, his universally acclaimed, crowning victory. But battles depend on circumstance at least as much as on planning. Thrommel wrote treatises about that, which was why he believed that, having communicated his plans to his generals, he was of no more use tactically behind the lines. He was needed where his influence could be instant, at the place where the battle was floundering.

In battle, he said—especially in times of great danger—he would become calm, like the ocean in a hurricane when a diver goes deeper and under. "Actually, I don't think I'm quite right in the head that way. I need people to tell me when running is a good idea. I had a soldier take an arrow through the eye for me. She was grabbing my horse's reins and saying, 'Prince, we need to go.' That, you see, is hellishly unnatural because I'm sure that the archer had aimed at me.

"If my calm comes from the heavens, then it must come from Hextor, who saves only those who will bring more death. Always, I seek to salvage a fight and ask my soldiers to die for it. My father cannot understand why I do not pray to Heironeous. Isn't it obvious? A lost battle always seems to me to have a last hope of reorganization and salvation, a final chance to force it into the history books. But if your soldiers no longer see it, you must yield to the larger wisdom. Else you rally them to death for a victory only you ever saw."

If there was a war, Thrommel knew that, as a prince, he had already failed. He wanted not the power that he had—to salvage a desperate situation in battle—but to keep people safe from such desperation. Perhaps that's why he needed Jolene and Wunsay. Thrommel was an intelligent man, near enough to Jolene's equal so that no one would notice ordinarily. But he was not quick; he pondered and made sure. If Jolene and Wunsay—the brilliant ones—could know his objectives, they could keep him from wars. It was Thrommel's generosity—more than any other, that word describes him—that made him want to rid the world of its need for his greatest talent.

He was King Belvor Ⅳ's only child. It was as if the gods had said, you have this golden one, and you shall have no other. When Thrommel vanished, it was not a only a prince, an only son, a provost, and a marshal that was gone; it was all hope in those few gods that believed humanity could make it.

Thrommel’s death and the Unified Kingdom’s failure reduced the central Flanaess to so much mistrust and misgiving that, when the Horned Society conquered the Shield Lands in 579cy, Furyondy and Dyvers did nothing at all. Four years later, when Iuz invaded in turn, the Shield Knight Commander, Earl Holmer, distrusted King Belvor so extremely that he chose to defend, his capital, Critwall, with only his knights rather than let Furyondian soldiers in the gates to assist. That fabulous error made the looming invasion of Furyondy inevitable: the Greyhawk Wars had begun.

Another monstrous threat existed south of Furyondy, where the memory of the Elemental Evil still horrified Verbobonc. While the Treaty of Reymend was in negotiation, only months after Thrommel’s victory at Tor Fens, rumors that the demon queen Zuggtmoy haunted the black temple’s depths were already rescinding Verbobonc’s hopes of security and peace. The prescience of those rumors was proved by the reappearance of the Evil in 579cy, and after that, the viscount’s decision to watch the fell temple from Homlett Castle built purposefully nearby led him to withdraw military patrols from Gnarley Forest and the Kron Hills, leaving the elves and gnomes unprotected in those places. His proclamation that “all enemies of the viscounty, both imaginable and otherwise” had then been eliminated was greeted skeptically by Verboboncans, who could find no security either in allying with Furyondy and Veluna because lingering doubts about the perpetrators of Prince Thrommel's disappearance meant that any alliance with one nation risked provoking the other.

Yet less than a decade earlier there had been hope. The Treaty of Reymend had awaited only the Canon of Veluna’s signature to annul the Archclericy completely; the Velunar theocrats would be restored to their spiritual calling, the Celestial Order of the Moons would govern Veluna in the name of Furyondy’s secular king, and the Unified Kingdom, not Veluna, would assist Verbobonc in defense against the border monsters. But the kingdom had failed; Prince Thrommel was presumably killed, the Celestial Order was subject again to the canon’s authority, and there was no hope of security in the forests and hills.

These are the inconvenient truths that historians methodically fail to recognize when they speak of Belvor and Hazen as friends and allies against Iuz, of the viscount of Verbobonc as a “willing vassal” of the canon, and of Veluna and Furyondy as beacons and bastions of hope and goodness against darkness and danger. None of it is true.

The truth is different. The Treaty of Reymend’s abrogation deprived the central Flanaess of a future security like none that had reigned since the imperial viceroyalty. Historians claim that the Kingdom of Furyondy's rebellion in 254cy had restored peace and decency to decadent Ahlissa, but had it? The concave illusion showed us the troubles that roiled the Flanaess for two centuries following the rebellion’s beginning. Never in that time was peace known. And, lo! I remind you, my scholars on watch against credulity, that although the illusion was mine, the history was taken from Histoire, C’estclos’ epochal study of commerce and war, not peace.

What else would it be? In all that time no allies were joined in the cause of peace and no grant of independence was freely made. The upshot of the independence movement was that individual nations took advantage of it; whether at the behest of monarchs, princes, priests, or merchants hardly signified because all were set free. The liberated did not question freedom’s purposes because they were under the constriction of a progressive empire and equated further progress with greater independence.

What, actually, was the freedom they sought? Furyondy tested its bid for freedom by withholding the Ahlissan tithe. The tithe was a due tax, so, refusing to pay it was essentially a tea party revolt, claiming the privilege of the tithe for themselves. The Furyondian revolutionaries preached freedom to the people but said not on whose terms, while they thought, “Why not mine?"

They wanted more and more. "A man's reach must ever exceed his grasp, or what’s a heaven for?" they asked. It was a rhetorical question, but we may ask it for real: Is heaven for attaining? May it be apprised of its rights? Is everything subject to someone's claim? A strange gospel for people that also said freedom is divine, and heaven, for the gods.

(From among the wondering students, a hand is timidly raised)

Excuse me, Professor?

(Returning to oerth)

Yes?

You said before that the Shield Knight Commander’s poor decision to defend Critwall alone against Iuz made the invasion of Furyondy inevitable and began the Greyhawk Wars. If you could skip over freedom and return to that idea it would be OK by me, because that’s where Iuz and Doraka’a will come in, and our adventure will come after that.

As you wish; although—I would ask you, before we return to history and leave off romance, to rehearse where the death of Prince Thrommel left us in 570cy?

Well, consulting my notes, Prince Thrommel was gone, the Unified Kingdom was abrogated, Veluna was nearly beheaded, the six nations didn’t trust one another, there were monsters everywhere, and Iuz was observing it all, I think.

Yes, precisely. I may refine things a bit. I have maintained that the Flanaess was a monstrous continent conquered in a prophesied quest for Oeridian glory; that the Vale of Luna was at that time refashioned into an Oeridian Raoan land; that the Raoan Imperial Church was prepared in anticipation of forming a theocracy; that the High Canon of Rao broke troth with the prince of Veluna (that was the king of Furyondy) by declaring independence for the archclericy; that a series of other independence declarations by former vassals followed, leading to violence across the Flanaess; that the king of Furyondy cooperated with Veulna’s conquest and occupation by Keoland until the occupying kingdom's expansionism threatened Furyondy too; that liberating Veluna brought a tenuous attempt to erase the archclericy (ecrasez l'infame is the thunderous phrase in ◒Histoire◓) and restore a secular national government such as Voll had long known; that the archclericy survived this trial; and that, again in C'estclose's words, “the Velunar College of Bishops convened in Mitrik to decide whether to break from the kingdom” of Furyondy for a second time, in 446cy. My illusion celebrated the archclericy's reformation with a fireworks finale that rose high into the concavity’s sky.

I ask you to consider, if the Archclericy of Veluna had been so near to a new subjugation to Furyondy that it needed to declare its independence once more, how close to subjugation had it been?

Very?

Of the two independence declarations, in 254- and 446cy,/span>. which is more directly related to modern Veluna and the Greyhawk Wars?

The second one?

Why?

Because it’s in between.

Sweet gods in heavens, yes, it is in between. And though you may think I am condescending, I remind you that historians persistently miss the fact. Why is 254cy so emphasized, when it was nearly cast into oblivion more than one hundred fifty years ago? The question closely relates to other points that I dispute. Why is the Canon of Veluna’s equivalence to the High Canon of Rao so essential? Why was the Crook of Rao lost, found, and placed in the canon’s hands? Why is Luna mechanical in Word of Incarnum? The only answer is that the Canon of Veluna’s authority must be perceivably divine and eternal. The necessity of it gets very near to the heart of the matter.

It is not obvious that something must be eternal to be divine. A blessing given today was not apparent yesterday but is divine all the same. The appearance of divinity is what’s necessary, and that is the problem.

It is very difficult to find a time when the canon appears to be a blessing. Whenever you inquire about it, you are referred to another time until you confront eternity. Apart from eternity, the canon’s holiness appears somewhat dubious. Nothing in the past as I’ve written it recommends his holiness, so, his sanctity and, in reality, his relevance to us must date to the history that we recommence in our next scenario. There he will appear for the first time as what he claims to have always been: a saint, a sovereign, a monarch, a theocrat.

I interrupted the history of his life and works to tell the romance of Mistress and Prince for this reason: so you may see how it will end. No one can write about history without a knowledge of where it is going, which is why the history of a recent time will be preliminary. But you, my allotted prisoners paroled by a dark fate, know in advance that Edmore Wunsay’s romance ends badly and is historiographically reliable. I tell you, too, that things will get worse. Prince Thrommel’s disappearance in 570cy coincided with Iuz’s escape from a demiplane under Castle Greyhawk, where he had been imprisoned since 505cy. Having his freedom, he hated Greyhawk and its friends. When he saw them frightened by monsters and ineffective against the puny Hierarchs of the Horned Society, it gave him ideas. Did he not have, if he could command them, the Horned Society’s army of discontented hobgoblins at hand? He did. This was his time.

The dismay of good folk following the prince’s disappearance would have seemed to Iuz, a god they had dared imprison and then failed to contain, much like the eternal goading by good folk of vanquished evil everywhere, like our disparagement the “red glowing eyes of the Pomarj that had look back to their ‘birthright’ and sought to reclaim it.” Directed at the demigod, we may as well have boasted:

To the Imp Lord Iuz.

In the Enfeebled Palace of Insanity Where He Squats over Sewers and Shit-gutters Wretchedly Shovelled in Hell.

In the Vaporous Stink and Cesspool's Belch of his Capital, Doraka’a.

In the Deranged Empire of the Identical Demented Enemy Doomed to Die Spitting Bile from the Wounds the Righteous Shall Visit upon His Deformities Moral and Physical.

Dear Sir, come and get us.

So, he did.

§

SCENARIO FIVE—VELUNA AND FURYONDY

§

Chapter 21: Return to the Short War

It was appropriate to close the previous scenario with a daring invitation to a demonic demigod whose power is beyond reckoning. Literary tradition commends ending an installment of fiction on a point of great expectation: always leave them wanting more. The device has been characteristic of serialized fiction from The Pickwick Papers to Game of Thrones and, when wrought to its tautist twist, is acclaimed a “cliffhanger.” But every tradition—like every person—forgets more than it remembers, and today few fans of fiction know that there was an original cliffhanger, in Victorian England, 1873, when an overly chivalrous Knight was left to dangle from a precipice for a month while awaiting his next installment. And I admit to you, my minute enrollment of tutorial interests, how keenly I regret that I am writing an historical monongraph and not a novel or—wishful bliss!—a gothic romance. Were I in your place, my life commandeered by a sinister agent relentlessly driving me to the Land of Iuz, I would not want (while on my way) to read the history of a canon I had never heard of. No. I would want star-crossed lovers separated by horrors and left to find their way in the darkness. I mean, right?

Another literary device is to begin in the middle of a story at a point of high expectation and delay the reader’s gratification by going back to the beginning to arrive, once again, before the end, at the middle. This is commencing “in medias res.” Unfortunately, my Interregnum on the mistress and prince began not in the middle and went to the beginning but started near the end and told you almost all of it, while the cliffhanger where I stuck you some time ago on a high stone needle—fire in front of (and below) you, hellfire behind you—has left you hanging for so long that I had to remind you where you are.

Oh! criminal negligence! Literary incompetence!

But, dear readers, I did it for you. I swear. I was torn between my role as your adventuring companion and my obligations as an historian under infernal contract. Your fate in Doraka’a depends, somehow, on fulfilling its terms and conditions. For one thing, I a to tell you the truth as I perceive it without reservation or mercy. But I felt (every day) how much you needed relief from the tedium and danger of your journey! All the way up the Ritensa River you walked only to reach the breadthless darkness of Fellreev Forest with nothing but a few goblins to kill along the way. Adventuring has often been said to be monotony interspersed with dicey encounters, and although you have survived them all, so far, the odds get longer with every step you take toward Doraka’a. And as for your mortal combats, I cannot help you because I am not there.

Every time this autograph opens to you by a magic of its own I fear that, this time, one of you will be missing from its pages. All my waking nightmares—I never weary, you will literally remember, and need no sleep—are haunted by the thought that you may die in a state of boredom! Can I do nothing? May I not, at least, entertain you? I am sure I could. Were I allowed to write like a romancer, I would take you briskly to my story’s hideous nadir: where Hazen triumphs over Iuz to attain world domination in the name of the holy trinity of Reason, Peace, and Serenity. I would then narrate the rest of your adventure, where you do your best to redeem the world and, just when you are about to fail, suceed! But—how great is my dismay!—my contract stipulates I am to write my history as concisely as possible. No romance for you, my friends.

But something occurred to me. Is it really necessary to instruct you according to the glum instrument of scholarship alone? Surely historical concision may coexist with adventure, love, and romance. I'm sure of it! And though this was a novel idea, it was liberating too. Novels, like histories, have limitations of genre. How much better it would be to cross fiction with historiography! That would be something new. I do not mean an historical novel to flirt with readers by using historical pick-up lines. Not like narrative histories, either, to subsume the past under fictional anachronisms. No, not like that.

But imagine: a novel whose narrator is a fantastical historian writing a fantastical history that the characters must read while the historian writes it! Now that would be dramedy. I only regret that I did not think of it sooner, before so much of the monograph was already done.

Still, you must not despise a late hour because it is not the whole day. Accordingly, I decided to bring the Unified Kingdom and the four romantics from near the end of our history to the middle before returning you to the past: in media res double-twisted with a reverse cliffhanger. In other words, my Interrgnum was meant for you, dear readers, by way of encouragement. Keep going! You’ll make it!

After all, Mistress and Prince is alike a romance and an historiogrphical resource. Wilna “Dastagirl” Pummenford has proved it. Too, it was already written by a writer better than me. A win for you, a win for me, a win for romance, a win for verbal economy; in general, a universal win.

Indeed, Mistress and Prince is near the heart of everything. If what you, my peripatetic fair, are now doing—the adventure you are on—is not a romance, I do not know what one is. And it occurs to me that, since you are almost illiterate, you may not know either. So, let me tell you.

Your adventure is romantic. It is a quixotic quest: it is not quite real, serves a noble and improbable cause, disregards causality, and will have an impossible ending where anything may happen, whether or not anything does.

Therefore, I recommence our story at the cliff it hangs on. The illusory concavity's hellfires are metaphorically your way to Doraka'a; the stone needle that maroons you is metaphorically the false security that it gave while you watched the concavity burning below. We have only to leap from the needle (one of us has done it before) into the unfastidious jaws of Iuz to land where the illusion re-situates us: at the magnificent (although ignited) Eademer Battistero, bursting like fireworks over the moon-bright city of Mitrik, where the College of Bishops is voting to break from the Kingdom of Furyondy nearly two hundred years after that had been done once before to, appartently, no lasting effect.

Why was it necessary for the bishops to separate from Furyondy again? Why, this time, the bishops, not the canon?

§

~The canonical apotheosis

In 438cy, after eighty-six years of military occupation, liberation from Keoland came to Veluna but did not restore the archclericy immediately. In the interum, a return to secular government was favored by Furyondy, the liberator, whose victorious armies had been formed into a cauldron "keeping Veluna safe" from its enemy by commanding strategic locations in the Fals Gap, the Velverdyva River basin, the Lortmil Mountains, and the Viscounty of Verbobonc. All of these were occupied by the King of Furyondy's men.

The ensuing contest between king and canon over the political future of Veluna lasted for eight years, until a conclave of Raoan bishops gathered in the Eademer Battistero to warn Veluna that she was choosing "apostasy” in her fling with secular government. The Velunar people were abandoning their god. The accusation was the last resort of the theocrats, whose political and spiritual powers had been spent by eighty years of national calamity. But the popularity of the bishops in contrast was high, especially in the south, and almost no one wanted to see the canon humiliated irredeemably. Chastened, the folk of the vale repented from secularism. But the Eademer Concordat, published by the bishops, did not return power to the archclericy as it had been. Public discontent with theocracy was rife. The people's love for the Raoan church and their grievances against the archclericy were a crucible in which a new archclericy would be formed at the behest of the bishops. The Raoan theocracy's restoration was equally its reformation.

The preparations for this historical crucible were depicted in my concave illusion. In 254cy, Veluna’s double-faced declaration of sovereignty—first turned toward Rauxes, then toward Dyvers—was never formally acknowledged by any other nation: not by the Great Kingdom, by Furyondy, by any of the other former vassal states, or even (except begrudgingly) by the archclericy’s own aristocratic Celestial Order of the Moons. Any acknowledgement of Veluna’s independence would have jeopardized the feudal trade routes between Furyondy and the Great Kingdom that every nation depended on; an economic jeopardy that took two centuries of wars and trade wars to resolve, until Furyondy’s liberation of Veluna ended the ambitions of both the Great Kingdom and Keoland in the central Flanaess.

Despite all this trouble, the timing of Veluna’s bid for sovereignty in 254cy had had been remarkably serendipitous in some ways. The Great Kingdom’s empire, against all expectations, was discovered to be politically unstable and militarily incapable of suppressing rebelion. Yet the cleanliness of the many rebellions that followed must not be overstated. The king of Furyondy had intended to be the prince of Veluna, and the consequence of that failure was fifty years of trade war between two imperfectly sovereign nations. Their troubles spilled over into other bids for independence by nations nearer Rauxes and the heartlands of Ahlissa that, in Keoland, prompted territorial ambitions north of the Lortmil Mountains

When Furyondy afforded its supposed ally, Veluna, no support or protection against it, Keoland settled in to occupy half the archclericy. Veluna's discontent with being anyone's vassal had surprisingly resulted in temporary sovereignty for the archclericy but also in instability there and throughout much of the continent.

The subsequent eight decades of occupation were enough for political struggles that were rending the Great Kingdom to stablize and for newly independent nations to come to terms. During those decades, Furyondy offered no fight against Keoland but worked with it as a trading partner. The posibility that trade might lead to their alliance forced other governments to settle scores and make peaceful arrangements. But Keolands attempt at militarily swallowing the whole of Veluna threatened an advance on Furyondy’s border. Furyondy committed to driving Keoland out and, surprisingly, managed it easily in the Short War (436-438cy).

Some historians suspect that the canon had had an influence on the king's decision, but their suspicion is surely delusional:

In 436cy, Keoland publicly threatened to annex the whole of Veluna. Whether the king of Furyondy decided to act due to agents dispatched by the canon or because the looming threat of Keoland had simply become too large to ignore, act he did.

Aside from informing the king when the looming threat became imminent, however, the canon had nothing to offer except bribes and other petty inducements; eighty years of continuous trade with the occupying forces absolutely prove it, and in fact, the king's reasons for liberating Veluna are inducible from the course of further events. To ensure independence for Veluna,

Bissel was conquered by the forces of Furyondy in 438cy, when the Furyondians and their armies advanced south to nearly the city of Hookhill, in Gran March. The throne in Chendl retained the office of Bissel's margrave but replaced the ruling family with nobles sympathetic to the affairs of the east. Distance from the Furyondian capital left Bissel practically independent, however, and in 477cy King Hugh ⅢI declared Bissel a "March Palatine" owing fealty to Veluna.

The palatine marquis was a ruler under the Furyondian king with the exercise of royal powers within the mark, so, the fealty pledged to Veluna is an extra obligation. It amounts to power sharing, the palatine marquis owing fealty to Veluna's canon while ruling the mark on authority from Furyondy's king. Milary forces from Furyondy and Veluna alike continued to occupy Bissel's capital, Thornward, until long after 477cy because of the continual threat of invasion by Ket from the west. The power-share shows that the cooperation and the supposed alliance of Furyondy and Veluna were enforced as well as trusted.

In the view of the commensurate folk of the Lortmil Mountains, the Kron Hills, and the Gnarley forest, Furyondy’s military presence offered protection not only against Keoland but against the monsters that constantly threatened the environs, a threat that became acute when Keoland retreated from those places. After the Short War, the viscount of Verbobonc went so far as to request that Furyondian soldiers be permanently stationed in the viscounty. Verbobonc had been a vassal to Voll (later, Veluna) ever since the Great Kingdom made it so in 119cy. Effectively, then, the request declared that the archclericy was unwelcome to return to Verbobonc following deliverence from Keoland.

The commensurate realms felt similarly. Traditionally, the dwarves, elves, and gnomes associated more readily with Verbobonc than with Veluna. Further, and obviously, the commensurates along with the humans of Verbobonc, Furyondy, and Veluna were the same “six nations” that Prince Thrommel the romantic would centuries later form into an alliance against the Elemental Evil. The politics at Castle Estival, where the Furyondian prince also met Jolene of Samprastadar, were rooted, old, and deep.

After Thrommel’s victory at Tor Fens, five of the six nations (and half of Veluna) favored dispensing with the Archclericy and creating the Unified Kingdom. This closely approximated to public sentiments following Furyondy’s victory in the Short War too. Many of the political instituions—such as the Gnome Assembly of the Kron Hills—in fact remained the same.

There is this difference, though, that after Tor Fens the six nations were pressed to ally against Iuz, while after the Short War there was no necessary arrangement at all. Peace reigned and, for a while, so did a measure of independence from the Archclericy of Veluna. For Veluna's canon it was a challenging time. The serene and eternal Shepherd of Veluna that we know today was not then in reputation. He was politically unpopular and spiritually suspect. The Celestial Order of the Moons and the Velunar merchant classes were against him because the trade wars and the occupation had cost them dearly. The bishops did not favor him because theocracy was a detraction from the primacy of the dioceses. Episcopal collegiality existed from long ago, but the College of Bishops was a novelty invented for the conclave in the Eademer Battistero. The canon claimed a special relation to the Church of Rao, the nation of Veluna, the Crook of Rao, and even to the deity, but to sustain the claim in public he neede to appear reasonable, peaceful, and serene while vying for political power.

We have come, at last, to the Canon of Veluna’s moment in history.

§

Chapter 22: The Eademer concordat

(In a courtroom come to order in a separate plane of exitence)

Leaving the villainous canon dangling above the unfastidious jaws of . . .

Actually, Professor, we were the ones left dangling, and we have already jumped down. And villainous? Really? Is that fair? You are judging him before we get started.

My objectionable pupils! You are on cue, on point, and just what the hour requires. Participants! And, yes, my dear, the Canon of Veluna’s villainy is no more than half proved. His conviction as a villain is pending. He has been villainous thus far. But there are one hundred fifty years of canoneering remaining to him, and he may redeem himself yet. The objection of my worthy pupil is sustained. I withdraw my comment about the Canon of Veluna being villainous.

For the record, my original prosecution of Hazen was as a “shepherd that has led us into so much delusion, war, and fear that I doubt his salvation.” Such a man need not be a villain. I say again, villainy may have no part in him . . .

Professor!

I withdraw the comment. Let “villain” and “villainy” be as if unsaid. Perhaps the canon is merely a mortal like the rest of us, tragically tempted by something larger than himself—say, the Canonry of Veluna—into acting against his personal avowal of Reason, Peace, and Serenity. The poor man, in that case, deserves our pity, not our villification. Indeed, there is nothing villainous about such pernicious banality. It . . .

Professor!!

Sustained! I have trespassed again on the bounds of historiographical judgement. Your pardon is begged. Although my new and innovative genre, the historiographical romance, is a sturdy vessel, yet my captaincy wavers, and an inexperienced captain needs a lively crew. You are most welcome aboard.

§

~County, nobility, diocese, and bishop

Shipmates—I mean, jury of the court—to understand the Eademer concordat we must know a little more about the provinces of Veluna, about the dioceses and counties, which are distinct but intertwined. Their names and geographical extents correspond exactly, the diocesan cathedrals are in the county towns, and our histories and sources all presume a basic knowledge of them. I may quote this, for example, from a sermon given in 440cy by the bishop of, in the cathedral of, in the attendance of the count of, in the diocese of, in the town of, and in the county of Devarnish:

In 355cy, Keoland’s Second Expeditionary Force captured Devarnish and the Crook of Rao with it. But today, praise god, the Keoish army has been dispatched from Velunar soil. Devarnish and its diocese are once again part of greater Veluna, and we rejoice for it. Yet this state of affairs may last but briefly, if Count Devarnish’s words were spoken in earnest.

Here, as you see, "Devarnish" signifies county, diocese, town, cathedral, count, and bishop. You need to understand this, although what immediately matters is rather the sermon’s reference to “greater Veluna.”

You, my historiographical percipients, will understand by now that when a Velunar cleric says that something existed “but briefly” it may mean that it never existed at all. And indeed, in 440cy, “greater Veluna” was actually unreal, merely a projection cast from Mitrik by prominent theocrats. Although it nominally included Verbobonc, Veluna City, and the southern counties of Devarnish, Valkurl, Kempton, Lorrish, and Falsridge, these could be considered parts of “greater Veluna” only by a stretch of the canonical imagination after the liberation of those places from Keoland's occupation. Even in Mitrik, not everyone was committed to the vision of "greater Veluna." The Celestial Order of the Moons was by then in Mitrik as well, forced to flee Veluna City when the Keoish army was poised to seige the capital in 355cy. After (or because of) eighty years of occupation, the Celestial Order was implacably opposed to the archclericy. Its grievances, which had brought Veluna to the brink of civil war when Keoland had first attacked, were still unresolved. Although northern Veluna during the occupation had remained under Mitrik’s jurisdiction, there was considerable doubt about the loyalty of its people to the archclericy. The northerners' repeated their affirmations of allegiance "to Mitrik," but that did not mean much when the Celestial Order was also in that city.

Keoland’s policy in the southern counties was to leave the functional institutions intact. The nobility's lands and titles were still inherited, the bishops continued to annoint new priests, and the participation of the northern bishops was encouraged in religious ceremonies. Keoland further encouraged the participation of the southern nobility when free Veluna held elections for plar and to the Celestial Order, causing some consternation among theocrats about the loyalty of the Order to the archclericy.

References to the plar and the Celestial Order appear very early in Veluna's recorded history, and the twin institutions are likely descended from the secular government of Voll when that had been in service to the overking and viceroy. The plar’s principle function had been a vow of fealty to the overking; his (or her, in the instance of a Supreme Mistress) authority was to ensure that the emperor’s instructions were respected. When the theocracy broke troth with the overking, the office of the plar became pointless, yet the nobility continued to elect one repurposed as their chief representative to the canon. The Celestial Order underwent a similar transformation: what had been a representative body in service to the plar and on behalf of the overking became a representive body in service to the archclericy but loyal to the plar, to the nobility, and to the work of secular government where it continued in the counties.

Because the plar and the Celestial Order were continuously associated with the governments of Voll and Veluna a fair amount is either known or is surmisable about their history; but that is untrue of the nobility, the counties, the dioceses, and the bishops, whose institutional origins predate vassalage in Voll and thus theocracy in Veluna as well. Local institutions were not of any evident concern to the historical (and mostly theocratic) sources that are available to us today. It is evident, nonetheless, that the counties and dioceses were remarkably egalitarian or, to respectivley apply more accurate descriptors, fraternal and collegial. Episcopal collegialtiy is inherent to the status and purpose of a bishop and was, as far as can be seen, indigenous to the old Vale of Luna. The bishops had ever been elected by their dioceses or by other organized groups that had very anciently taken on a diocesan form. The land and titles of the nobility were inherited, of course, not inherent, but the members of the Celestial Order and the plar had always been elected, indicating a collective authority paralleling that of the bishops.

During Keolad’s occupation, the southern counties and dioceses had been dissassociated from Veluna’s national superstructure—from the Celestial Order, the plar, and the archclericy—and Keoland had sought to subsume them under its monarchy. Keoland’s governors promoted the participation of southern lords in elections for plar and to the Celestial Order, and they allowed northern bishops to participate in annointing new bishops to fill vacant southern sees. The canon and the archclericy had no legislative or ecclesiastical standing to prevent it, and therefore, there was no guarantee that following liberation a majority of nobles and bishops would welcome the return of theocracy. This was true even in the north.

Indeed, had the archclericy’s restoration been widely agreeable, the Eademer conclave and concordat would not have been necessary. But that was far from the case; the work of the conclave was equally as decisive and definitve of modern Velunar history.

In conclusion; I submit to you, my fair-minded jurors, that the evidence stands in favor of the plaintiff, Professor Annalo Bifurcati, in accepting the greater importance of Veluna’s second declaration of independence from Furyondy, at the Eademer Battistero by a conclave of bishops in 440cy, over its first, at Mitrik, in 254-, by the defendant, the Canon of Veluna, aka Shepherd of the Faithful. Case dismissed.

§

~Leading to the Eademer Battistero: The Diocese of Verbobonc

I find it expedient to remind you, my meandering coterie, that the route you are taking to Doraka’a goes indirectly. Traipsing the Fellreev Forest adds weeks to your journey. You might have gone by good, straight roads from Law’s Forge to Ixworth and then to Kin Dell, taken the Long March to the Opicm River's mouth, followed the Whyestil Lake shore to the gates of the blighted city, and, if you had, by now I would probably be free of my horrid contractual obligations, which are void on the event of the death of the last of you.

Had that happened—should it yet, even partially—I doubt I could go on. Seeing you arrive at the Sewers and Shit-gutters of Doraka'a is important to me. Not much else matters anymore. There is another thing, yes, that I might have done, a place and a someone I know, but that’s likely over. There’s only you, the road we take, and what the next turn will bring.

It's gonna be great, Professor!

Undoubtedly. And to ease the burden of thinking about it, I will tell you something you do not know. If, right now, you vere east for ten miles off your current trackless way, you will come to a broad path going north. Take it, and you will be granted two boons. One: you will soon depart from the domain of Verithmirax, the terrible green dragon, where you are right now without knowing it, and avoid the castle of Dahlvier, the vampire, where you are headed unawares. This will lower the odds of a fatal bereavement among you. Two, the northern path will take you to the precarious, impecunious, yet widely renowned outpost of Grimwood-under-Sky, wherewith in a scant clearing in the forest’s depths you may find food, rest, and entertainment at the High Moon Inn, a destination for storytellers, fantasists, adventurers, and various exponents of alternative truth. Will you go there? If you need further encouragment you need, I promise to provide you with a tale to tell at the High Moon.

(A general shrug)

I suppose, why not?

Excellent. And regarding your group's use of forestrial misdirection in making your way to Doraka'a, I approve and even find it instructive. It has convinced me that a due appreciation of the Eademer Battistero concordat will come easier if, as on your way to Grimwood-under-Sky, I take you on a topical detour, too, leaving the main highway of canonical history to make a local stop at the Diocese of St Cuthbert, in Verobonc Town. St Cuthbert's is the only diocese in all the Flanaess that exists outside Veluna, and the reasons are significant. Plus, you ought to see Verbobonc, a leafy locale caught up in the magic of elves and gnomes and, therefore, not much given to written history apart from aureate verse and practical joking. Fifteen years ago, Gary Gygax wrote that “The history of Verbobonce is hardly worth a mention.” He was wrong and ought to have said it is not not much written about; because humans, although they do live in Verbobonc, are too contented by their environ to do to it properly.

Some of them do, of course. One man, in particular, wrote volumes (and volumes) (and volumes) about mid-fifth-century Verbobonc. His career there as a Cuthbertine priest and bishop extended from ten years prior to the Short War to forty years beyond it and featured prominently in the events leading to and from the Eademer Concordat. He was that pleasantly rare type of man, a Cuthbertine memoirist. Lights and Shadows of a Loooong Episcopate was lent to me fifteen years ago by an elf that lives in an ipt treehouse in Verbobonc, where he keeps a private library. He (elf, not bishop) hosts parties of mixed elven and human company and has a fascination for humanity because he sees it for longer than we do. In 479cy, he purchased the entirety of ◒Lights and Shadows◓ (at the time, it was momentarily topical) and finished it eighty-two years later. He assured me that the opus, although widely unread and tedious, contains a wealth of information in the same way mud flats contain pearls. He knew how accustomed I was to wading the murky shallows of tedium to obtain nuggets of information, because my academic specialty is . . .

Wait a sec, Professor. Who was the memoirist you mentioned? I didn’t get the name.

No doubt, my dear, because I forgot to mention it. He was Cornelius Speiknhammer, the initial Bishop of Verbobonc and a grand pedantic in the Cuthbertine style. The Cudgelites employ common sense by rote, you know, and it is a great labor to pry the tough shells of their prose open and look for a morsel of writ. And because you, my heroes now hastening to doom, have little time to spare, I have husked ◒Lights and Shadows◓ for you and strung its salient points together. Here, then, is the nacre of the seventy-eighth through hundred-and-sixth chapters of the forty-seventh volume of Speiknhammer’s memoir:

St Cuthbert’s Diocese of Verbobonc was created by the stroke of my appointment as its bishop. Its constitution was such: Subsequent candidates for bishop would be nominated by the viscount subject to approval by Cuthbertine monastics and the temple priests. Rao's Titular Bishop of Veluna was banished from the viscounty along with his overseers. The eight Cuthbertine abbots continued as heads of the Cuthbertine monasteries and were given supplementary appointments as the Bishop's Abbot-executives. In the future, the monks would elect abbots subject to the bishop’s approval of the consequent abbot-exec. The abbot-execs were to appoint one Bishop’s High Knight-protector and one Bishop’s High Ministerial to each of the provinces of Verbobonc under their assigned jurisdictions, and they in turn would appoint staffs of knight-protectors and ministerials to protect and serve the citizens of Verobonc. Such appointments would be made from among St Cuthbert’s Billets, a chivalric order dedicated to ordinary service, not combat.The bishop was vested with the power to dismiss an abbot-exec (subject to the monks agreeing to dismiss their abbot) and, also, any billet under the authority of an abbot-exec, on the grounds of being unsuited to the viscount. To cap the arrangement, a magisterial power was vested in the viscount to abolish the bishopric and diocese wholesale on grounds of their being unsuited to him. Taken as a whole, the constitution satisfied all concerned parties by assuring that: the temples and churches remained free of the bishop; the monasteries remained free (in part) of the bishop; the bishop had control (in part) of the monasteries and the Billets; the billets were established as protectors and ministerials serving the people of Verbobonc; and the viscount, if he deemed it necessary, could repent of the infliction on his viscounty of the entire Cuthbertine establishment.

Marvelous agreement! I am proud to be a Verboboncan, where at least I know the Cudgel.

As you will understand, this literary oyster must be opened to be digested. Therefore:

⚜

In those days, as today, great numbers of St Cuthbert’s adherents lived everywhere in the Flanaess and many bishops of St Cuthbert were dispersed throughout Veluna—but the lone Cuthbertine diocese among them was the one in Verbobonc. Apart from it, there were (and are) no dioceses of any kind save the eight in Veluna, which were Raoan and differently constituted. St Cuthbert's bishops oversaw temples in Veluna, not cathedrals, and were appointed to the office, not consecrated. The only geniuinely diocesan system—comprehending a catholic church organized into dioceses and united in episcopal collegiality—in the Flanaess was the Church of Rao: seven dioceses and an archdiocese overseen by seven bishops and an archbishop. There were Cuthbertine bishops resident in Veluna— one for each of the saint’s temples—but they were not consecrated in episcopal collegiality. They were temple head priests, appointed by the other priests and the acolytes.

A Cuthbertine bishop in Veluna resembles, quite remarkably, a Raoan high canon at the head of a chapter of junior canons on a cathedral staff. The whole profusion of temples, churches, monasteries, bishops, cathedrals, canons, high canons, and chapter houses may even have originated in an ancient, proto-episcopal, Raoan tradition native to the Flan when Rao was still Lord of Peace in the great Vale of Luna.

In Verbobonc, St Cuthbert's diocese was synthetically conceived, a hybrid. Its bishop was appointed by the viscount, not consecrated by fellows, and extraordinarily, priests of St Cuthbert were not all under episcopal oversight. The churches, temples, and monasteries were not, either, and abbots were overseen only in their capacity as abbot-executives. Episcopal authority in clerical matters was restricted to abbot-executives, High Knight-protectors, High Ministerials, and billets on staff. The viscounty's citizens, however, were each and every one members of the diocese by law whether they worshipped the deified saint or not.

We may say, to sum up, that Verbobonc had established the diocese of St Cuthbert but not the faith. It differed in this from the Raoan establishment, although the two resembled one another in other repects. They alike provided for the spiritual and temporal welfare of their nations' citizens by supervisizing a network of religious and political institutions that together met the nations' needs. Certain taxes, for example, were collected by the religious establishments on behalf of the political states, which was also true vice-versa. Sacred and secular things categorically cannot be mixed, yet in life, religious and political authorites do mix spiritual and temporal activities. They do it all the time. That's the whole point.

Goodness, Professor. The whole point of what?

Of an establishment—what I'm saying. Try and keep up. In the early third century, the Canon of Veluna began dispatching a Raoan titular bishop (a bishop with no diocese) to Verbobonc as the archclericy’s political representative to the viscounty. The titular bishop, although he had no see, was collegial with the diocesan bishops in Veluna. His office was politically significant, because he and his network of "overseers”—some of whom were priests of St Cuthbert—were the archclericy's only representative presence in the viscounty, where the Raoan church was little known and the faith of St Cuthbert was predominant. The dismissal of His Titularity (as the monks began to call him) from Verbobonc was tantamount to a rejection of the archclericy's right to rule following Verbobonc's liberation' from Keoland. It left the Raoan establishment with no authority in Verbobonc beyond the old feudal allegiance of the viscount and the canon, which the occupation had reduced to vestigial.

The point, if you will, is that St Cuthbert’s diocese resembled Veluna's episcopal system for a reason. Verbobonc wanted to become something like an eighth province of Veluna and dissolve their feudal allegiance. It seemed a good idea (if you were not an archcleric) because Verbobonc was working with Furyondy and the Celestial Order of the Moons to replace the archclericy with a secular government that would likely be organized into counties and dioceses as old Voll had been. The best opportunity to advance this revolution peacefully within the archclericy was to create a Verboboncan bishop roughly equivalent to Veluna's and, therefore, eligible for participation in episcopal collegiality. This was the original motive for what later became the archclericy's College of Bishops, a representative house of congress reserved to Raoan bishops only.

The viscount wanted to be a member of the Celestial Order of the Moons, too, which was easily achieved when the plar proposed it and the members voted for. Like the College of Bishops, the Celestial Order would also be refashioned as a house of congress comprising representatives of the seven noble families, although it differed from the College in not being exclusively Velunar. The viscount gained a place in the Order while Verbobonc's bishop had none in the College.

Those of you capable of paying attention will have noted that these developments gave the projected secular government of Verbobonc an attainable form. Episcopal collegiality was a way to unite Veluna and Verbobonc by letting bishops and aristocrats share temporal and spiritual power in replacement of the archclericy. This was consistent with Velunar government as it had been in Old Voll. The unsettled details . . .

Oi! That's just like the Unified Kingdom! I do pay attention!

No, it isn't. Would you like to try again? Please, keep up. It isn't like the Unified Kingdom, because it didn't formally involve Furyondy, granted the bishops a measure of temporality, and proposed an interfaith episcopal collegiality that sowed the seeds of a potent dissent. The Raoan bishops promulgated their objections in the Eademer Concordat, calling the plan a national apostasy and turning the political tide against secular government. The Unified Kingdom's constitution was intended . . .

I do keep up! The whole point of the new government, obviously, was to make the bishops secular.

Not even nearly.

What, not even?

The bishops wouldn't be secular, silly. Only temporal.

Same thing!

Not! When a bishop act spiritually, that's one thing, and when he acts temp . . .

Yes—but before we make a fuss over it, let's conclude my lecture. Shall we? In 445cy, five months before the Eademer conclave, Furyondy announced the king’s intention of withdrawing his military forces from Verbobonc, which left the viscounty in need of an independent militia to serve and protect its citizens. The billets of St Cuthbert had by then been established as knight-protectors and bishop's ministerials organized for public service and therefore a likely resource for the militia. But St Cuthbert’s creed is notoriously belligerent about making people follow Cuthbertine precepts. The billets were the least militant of the saint's priestly chivalric orders, but even so, the bishop had sworn them to “protect and minister to the faithful” of the viscounty, a broad mandate in a polytheistic society where everyone was by law included among the faithful whether or not they worshipped the saint. If the billets were to serve the people, not the faith, the notorious Cuthbertine zeal (“the Cudgel”) must be curbed.

This was a matter of distinguishing “Cudgelite values” from those of the larger society and subsuming the former under the latter. The priests of the Chapeaux and the Stars—St Cuthbert’s other chivalric orders—objected to the subsumption, but most billets viewed public service as a feather in the cap of an order often looked down on as servile. To pluck the prestigous plume, however, the billets of the “civil diocese” (as the establishment was commonly called) needed to compromise civic duty and the fervency evident everywhere in St Cuthbert's temples, churches, and monasteries. But according to the diocean civil constitution, these groups were not within the episcopal jurisdiction. Bishop Speiknhammer could not control . . .

(Another interruption, this time from the front row . . .)

(. . . and more welcome)

Don’t call me that. If they were all free of the bishop’s oversight, what was the bishop for?

Well, young lady, that’s right. Good question. He was “for” a police force and a civil service but must be a bishop to mingle and convene with Raoans in Veluna. Ordinarily, a diocese will encompass the faithful within a particular geographical area. But there was precedent for its utility in defining a political encompassment, not a spiritual one. Since the second century, Raoan ecclesiastics had . . .

The Verboboncan sky grows desolate—the universe grows cold. For the life of me, I . . .

No, no, no, no, no, no, no. . . . Well, yes. Really, it was done by expediency and precedent, not by legislation. For two hundred years, the titular bishop of Verbobonc had been sending Raoan overseers into the Cuthbertine monasteries to press Raoan interests into training Cuthbertine billets. Traditionally, the monks urged the Cudgel's priests to true zealotry, so, the overseers encouraged the billets to be particularly zealous in keeping the viscounty peaceful and serene, as the Imperial Raoan Church had done in the old viceroyalty except by chudgel this time, not by reason. The viscount had co-opted the authority of the titular bishop by establishing a diocese and substituting abbot-executives for Raoan overseers. The abbot-execs eagerly pledged loyalty to the bishop because the abbot's wanted to be rid of any association with the overseers. No one asked how it worked because it was ready to go. Everyone gained an advantage even if the advantages were contradictory. None of it dimmed the heavens; it was a gods’send to all.

(A general lack of conviction)

Keeping it afloat depended on the captain (the viscount) and his XO (the bishop), which tied their hopes to the same mast and gave them a unanimity of command although they sailed in somewhat different directions.

While voyaging that vale, the Raoans and the Cuthbertines had created spiritual and temporal institutions that were much alike despite their episcopal variations. And all the while . . .
