Indeed, it's confusing. I could explain it to you in detail, but that would only lead to a detailed confusion. The Archclericy of Veluna was born to, and has lived in, a great confusion of fidelity split between the Great Kingdom and Furyondy, of a collapsing empire’s troubles, and of a proliferation of free nations not in an "independence movement” but in a broken series of seized opportunities.

Following their liberation from Keoland, the bishops and the monks in Verbobonc and Veluna were curiously placed. They were proffered independence from the archclericy by choosing a secular government, and of course, they remembered the old ways of the Vale, when bishops hhad taken precedence over their canons and monasteries had been free of overseers. But the bishops and the monastics reclaiming power was not what happened. The Archclericy instead worked a reformation and a restoration.

Why did that happen? What does that tell us about the Canon of Veluna's past?

§

~The Eademer Concordat

By 445cy, the King of Furyondy believed he had enough support in Veluna to overthrow the archclericy. In a gesture of good will, he withdrew his military forces surrounding Veluna and promised benevolence and independence to the reprieved nation, whose gratitude, he believed, would make him Prince of Veluna at last. The unpopular canon's last hope was to rally the bishops, whom he gathered in conclave to decide the issue. We follow events by excerpting ◒Lights and Shadows◓:

There had been no episcopal conclave since before the Archclericy's independence from Furyondy, and never before had one been summoned by a canon. For these reasons it was called an extraordinary conclave, not because it was great but because it was unprecedented. It was not at first even expected to happen, because it required a majority of bishops in favor and that was uncertain. There was no archbishopric yet, and the titular bishop was a recent, canonical innovation of uncertain standing. In the end, because the titular had been consecratted to office by his fellows his voice was heard, making him the fourth bishop in favor of conclave with four opposed; in the interest of episcopal collegiality, this was deemed sufficient.

The Exraordinary and Episcopal Conclave of 446cy was convened in the Eademer Battistero, in Mitrik, to discuss the fate of Veluna, which many religious men believed was controlled by greedy Furyondians driven by secular goals. Although cool heads opened the conference, a contingent of orthodox Cuthbertine overseers rallied the more conservative Raoans to their cause, urging that Veluna formally cede from Furyondy to oppose the growing apostasy being fomented by wartime expansionism and imperialism. In an agreement known as the Eademer Concordat, the members of the college voted overwhelmingly to break from the kingdom.

The vote was not overwhelming; it was unanimous, eight to nothing—but Speiknhammer had taken sixteen chapters to explain that

although seven diocesan bishops plus a titular went into the Conclave of Eademer, yet seven diocesan and an arch- had come out, tit- being translated to arch-”,

and he wanted to elaborate the point. The comment drew violent objection from Raoans when it was published for reasons that must be understood; they explain the vote's unanimity and . . .

Oh! Oh! Professor, I’ll explain it! I’ll explain it!

Really, my dear? But you haven’t . . . well, have a go.

Only diocesan not titular bishops traditionally had a vote in the conclave, which had been in existence since the beginning of Voll. But of the seven dioceses, four had been under Keoland’s occupation and only three had not, so, the vote to reform and restore the archclericy would likely have been four to three against. To avoid this, the titular bishop had to be given a voice, but even at that, the bishops were likely at a stalemate, four to four, which would fail to gather the conclave, denounce the apostasy, and resolve the political crisis. The tit- had to be an arch-; the arch- would break the tie and be reliably pro-Canon. But if the tit- were translated the theocracy's only representative office in Verbobonc would be vacated, and consecrating his successor would be controversial. The tit- must be an arch- in some other way, but no manner was ever decided; the arch- was simply proclaimed. When Speiknhammer called it translation, objections were brought loudly without really saying anything, and since people stopped reading ◒Lights and Shadows◓ soon after it was published, the controversy passed quietly away. Calling the vote “overwhelming," not “unanimous,” let Speiknhammer point out that the bishops had not been in agreement; they had followed the episcopal custom of having minority protestants switch their votes in the interests of apparent fraternity. Eight to nothing!

Oh, my. My dear girl. That was simply bril . . .

But Professor, there’s so much more!

Really, my boy? You too?

Astonishing, isn’t it? The Cuthbertine Bishop of Verbobonc’s request to be collegial among the Raoans could have been restricted to the College of Bishops, a temporal house of congress without any properly spiritual function. But the college was at first an extraordinary conclave; so, proposing the inclusion in fellowship of a Cuthbertine bishop could be seen as a renunciation of Raoan faith, the sharpest point of apostasy's dart lodged in the heart of Veluna. This proved that seclular government meant the renunciation of sacred power from within —a sacrilege. Accusing Veluna of apostasy was, at the moment closest to its surrender, the archclericy’s final thrust, a reaffirmation of the original unity (although apocryphal it may have been) of Velunar government and Raoan faith.

Denouncing this national apostasy required more than denying the Cuthbertine bishop’s collegiality with the Raoans and remedying the ill itself. “Greedy Furyondians with secular goals” were denounced by the Eademer Concordat as instigators of a “growing apostasy fomented by wartime expansion and imperialism.” The denunciation avoided a condemnation of Veluna's vassal, Verbobonc, and restyled Furyondy’s liberation as a sacrilege barely eight years after the happy event. Liberation had become desecration in the interests of secular rule, but sacred Veluna was spared by a divine authority in exercise of its temporal power, theocracy's vindication.

Had the accusation of apostasy failed, the archclericy would have ceased to exist. But Veluna repented at the call of its shepherds. The King of Furyondy and the Viscount of Verbobonc prized political stability in Veluna above all else and quietly conceded. Resistance would only have widened the “overwhelming break from the kingdom” the bishops had propsed and the triumphant archclericy could have arranged.

Dear me! Oh, my! My wonderful adventurers, my armor plate against error, you perhaps believe that these, my tears, are of the joy that only pupils can bring to a teacher’s eye, but you are mistaken! I cry, I weep because you have spoken so concisely what I had intended to lecture at considerable length! O! what misery. What use for my long night spent making this lesson?

(Disbelief and amazement)

It's hardly fair to complain. You never weary and you need no sleep.

That’s hardly the point. My notes must not be wasted. Let me see, there must be . . .

Oi! You forgot to mention that ever since the Eademer Concordat the Raoan archbishop has been chosen by the canon for consecration, not elected by the priests and the citizens of Veluna City. By commanding the archbishop, and by establishing the Celestial Order of the Moons and the College of Bishops as representative houses of his congress, the canon reached his full stature. At last he condescended to the nobility and the episcopacy, an odd thing for a canon to do, and what he had not been sure of before.

Yeah, yeah. We would have thought of it. I mean, it took you all night, right?

The Archclericy of Veluna depended on the Eademer Battistero in 446cy. It is not eternal, therefore, and the Canon of Veluna likewise is not. The Eademer Concordat, the Archbishop of Veluna City, and the subordination of the Celestial Order and the College of Bishops were each a product of the battistero conclave. Look deeper, and you will further see that the authority of the conclave rested only on itself. It was an original, like Raoan scripture, the Crook of Rao, the foundation of Voll, and the independence of Veluna. These things' origins are murky, and the murk hides the canon's origins too.

And so, dear students, you confront the Canon of Veluna’s foundational dilemma: How to costume his ambition in guises of Reason, Peace, and Serenity. Having reached an immovable, mountainous height in these regions, yet his supremacy must be hid for the unhappiest of qualms. His canonical peace was well endowed (speaking metaphorically) by an olive branch so large no fig leaf will conceal it. His reasoning bulges with a passion so concupiscent no euphemism will trouser it. His serenity burns with a desire so unsavory that only some like it hot. What would you, my salacious readers, have done in his stead? Bare your magnificence (supposing you possessed it) to the world—or pants it modestly and closet your perfidious abundance? Deflate the extremity of your longest extent—or measure it proudly amongst the mighty? Arouse the high standard of your pride—or leave it corpuscularly diminished? Fortunately for us without the stamina to requite such questions, the canon has wrestled the horns of the dilemma and straddled it:

Maintain your public modesty at all costs; treachery is a boast made more massive in private.

§

Interlude: The High Moon Inn, a hero adventurer’s recital

In Grimwood-under-Sky, the High Moon Inn hosted a sleeping man that always smelled of beer, a bottomless beer that the innkeeper provided. The guests of the inn, transient and resident alike, gave the man always a wide berth at a corner table less out of consideration than out of disappointment and consequent resentment. The sleeping man was known as The Sage, and he was the heart of village life, giving (he long had) relief from the “Grim’s life” (as the villagers told it) of foraging in the forest to find what sustenance the clearing sporadically provided, cut too deep within a forest that disrespected the pale of Grimwood-under-Sky.

Things came out of the forest and trespassed the clearing, natural things very often but not always so. The unnatural were the dominion of The Sage; he told Grimwood-under-Sky preposterous tales about things they knew were all too real, although the stories were sufficiently ridiculous to laugh at. The drunkard was ridiculous, too, and the levity he provided was what the villagers needed to get by. In fact, for a while they had more than got by. Grimwood-under-Sky had formerly prospered from public traffic the drunken Sage had brought to the High Moon Inn. People from hundreds of miles came to hear, and they, in return for a little hospitality, could be very generous. Some came to tell tales of their own, and of those, some chose to remain in the village. A community of tale-tellers and an industry of tale-telling soon defined a place so remote that only the wealthy and the adventurous ever reached it. There is no better way of adducing the old addage about wealth trickling down than to point to the prosperity, such as it was, of Grimwood-under-Sky.

Tonight, among the adventuring transients there are several from Law’s Forge, where no one here is known to have been from before.

“That is because,” the newcomers said, “it’s a devil’s prison.”

They were almost children, hardly more. They had a friend, they said, that lived in a book. And there was no doubt that they had a book, because one of them was going to tell a tale written by it. The book had sent them to Grimwood-under-Sky for that purpose, they said. The High Moon Inn laughed and shouted for joy. Rarely had a storyteller come with an introduction so inventive and rich.

It was a tale of Prince Thrommel, and even in all-knowing Grimwood-under-Sky, that is a tale worth hearing. The child began.

§

~The prince and the kidnappers

“About Prince Thrommel everyone knows three things: his last words; he did not die, he disappeared; and becase there is no body, there is no tomb. Plans for an empty mausoleum were mooted when Lucidides, Thrommel’s biographer, had boasted that ‘A hero like Prince Thrommel has the whole oerth for his tomb.’Every year since, on Whole Oerth Day, Furyondians have planted trees and cleaned the environment.

“Lucidides also wrote the official account of Thrommel’s last words, which is this:

“After his victory against the Sea Princes, the prince’s wounds were dressed and he was given a sedative. As he fell asleep, his captains debated ‘whether His Highness’s civil or military excellence was the superior example of his virtue.’ Thrommel sat up and rebuked them, saying, “I boast only one thing, that no Furyondian ever wore mourning because of me.” Thousands of men, women, and children had died at the marshal’s command, but Thrommel believed he had been a scrupulous soldier and only fought when necessary. Popular sentiment and historical judgement have agreed.

“That night, unknown assailants overcame the night watch and abducted the prince, leaving witnesses to the event and purportedly alternative last words. Singling out the most commanding, villainous, and brutal of the assailants, Thrommel had said, ‘Et tu, amica?’ Which means, in the common tongue,

‘You too, girlfriend?’

Something was wrong. I awoke but could not rise. My hands (in their dreaming) gripped the wrist of my attacker but could not force his hand from my mouth. His strength and weight were on me, keeping me down. I could not scream. Yet his eyes (this was odd) were reassuring to me; the forefinger that he brought to his lips soon obviated my struggles.

Who was he? What was he? He looked left, he looked right.

So did I. Our tent admitted no heaven; everything was dark within. Yet shapes of absolute darkness were there that lacked any fathom and sound. Under their weight were other, more cognizable things held prone. I looked again to my assailant, who was becoming intelligible to me.

It was Victoro, captain of our second battalion. A knife in the grip of a void notched his throat, and we, a moment ago Victoro's fellow captains and dreaming of victory’s delights, were now captured. Our tent was a hatchless dungeon.

Which (nonetheless) hatched a torchbearer bringing three further figures in tow. They wore the black costume of their comrades, two adorned by flaps on their hoods like the ears of Nubian goats, the third with a tiara of satin strips falling over his head like a skirt of pheasant’s feathers. The torchbearer cleared a way to the only man in the tent still sleeping: our sedated prince, ignorant as a napping babe.

‘Rouse him.’

The Nubians brought him to his feet, and with eyes still sealed Thrommel gave the atmosphere two sniffs. ‘Rosenrantz and Gildenstern, as I breathe,’ he professed, unlidding his eyes with disdain for the attackers. ‘Hooded? For real? None of these men know you. Are you bigger fools for admitting that I do?’

One of the goats removed its ears. ‘Yo, prince. Rejoice! You see me happier this night than I have been this past year, may it ever be forgot.’

‘Your friend is reluctant.’

‘He’s just stubborn. I’ll help him.’

The second man, unwillingly unmasked, brought a lecherous grin to his cleft lip; a wound that, on his face, denoted an ill spirit.

‘How are you, my lord? Perhaps you’ve had better evenings?’

‘All that saw nothing of you,’ reconsidered the prince, who next attended to the pheasant, the chief, who stood three steps back, a man of ponderous strength like an anchor of malice. The prince grew disenchanted.

‘You too, girlfriend?’

There was no reply. The pheasant was still; slowly, slowly, hope and meaning diminished.

‘Rope up his friends.’

We captains were herded and cinched together, shuffling our feet in maintenance of an awkward common balance. The pheasant spoke words, raised a forefinger, drew a circle in the air, sealed his lips, and stunned the tent into a silence so profound that I could not find my thoughts. The torchbearer pulled a bomb from his garment, lit the fuse by the torch's flame, and tossed the device at our feet, which were combined so we could not kick it out. The pheasant incanted again, and with Thrommel, the clefted lieutenant, and the torchbearer he vanished. The prince, guessing our fate, grimmaced as he disappeared.

The remaining assassins withdrew and left us captians in a magical zone of silence. The fuse burned down, and—

Nothing. We lived. The tale is told. And I, Captain Lorenza D’Amico, swear that it is true. You have been a wonderful audience.

“The tavern cheered. The innkeeper served me a beer that I pushed at the drunken sage in the corner as I sat down beside him.

“‘He won’t take it unless he drinks in a coma,’ said the innkeeper, who had followed me there.

“‘How long will he be like this?’

“‘Two days.’

“‘Why?’

“‘The brew don’t wear off; he stays lost in his thoughts.’

“‘What are they?’

“‘That he once lived in Doraka’a, and it gives him bad dreams,’ said the High Moon’s proprietor, leaning toward me and winking confidentially. ‘I’ll tell you. He has stories to tell. The clientele is mad for them. He’s worth a bit to me and mine. I got a wife, you know. I got kids.’ He grew more confidential, his eyes gleaming bright like the lamp of a miner you see trapped way down. ‘The folk liked your story a lot. How many more of ‘em you got in that book?’

“‘None. I want to know what he says about Doraka’a.’

“‘That there’s demons and necromancers and goblins and graveyards and citadels of terror. But if he’s talking about Doraka’a, he always ends up talking about Iuz. He says he’s seen Iuz.’

“‘I need more detail.’

“‘Why don’t you stick around? Let him tell you. Maybe read a few more stories from that book?’

“Impossible. We have an appointment to keep. Come on, tell me more.’

“‘He’s mad. You can’t believe his stories. The wildest one’s are about Halga. You know, the High Priestess of Iuz? the Bloody Hag? The Witch-lover of the cambion god? Now, get this.’ I hadn’t thought anyone could get so confidential. ‘The Sage says she’s innocent. He says its lies about her and that we got her wrong.’ The fat man set down his belly, half on the table and half on me, and leaned across to take hold of the drunken Sage still sleeping opposite. He reached inside the Sage’s shirt, fondled for something down there, and pulled out a hideous, veined, dried, flesh-and-blood eyeball on a string. ‘This is a Iuz’s Eye. Iuz’s priests got them and use them to see things, to scry far off. That’s true enough. The Sage says he got this one from Halga. But Iuz’s Eyes move and blink when they look about, and this one hasn’t moved in the twenty years I seen it. The Sage just found it somewhere in the forest, picked it up, and brought it here. He showed it to us. I gave him a beer. He told us a story. I gave him a beer. He told another one, and—you get the picture. He’s pretty imaginative. He’s told hundreds of stories. But they’re starting to get repititious. The best ones are about Halga, and now he’s gotten peeved. He won’t hardly tell them no more. He’s drunk all the time, and his imagination’s run dry. People are noticing.’ The proprietor scraped his belly off me and gave a heavy sigh. ‘I got the future to think of. The Sage is unreliable. How much do you think that book is worth?’

“‘Nothing. How do you know that he makes them up?’

“‘Because Halga visits these parts. People have seen her. She’s tall. And we’ve seen what she does. She’s into bowellismsm.▽Bowellism – not to be confused with disembowelment – is removing the innards from the body cavity while leaving the organs functional although external. The objective is to keep the patient alive and perambulatory for as long as possible. In principle, this is similar to (and may have inspired) the architectural school of Bowellism, which places the functional systems of a building – ducts, elevators, stairwells, et ecetera – on the outside, e.g. the Centre Pompdou, in Paris. Anatomical bowelsim is more difficult to achieve, and magically prolonging the viability of victims is cheating. (Eds) That guy’s sister was boweled. And Halga disembowels too. You know the intestines on the walls of Wormhall, right? That’s not a hundred miles from here. Folks have seen it. Halga put them there. She still does. People can see her, because she does it right out in the daylight. She has a glue made of mostly human innards and demon’s blood. Nowadays, she goes about hooded on account of her eyes. Blood drips from the witch’s eyes, you know, a little more each time she kills. It’s buckets by now. So, she hides her face but it soaks through her cloak. Does that sound innocent? People don’t like him saying Halga’s innocent. They know better. They jeer him for it, and it makes him mad. He gets peeved. He’s starting to clam up. After twenty years! So, I’m telling you, friend: that story about Thrommel is new. There’s plenty of tales about Thrommel’s last words, but that one is new. Original, like. How many more you got in that book? Because I think it must belong to the High Moon one way or another. See?”

“No. But I have one more tale to tell. I’ll tell it, and then we’re leaving, and you are not going to mind, friend, because I’m telling you: We’re not innocent either. Not any more.”

§

Chapter 23: Tranquility College

I have news for you, my hero adventurers. This day I have obtained The Compleat Compendium of Monsters Illustrated Edition, because I wanted to know more about the dangers that await you in Fellreev Forest. I have long lamented being of no use against the terrible villains and horrible horrors that you encounter (by statistical averaging) on a bi‑weekly basis, although I never hear about them until later. The most recent occasion—six days after leaving Grimwood‑under‑Sky—was your campsite attacked by assassins at night. Why did they do it? Who cares so much about you? What would have happened if your sentry had been asleep in that tree? If your healer hadn’t learned protection from poison a fortnight ago from a thieving drow pressed under your blade and pleading for her life? What if you hadn’t allowed her live after you had vowed to? Lolth, the spider‑goddess of the drow, might have cursed your spell and allowed the eerie poison of the assassins to do its work. Instead you had earned the demon goddess’s unblessing, a necessary thing when you consider that the venomous poison had a resistance to the cure. By the ungrace of Lolth you live today!

It's too terrible to think about. And who’s to say that something worse won’t happen? I’m no prognosticator. I cannot foresee your future, and in addition to the plain impossibility, my contract forbids it. But last night, while working tirelessly on this chapter, it occurred to me. Am I forbidden to know something (by natural means) that I might happen to mention to you accidentally in the nick of time? On the contrary. All the conventions of fantasy and romance require it! How unnatural of me not to know something (incidental to my wide‑ranging scholarly interests) about what might be lurking near you at a time and place no one expects, and that I may have included this knowledge in my history book, so, you are proved fortunate in surviving a mortal encounter? It is so unnatural that the Fates (who are avid readers of romances) may be getting suspicious by now about why nothing like it has happened so far. The only time I remember was when I diverted you from the domains of Verithmirax (the dragon) and Dahlvier (the vampire) and sent you to Grimwood‑under‑Sky; where you told my tale about Halga, the High Priestess of Iuz, who resides in Doraka’a, where you are going. No harm came of that, right? So I thought, let’s give it a go!

You now approach lonely, lovely, deadly Lake Aqal. By luck, I happen to have sent advanced payment to Clerkburg Inscribers, in Greyhawk’s High Quarter near the University of Magic, to request that a copy of The Complete Compendium should reach me by today at the latest via teleportation. You see, the postcard about Verbobonc that I sent you earlier got me thinking about the ancient elves that live on Lake Aqal, one of whom had written about the water’s indigenous monsters in a series of notices that happened to have included reminiscences of her former life in the Vale of Luna long ago. The notices have been incorporated into the Compendium, although I cannot remember into which entries in particular. The Compendium arrived today, and not knowing any better, I naturally began at the beginning, and lo! the second alphabetical entry of the seven hundred and eleven composing it is the Aboleth, a tubular aberration that (for all I know) may exist as a black, ten‑foot, tentacled, wet, spongey‑skinned, squid‑ or phallus‑like and dismembered appendage (my apologies to the ladies) that lives and slithers in the lake’s waters and on land nearby. So, dear students, take heed: near Lake Aqal, if you begin to feel in your mind a compulsion to be generally subservient to nothing in particular, turn and run back the way you came, or it will be too late!

The Compendium was not cheap. I almost had to mortgage my desk. But I wanted to share your adventures as far as I might, and you must admit that the bit about the aboleth is timely. Nonetheless, I have set the Compendium aside and placed before me tonight’s work, which includes a little scrivening of my own, transcribing a bifolium—a pamphlet— written two decades ago that few people have ever read, although it is widely notorious. I thought about sending the autograph to you, but it is a fairly popular request among the Divergent Underground (for whom it was written) and too precious to be lodged in a book that no one will ever see.

The bifolium in question—“What I think about my great‑great‑great‑grandfather”—was written by the great‑great‑great‑grandson of Bromides Authenticeus, the former Bishop of Devarnish from whose widely‑known sermon, delivered ex cathedra in 440cy, I blockquoted an excerpt several headings above that spoke of the bishop's hope in restoring “greater Veluna, which hope may last but briefly.” Historians have always considered the bishop a wily advocate for restoring the archclericy, a key agent in Mitrik’s triumph, despite his see in the south. But according to “What I think,” it was not so. Passages from the sermon have allegedly been lifted out of context to misrepresent Authenticeus’ true support for the cause of “county and diocese,” not for the cause of theocracy. To posterity, nonetheless, Authenticeus’ reputation has preceded him: he is universally known as an establishment hero at the Eademer Battistero. No one imagines that it was infirmity and hopelessness, not his genuine consent, that put the bishop’s signature to the concordat.

Or so claims Professor Authenticrates Minerva, the great‑great‑great‑ grandson of Bromides Authenticeus. Minerva was the Historical Conservancy Professor of Modern History when I was at Grey and until his retirement in 586cy. The Historical Conservancy was (and still is) a Velunar conservative foundation, and Prof Minerva was a bit apologetic about that and about his great‑great‑great‑grandfather too. And well he should be, because “Doctor Authentic” (as we called him) was a closeted member of the Divergent Underground, a closet where such bastions are very lowly shelved. The Doc took a lot of ribbing because of it, but we were flabbergasted to discover, when we read his ◒Bifolium◓, how personally he had taken it.

My Apology to the Club:

You quill‑dicks and spunk blotters may say what you want—as you do—but my ancestor wasn’t like that. Signing the Concordat saved his see for the diocesan cause. He would have lost Devarnish had he spoken his mind, and history would be very different.

I am telling you. When Devarnish was liberated, in 438cy, it had been occupied for eighty‑three years and Bromides Authenticeus had been bishop for fifteen. Southern Velunars had known happy days during occupation. The Keoish had governed openly and confidently, and why not? The demarcation line with Veluna was secure; the occupiers did not fear rebellion because so few Velunars wanted it. The archclericy had never been popular. Theocracy had brought trouble to the counties, and occupation had returned peace and prosperity. The south believed that it was better off than the north and had become an entity apart.

The beginning of the Short War came tinged by patriotic hope but even more by uncertainty. The war proceeded roughly from west to east, so that Devarnish was the last diocese freed. The four southern bishops— Falsridge, Lorrish, Valkurl, and Devarnish—▽Minerva refers to the bishops by the names of their dioceses. (Eds)stayed in touch until, one by one, freedom stilled their voices. They had wanted to adopt a common stance facing Mitrik and the victorious Furyondian king, but points of divergence frustrated their agreement. Falsridge was afraid his county would be caught in a long border war in Bissell and intended to accommodate the king as a precaution. Hibit▽Myckal Hibit, Bishop of Valkurl. (Eds) quit Valkurl prior to liberation in a demonstration of loyalty to Canon Raowen, which his see depended on. Lorrish hoped to advance his precious liturgical reforms and would accommodate Mitrik for that reason. But the four agreed on one point: episcopal privileges had flourished during the occupation and ought to be preserved by the archclericy. In practical terms, this agreement accomplished nothing because of the bishops' differences, but nonetheless, after the Eademer Concordat, it became the diocesan movement’s guiding spirit and the font of southern Tranquility, Tranquilitism, and liturgical innovation.

Of course, the diocesan spirit was incompatible with the concordat that Authenticeus and the others had signed in the battistero. But by the time they signed, the College of Bishops was a fait accompli. The king had made clear that he would not intervene in Velunar affairs, and Titular Bishop Cranmerra, translated into Archbishop Claud, awaited his public consecration. Within the battistero, the old temple was cold and damp, Authenticeus was sick, Devarnish needed attention, the other bishops had given up, and my great‑great‑great‑grandfather had made crucial other plans. He signed.

But you are always so flippant, aren’t you? You do not understand. You see everything badly. You see history streaming in a great current and cannot imagine that it was not so. History does not flow; it converges and diverges. Always, convergence is a gain by which much is lost, and divergence brings new directions, not more of the same. We know historical appearances by following before and after, not by pinning them down. This is true, even if it spoils your fun.

Bromides Authenticeus signed the concordat yet saved the diocesan spirit by directing it underground to part from the Archclericy’s gathering waters. Had history depended on Falsridge, Lorrish, and Valkurl, diocesanism would have dispersed into the mainstream. There would be no Tranquility College, no Tranquility movement, no Cardinale Newman, no church reform, no Fountainspring crisis, no independent Dyvers, and possibly, no Greyhawk Wars.

When I say it, you laugh. You are always laughing at me. “But Doctor Authentic, those things all came out of the battistero! Tranquility was founded by Authenticeus as an archclerical college! The archclericy supported the liturgical reforms!” You jest and you think very freely but not very well. How could an anti‑Erastrian movement such as Tranquilitism have come from Mitrik? Where could it have come from? Where dfo you find its source?

You think of the archclericy as a thousand‑year‑old stream that inevitably gathered strength and took everything in. You do not see convergence and divergence. My great‑great‑great‑grandfather signed the birth certificate of the gathering stream, that’s true, but he swam in the underground current, too, with its divergence at the battistero conclave. The diocesan spirit flowed under the archclericy, at least for a significant while, and that has made all the difference.

Do you know the history of Tranquility? You think so. You say, “It was founded by the College of Bishops. It’s an establishment school,” and you are done with it. But I ask you, Who was at the college? I remind you, the faltering three southern bishops (I call them Wilso, Stillso, and Creedalong) and my ancestor Bromides Authenticeus were in the battistero too. Tranquility’s foundational grant came from Mitrik, yes; but after that, the southern dioceses were its benefactors. The south made Tranquility wealthy and influential.

What was it that made Tranquility an anti‑Erastrian school? Was it the money from Mitrik—or the diocesan ideal, the southern ideal? You know nothing about it. You hear nothing of it. You are bad historians. Those of you who are historians, doubly so. I possess the documented evidence of what I say. It is my family that knows it. Yet, you do not listen to me. You are jokers and tell your jokes.

In fellowship despite it,

Authenticrates Minerva, Conservancy Professor

Moonday, 3rd Patchwall, 574cy

I possess the dated autograph of this text, handwritten six months after the undated bifolium was first distributed, in Growfest, 574cy. By then the autograph had been transcribed dozens of times by members of the informal “club” (it was not yet the Divergent Underground but its forerunner, known variously as “the Subversionaries,” “the Antithesizers,” “the Assassins of Magesteria,” “the Quiblers,” etc.) that Minerva addressed. This was a loose collection of Grey College scholars that relished cow‑tipping authoritative exegeses. The club had much fun at Doc Authentic’s expense, it’s true, because he could not contain his love of family honor. Ha ha! Our jests were private and soon blew over, but the Tranquility bifolium was so good that it blew into public view, where the Historical Conservancy frowned on it. The conservancy even expressed an interest in confiscating the documents that Doc Authentic had claimed to possess. I know all about it because I got acquainted with the good Doctor that autumn in Dyvers, after I had interviewed him for my doctoral research into . . . Oh, do you have a question?

Yes, please. Professor Minerva’s pamphlet . . .

Bifolium!

. . . bi‑fo‑li‑um presumes some knowledge that we adventurers don’t have, apparently; for example, those anti‑erasers . . .

Erastrians!

. . . and things like that, maybe you could explain them?

Hmm. The pamphlet covers a lot of ground that you don’t need to see. I hadn’t thought to take the time. But coloring in the outlines won’t do any harm, I suppose.

In fact, it’s a good idea! It is past time that I acquaint you with Raoan popular religion and the proper rites of Reason’s church, which are not the same things although each has its attraction and beauty. I could make this lesson into a history of Tranquility College, Tranquilitism, the Tranquility movement, liturgical reform, and—if I sneak the anti‑Erastrians in—answer your question superbly!

§

~Tranquility College and the Tranquility movement

Despite the one thousand years that have passed since its origin in the Vale of Luna, the popular Raoan faith that people experience today remains tethered to the faith of the Flan pastoral folk from long ago. The valley is more settled, of course, and the people are too. The land they lived on in common is now all privately owned, and their ancient shrines and temples have been incorporated into churches, so an apse or a sanctuary in use today may be a temple’s relic. These old “blisters”—so called because they often look like bubbles swelling from a church’s exterior walls—accommodate ordinary festive and occasional days in popular ceremonies that do not require a priest: personal prayers, private remembrances, talismans, thanksgivings, and feasts such as hock‑carts, may‑poles, mid‑winter, and mid‑summer. Priests may be present on these occasions but they do not preside. A harvest‑ king, a may‑queen, or any such a one takes the lead by popular acclaim and gives thanks to Rao on the day.

The distinction between church and blister is of consequence. It exhibits the gradual imposition of church manners onto earlier Raoan things: first, on a shrine, a temple, a church, a parish; then, on a diocese, an establishment, a cathedral; later, on a high canon and, at last, on a government. Church and blister exhibit how local customs, occasions, ceremonies, and rites have survived with a national church superimposed— a diverse but still catholic Raoanism.

Keoland’s occupation of Veluna lasted from 355‑438cy and prompted a transformation of Raoan religion. Actually, there were three remarkable transformations, one each in the free north, the captive south, and the restored “greater Veluna” following liberation. In the north, during occupation, the archclericy persisted as the national government but the perception and nature of its authority were changed. At its founding, the theocracy’s authority had been vested in the canon (and many lesser high clerics) and was dependent on the cooperation and tolerable good will of the dioceses and counties. But occupation reduced the theocracy's extent to a lesser fraction of itself, and though it still claimed to legitimately rule all the seven counties and Veluna City, the difference between claim and reality was apparent to everyone and had a corrosive effect. After liberation, the theocrats suspected disloyalty everywhere, and to suppress it, they exerted political power forcefully top down. The immediate vertical control was felt everywhere, prompting the mocking overtone of most contemporary references to “the free north.”

In the south, the bishops (other than Kempton, who fled to the unoccupied portion of his diocese) had remained in their cathedrals even as Keoland’s armies closed in. But they ceased excercising their authority ostentatiously. On the contrary, at first they had expected to be arrested each passing day. But the Keoish governors discovered the ambivalence of Velunars toward theocratic government. They tempted the southern bishops to separate their sees from the archclericy while maintaining continuity in provincial parish life. Popular local customs—especially those tied to the blisters—were encouraged while great national observances were not. The theocracy in Mitrik took the opposite approach; the bishops were caught between the local and the national Raoan faith. We may say that, in the south, the faith of the blisters would be invited into the churches; in the north, the faith of the churches would expell the blisters.

Consequently, in the south the bishops came to embody unity in the variety of popular rites, while in the north, they represented ritual conformity. Two very different understandings of episcopal authority had taken hold. Southern bishops were styling themselves as equals and believed that Raoan catholicism was embodied in episcopal collegiality; the northern bishops derived their authority from the Canon of Veluna and understood catholicism as proceeding from canonical good graces.

After liberation, these two ecclesiologies were synthesized by the episcopal conclave in the Eademer Battistero. But the synthesis was neither clean nor clinical. The big losers were the local parishes in Veluna City that during occupation had been treated as a rabble (they had no bishop) and been placed directly under the canon’s authority. But the three northern bishops (Whitehale, Grayington, and Kempton) were also submitted to canonical authority, and they would support the canon’s man, the titular bishop of Verbobonc, when he was made the Archbishop of Veluna City.

The southern bishops accepted their archbishop after gaining two concessions. First, the canon’s authority would not be superior in the dioceses and the archbishop would not be a monarch among bishops. Second, each of the southern bishops was given something he wanted. Falsridge received assurance that his county would not be involved in Furyondy’s annexation of Bissel. Lorrish obtained the official sanction of his liturgical reforms (we will discuss these later). Valkurl—the poorest diocese— received a permanent financial consideration from the archclericy. And Devarnish—the see of Bromides Authenticeus— was granted Tranquility College.

It was because Authenticeus got so little—a college founded by a donation from the canon’s treasury—that he was understood to have been the canon’s man. But Canon Raowen had wanted to found what he had proposed to call “Canon’s College,” and Authenticeus' Tranquility would prove—as his great‑great‑great‑grandson Authenticrates maintained— more important to Velunar history than the other concessions combined.

The difference between Canon’s and Tranquility was not a school by another name; it was a different system of patronage. Canon’s would be funded by the archclerical treasury; Tranquility would be funded by diocesan bequest. Everyone understood the difference, but Raowen conceded because the canonical coffers were poor and Bishop Authenticeus’ signature to the concordat was the last one needed to restore the archclericy.

Canon Raowen did not expect the emphatic commitment of the southerners to Tranquility—not to its endowment and construction alone but to the supply of its faculty, administration, and student enrollment. Within thirty years Tranquility College was large and rich, almost Veluna’s pre‑eminent institution, third only to the Canonry and the Archclericy.

In 461cy, Tranquility’s great rival was at last founded in Mitrik. Canon’s quickly became a minor priestly seminary and a major school of law, while Tranquility flourished as a humanist school centered on the Raoan tradition. The rivalry would inform the first of the great sixth‑century troubles that befell the western Nyr Dyv region:

The Tranquilitarian controversy.

§

SCENARIO SIX—THE TROUBLED SIXTH CENTURY

§

Chapter 24: The Tranquility movement, Dyvers, and the “obscure D”

It was laws and taxes; that’s the standard view. And presumably, it’s true. Taxes are proverbially certain, and of course there must be laws to collect them. The logic speaks for itself. And, so, in light of necessity, I commence my history of the troubled sixth century by heeding sage advice: “Follow the taxes.”

Eight years ater Veluna’s liberation, the teetering Raoan archclericy was given its second foundation by the unanimous vote of eight bishops in the Eademer Battistero, in 446cy. Gratefully, Canon Raowen requited his saviors by implementing tax and legal reforms in the provinces; the seven counties of Veluna were each of them subsumed under their coextensive dioceses while Veluna City was received into the purposefully created archdiocese, making the bishops the reformed theocracy’s judges and tax collectors. Extensive legal reforms were implemented to effect this transference of civil authority. The county courts, which had never before been subject to appeal, were deferred to a supreme court for further adjudification according to a secularized code of canonical law, and gradually, the "canon’s code" was reached into the lower courts. Under the new archclericy the counties—judges and tax collectors in Veluna since before the founding of Voll—were semi-autonomous provincial governments no longer.

Raowen then reduced the Celestial Order of the Moons, which had nearly been the secular national government a few years before, to a representative house of congress with no more constitutional authority than to advise the canon on matters of interest to aristocrats and wealth. Although it had taken four centuries longer than historians will credit it, the tax and legal reforms that followed the Eademer Concordat would lift the Canon of Veluna at last to the level of a theocratic monarch, the realization (so it would seem) of his schemes.

Despite the Celestial Orders nominally equal staanding, the College of Bishops’ greater importance was obvious from the first. The bishops effectively displaced the noble families as peers of the realm. The princes were now subordinate to clerics, and although the bishops were also subordinate to the canon in many respects, yet they had won concessions in the battistero that would allow them often to act independently.

Taking on political authority as an archclerical house of congress had been a gambit played by the bishops no less than by the canon, mixing as it did the national politics of the theocrats with the politics of the provinces, whose prerogatives had been removed to the bishops from the princes. Although the constitutional role of the college was only to advise the canon, yet the bishops (especially in the southern dioceses) were much nearer to the popular faith of the people than was the canon at this time. The bishops' appeal to Veluna's faith had saved the theocracy from abolishement, and afterward, the advice of the College of Bishops still carried political weight. On the other hand, the bishops risked associating with the unpopular theocracy and allowing the political canon to display a spiritual concern for his flock, more like the shepherd of Veluna today than he had been before.

Calculation was everywhere.The nobles had been set aside as the archclericy’s third wheel, and with secularists also marginalized, the canon and the bishops contended for control of the tricycle. The Archclericy of Veluna had been nearly void going into to the Eademer Battistero, and the bishops had restored it. Yet how much theocracy was needed for a national administration whose political responsibilities were being shifted to the dioceses? The theocrats seemed set adrift and without purpose, yet we have met the new anchors of their support: canonical law in county courts and, in Mitrik, the new Supreme Court and the school of canonical law at Canon’s College. Surprisingly for a nation whose history had long been about spirituality and temporality, legality was the center of things as the fifth centurycy became the sixth.

These controversies took fifty years after the Eademer Battistero to coalesce into one decisive contest: the Temporalities Decree. In 497cy,. the supreme court ruled that “the Temporalities” was a legitimate exercise of political power that had been invested in the canon with the consent of the bishops in the Eademer Battistero. The ruling brought on a crisis of conscience in the Raoan church that the bishops, in their capacity as diocesan shepherds, had to salve. The Temporalities Decree affirmed that the dioceses and other Raoan institutions were the Canon of Veluna's financial responsibility, endowing him with the authority to reform them when necessary under advice from the College of Bishops. In the Supreme Court's decision, the bishops had agreed to this in the battistero and in principle when financial donations from the canonical treasurey had been accepted in perptuity by the Diocese of Valkurl and by Bishop Bromides Authenticeus in founding of Tranquility College.

Did the Canon of Veluna have responsibility for reforming spiritual institutions, even to the extent of reforming them completely? Did the Temporalities require the canon's interference in the bishops’ personal and spiritual conduct too? Could the bishops reject that interference despite their subordination in spiritual matters to the archbishop appointed by the canon?

In 499cy,. five of the eight bishops of the Church of Rao accepted the Supreme Court’s ruling in favor of the canon and the Temporalities Decree. The Raoan episcopacy was subject to the Canon of Veluna, and many of the ordinary priests and of the faithful of Rao were made to see the bishop’s legislative advice in a new light. The College of Bishops had become spiritually problematic.

But the Tranquility movement was much more than an ecclesial regret. It had far-reaching social, commercial, and political repercussions that the reformists and the Tranquilitists were very aware of. I have seen the best evidence of this, although as things stand I can produce only a part of it, the first and last sheets (in autograph) of a journal kept by Sir Porrish Poundlace over a six-week stay, in 514cy, at Belickling Hall, the splendid estate on Tempton Water inheritent to the female line of the notorious Mrs Plimpson, later Lady Broile, the Baroness of Broile, Sir Porrish’s friend.

§

~The Belickling Hall diary

Porrish Poundlace had been a vagabond esquire and a racy novelist from before his boon companion Prince Thrommel (not the one from Mistress and Prince but his grandfather that would be King Thrommel Ⅱ) enobled him. The vagabond and soon-to-be-Sir Porrish kept journals about his life among aristocrats as storage for the furniture of his books; his stay at Belickling Hall upholstered a front row seat to the enduring affair of His Royal Highness and the aforementioned Lady Broile (aka Lady Plimpson, Mrs Plimpson, née Liberta Purchisse), and the journal records a time when the celebrated divorcée was much less infamous (and rather less a lady) than she later became.

I will tell you how I obtained the autograph sheets once you have read them. Poundlace, you will notice, economized on sheets by not indenting paragraphs, writing on both sides, and crossing on one.

(First sheet)

Waterday, 5th Reaping, 514cy

Belickling Hall

I have avoided all further expense of entertaining HRH and his accomplice Lord Landlard by transporting us from Kissail Town to Belickling Hall, where the Plimpson-Purchisses may better afford them. Legal (WARN your readers to pronounce his name LEGgull) and his sister ▽Legal and Liberta Purchisse were the children of wealthy Raoan Churches merchant Sir Highrose Purchisse. Liberta (aka Lady Plimpson, Mrs Plimpson, and Baroness of Broile) married Lord Hoemer Plimpson, Baron of Broile (later Lord Plimpson, Baron of Aimesup and Duke of the Reach), in 514cy. (Eds) are ecstatic to have the prince, so, I have combined their service and my advantage by deferring my costs to Belickling for the duration. Landlard brought Prince Thrommel to Kissail, I doubt not, to pump me for information about the Raoan Churches. HRH fishes for a quiet introduction to Legal, which is why he was being so damned expensive in town. I will pretend to be ignorant of my suspicisons while here, though, because if HRH is interested in the Raoan Churches it’s because he intends to tax them. I wonder if Lady Liberta can charm him out of it? She has that reputation, although I have never appreciated it. She’s short and plump, to my eye. Her lord fell head over heels, yes, but I think he’s recovered by now. The lady was modestly, almost plainly dressed when she greeted us. But after dinner (and our fourth glass of wine), the gentlemen—I am liberal enough to include myself in their company—were all besotted. Damn me, those blue eyes! The way they wink, nod, glide, and roll! Libby tells jokes like a man in the voice and vocabulary of girl. I watched her closely, and every quarter hour she favored HRH with a few more glimpses and smiles, damn me if she didn’t. By the end, we (the prince, Landlard, and I—I admit no reference to her husband or brother) had felt the lodge of Cupid’s dart. In the morning, though, we were in our proper places. Lord Hoemer suggested a walk to the church and Legal seconded it: “Yes, St Sophia’s is my sister’s project. She’s renovating it in the gothic style. We must go. Libby’s quite into this Tranquility business, you know.” I was right, then: the prince’s visit is about imports and tariffs. The talk on the way was all about Tranquility, and I must say that, although I keep informed on the business side of things, I

←(over)→

took a lesson in what motivates the religious types to buy our trinkets. There are shelves of them in St Sophia’s reconstructed blister: Canon’s candles, crook-snuffers, peace pipes, serenity sticks, wisdom books, sensible beads, etc. for sale on the blister steps. When Lady Liberta showed us their rituals and purposes I was nearly moved to participation, despite that I had supplied every trinket myself. In the end as a donation to our cause I bought a venture cap with “Sir Porrish Poundlace, supplier” sewn in. St Sophia’s has become very solemn. I’d seen it many years ago, when it was barely a stone cabin. The church now has excellent nooks and crannies filled with saints’ statues, window depictions, a flowing font of wisdom, and many things besides, each with its proper rite and habbit for purchase or rent in the vestibule. As Lady Liberta explained the mysteries she whispered them so low that we could scarcely hear her, angling her mouth toward Prince Thrommel’s ear all the while. It’s too late for him—he’s converted! When the sorceress draped a white surplice (taken from the church’s fabulous sacristry) over her black dress (like widows-weeds that reveal too much), swinging the folds by swaying her arms, she made a tempting devil! Did I say, short and plump? Lady Liberta will reform your ideas of love and beauty. When she showed the church’s new organ, playable although not every pipe was up, she showed it to advantage. By chance the builder was “John Pope, Organ-maker by appointment to HRH Prince Thrommel, Duke of Freeborough,” the identical HRH that then handed her up the steep steps to the loft where she, seated at his organ, pulled all the stops out on “Lo! he comes, with cries ascending,” and lo! as the regal hymn spent its last gasp, at the holiest of moments, a thunderstorm broke upon St Sophia’s and a resounding, bellowing, blowing, pouring rain overcame us. Nor passed the storm too soon but dwindled to a sullen, soaking downpour that stranded us disconsolately a wet mile from Belickling. The prince, a little stupid at the bast of times, was soon bored, but fortunately his boon companion Lord Landlard is a practiced hand and was equipped with playing-cards. “But damme,” said the mildly heartened royal, glancing implausibly toward the church-builder and the foreman (commoners from outside that had come in from the rain), “if we aren’t two players short for Ups and Downs.” This parlour game, which is ruled

↑(cross)↓

so as to pair couples off for bed, can be played in a group, and the prince was up for it. Fortunately, Lord Landlard had the resolution of this difficulty, too: “We will call the prince “my lord” and each other “sir” and “lady” except for Legal, whom we will call “mister,” so making everyone at table comfortable and the necessary party of eight.” In that arrangement we played through the storm, and if Lady Liberta had seemed briefly transcendent she was one of us sinners now. On the game’s final round, the prince produced a seraph and thought he had won her, but the lady cried out, “Ha! the deuce takes you!” and trumped his one with a two. (I wonder who dealt her that duece; her husband, most likely.) The hand would have coupled the prince and the lady either way, but the prince seemed pleased to have Lady Liberta win him. The rain had stopped, and so, bidding goodbye to St Sophia’s, we trumbled back to Belickling. The bedrooms that night began with their correct occupants but I doubt they stayed that way. Whether or no, in the morning Lord Hoemer remembered he had business in town, and from that day . . .

the sun had gone down by the time we left the courthouse, and like the streets of Kissail, Prince Thrommel was in the dark. “How,” asked he, “can those candles be leased? You cannot lease a candle.” Why not? “Because they burn down. You can’t lease a consumable!” We don’t. It’s a renewable. “You told that to the judge. But, damme, the candles burn down just the same.” It’s not the candles, Your Highness. We lease the blessings. “Damme, if blessed candles don’t burn the same as others.” The candles, yes, but not the blessings; those are renewable. “But in the courtroom you said they’re no good anymore.” Hah hah! No, we didn’t. The spent candle is no good. The blessing is just fine. “But you told the judge it expired.” A blessing never expires, my Prince, only its effect. “Its effect? What good is a blessing without an effect?” The effect must be renewed. “By lease?” Exactly! “Oh, dear gods. I won’t have this. You Raoan Churchers are leasing your blessings!” You cannot lease a blessing. You renew it. “How, in the gods’ names, except by paying the rent?” By burning a candle, Your Highness. “But the candle must be . . . bought?” Naturally. “Where?” From us. “So, you’re SELLING the blessing.” No, only the candle. “But effectively, the blessing comes with the candle.” No, the effect of the blessing is renewed per the lease. “So, the blessing is leased!” No, the effect. “A blessing IS an effect. I bless you: you are blessed. You cannot help it.” You cannot help the real effect, of course. But the effect remains virtual unless you lease it from us. “A virtual effect?” Yes. It’s a manner of delivery. Of logistics. Suppose, Prince, that you are far, far away. “What does that have to do with it?” True. An error on my part. Suppose, instead, that you are too busy to give the quantity of blessings that everyone wants. “I’ll bless everyone at once.” They don’t want to be blessed all at once. They want a blessing of their own. "Why can’t each get their own all at once?" That would be impersonal. Think about you and your subjects. They want to see you up close and personal, right? Well, it’s the same with the Canon of Veluna’s blessings. “Damme, the people are nowhere near him. It’s a candle.” It’s a blessing, made and renewed by the canon according to the sacrifices people make. “What sacrifices?” Oh, Your Highness! The sacrifice is burning the candle. “Holy moley!” said the prince after a long, royal pause. “I see it! Yes, I see it all! The people are virtually buying a blessing and

←(over)→

thanking you for it on a monthly basis!” Leasing it. They lease the blessing. “Ye gods! What a remarkable scam!” Scam? No, it’s a delivery system. It’s the system we operate, an operating system for the virtual delivery of effective blessings. “I see! I see! Your operating system allows everyone to renew their personal supplies of candles for sale and of blessings for lease on a monthly basis. People receive all of this without getting too much, because they won’t be getting the real effect of the blessing until they burn the actual candle per the terms of the lease.” Yes, my prince. And there is more. Virtual delivery won’t be restricted to candles and blessings. We can lease anything to anyone in the same way. We call it ‘streaming content’ or ‘content delivered in a virtual stream.’ The real effect of a virtual blessing is only the beginning. Once we have established, as a principle of law, that the Raoan Churches of Furyondy has the right to lease its real effects, we can make this work for all kinds of things, not only for consumable products. For example, if people want the real effect of virtually viewing our stained-glass windows, they will lease virtual admission passes before virtually accessing the streaming content of our virtual churches. The real effect is our property, after all. We hold the rights to any real effect that our content may provide, and we may lease the effect to anyone that pays. Content will be streaming within a decade, effectively, and otherwise, any effect of any content that our virtual OS may provide would actually belong to someone once they had really paid for it. “True,” said the prince, “and we don’t want that. But, hang on a minute. If everyone is leasing your church’s content, what will happen to my excise taxes? What will happen to sales tax? The Royal Treasury will go broke.” “Oh, la!” said Lady Liberta, soothing the prince’s doubts by tickling his ear, “the treasury may do better than that. Really, pookie, we can help you. We’ll just redefine leasing as buying, and the excise will come back. We’ll do that for you, because we’re friends, right?” “Yes, pookie,” His Highness admitted, “we’re very friendly. But I’m not sure that my father, the king, will go for it.” “Oh, no problem,” cooed his mistress. “We’ll get him to agree to it by taking one, little, legal action at a time. He’ll come along, you’ll see. Together, the king and the Raoan Churches will master the cloud.” “The cloud? What’s that?” “Think of it as the place where real people keep virtually everything that virtually matters.” “I see.” “Oh, pookie, of course you do!”

“It’s not funny, and let us hope your disbelief does not carry over to the next point I make, because it’s important. The lawsuit mentioned in Porrish Poundlace’s Belickling journal really took place, and the journal, read in its entirety, proves the legal proceedings to have been the effective cause of a momentous historical event: the independence of Dyvers, the City of Sails and capital of the former Viceroyalty of Furyondy, from the Kingdom of Furyondy, in 526cy.

§

~The Free Lands of Dyvers: A precursory Mistress and Prince

Although it has proved (I have private information showing it to be so) greatly significant, historians still gloss Dyvers’ independence in the way it had seemed to be at the time—so nearly unaccountable and insignificant that it almost need not have happened:

The city had contributed heavily in money, goods, and men to the establishment and prosperity of Furyondy. But because of Fuyondy’s alliance and close ties with Veluna, whose policies the Gentry of Dyvers saw as restrictive, the city declared its independence in 526cy. King Thrommel Ⅱ allowed this act to pass unchallenged.

The city had been an important trading center, with lake and river traffic from Bissel, Nyrond, Urnst, and even lands as far away as Perrenland and the Theocracy of The Pale. But Dyvers proclaimed itself a free city in 526cy,/span>. alleging that it was uncomfortable with Furyondy allying with a state (Veluna) whose policies Dyvers found overly restrictive. This was probably just a pretext, but King Thrommel Ⅱ of Furyondy allowed the secession to pass in return for Dyvers continuing to contribute taxes and levies to Furyondian coffers.

Dyvers had been the capital of the Viceroyalty of Furyondy and still served as a welcome port to goods and travelers. The palace of the viceroy rivaled that of his colleagues in the west, and its domed central structure and austere stone towers are cited in travelogues as among the finest examples of Oeridian architecture. But Furyondy's relationship with Veluna troubled the freethinking folk of the city, as Veluna's clerical rulers were highly principled, rather ascetic, and encouraged great donations to church coffers. When many cities in Furyondy established a code of "canon law," replete with church courts stocked with Raoan doctrine and Cuthbertine punishments, the Gentry of Dyvers decided that enough was enough. Preparing for the worst, they informed the crown of their intention to split from Furyondy in 526cy. Perhaps because Furyondy feared the growing power of Greyhawk and felt it needed to ally more deeply in the region, Thrommel Ⅱ, the reigning monarch, allowed the secession to pass unchallenged.

This is nonsense. No king or kingdom allows its largest, most prosperpous city to declare independence so casually. True, Furyondy’s political relations with Veluna were as much the pretext as the reason for Dyvers’ independence, and, true again, ever since the Eademer Concordat the difference between “canon law" and secular law had grown thin in Veluna. But this would not have been a problem for Furyondy and Dyvers except on other, historical considerations.

Although the archclericy of Veluna and the secular kingdom of Furyondy have been separate and sovereign governments since Veluna declared its independence in 254cy, many Raoan churches continued to exist in Furyondy although not as part of Veluna's Church of Rao. These churches had originally composed the Imperial Church of Rao in the viceroyalty and been reconstituted as the Raoan Churches of the Kingdom of Furyondy—one in faith (they claimed) with Veluna's church although unbeholden to the archclericy, which the Raoan Churches regarded as an ecclesiological institution, a matter of church polity inessential to faith.

But differences of polity often settle into differences of faith; the Imperial Raoan Churches had always appealed and continue to appeal to wealthy and aristocratic citizens primarily, while in Veluna, due to the archclericy’s political volatility, the church leans heavily on popular faith. But the social values of elites and populations will differentiate very quickly, so, today for example, the elite and liberalized Raoan Churches ordain women while the popular Church of Rao does not. Similarly, the liturgical reforms that over the past century have incorporated most blisters in Veluna into churches only recently reached Furyondy where, historically, blisters had barely existed.

A great gap, nearly unbridgeable, had been opened between the Church of Rao and the Raoan Churches by the Eademer Concordat's declamation against “greedy Furyondians fomenting the apostasy of imperialism in Veluna.” Thoroughly in disagreement, Furyondy’s elites had decried the archclericy for its abuse of sacred power in attaining secular ambition. As Canon Raowen’s legal and tax reforms were more and more interwoven into Veluna’s civic affairs, the Raoan Churches objected in the interest of Furyondian liberality in politics and religion.

But the reforms that were initiated by the Eademer Concordat did not concern only law and taxes. They brought liturgical reform as well and a reconsideration of how tariffs may benefit not only lawyers and merchants but the Archclericy of Veluna and the Church of Rao. In Furyondy—where Raoan faith remained more influential than elsewhere in the former Ahlissan empire—the new tarriffs offered liberal elites in the Raoan Churches a way to make money by importing from Veluna the material and practical aspects of a spiritual reform.

Sir Porrish Poundless’s journal at Belickling Hall captured the first retraceable currents of these reforms in Furyondy: a litigation before the Furyondian Crown’s Court Civil over new legal principles for importing and retailing liturgical appurtances in Kissail, a city and Raoan Churches stronghold on the north side of the Velverdyva River. By the day of the trial, in Reaping, 514cy,/span>. the spread of “old Raoanism” in Furyondy had reached from Kissail along the river north to Caronis and Baranford and south to Verbobonc and Dyvers. The wealth and influence of the Raoan Churches brought this to the attention of Prince Thrommel Ⅱ, who went to Kissail to see for himself.

§

~Liberalism and liturgical reform

The spread of Raoan reform went less noticed in other places, but Dyvers was an extraordinarily mercantile and free-thinking city with centuries of settled commercial law that resisted the innovations. The City of Sails disparaged the Raoan mixture of ritualism, legalism, and commercialism as “liberal religion,” a reference to the “liberties” taken in theology and law by wealthy Raoan Churches merchants under the influence of canonical law and liturigical reform formulated, in Mitrik, at Canon’s College and taught, in Devarnish, at Tranquility College. These two schools were opposed to each other in Veluna but were identified as one and the same in mercantile, free-thinking Dyvers.

I do not know the city that well know people that do. Dyvers is generally considered a fine place; I count among its admirers. Its libraries and museums contain the most important of the ancient documents and artifacts of historical significance to the central Flanaess, stowed away centuries ago and far from where they had been looted in the interest of “preserving viceregal heritage.” These warehouses are frequently the starting points of my historical research. The earliest documents and artifacts (among which I prowl) are erratically catalogued and may take days, weeks, months, or—may Lendor anesthetize me, the memory hurts!—so long as a semester to discover.

I have been urged by medical researchers to advise you, my adventurous documentarians, of the following item: Anyone disinterring the recumbent dust and particulate aerosols of those deathly scrolls will contribute to experimental knowledge of the effects of the Acari (a subclass of the Arachnida) on pervious human tissues (the lungs, eyes, hands, nose, and scalp) that said Acari might otherwise never perv. Such is the consequence, my neophyte paleographers, of boldly going where no one has been in a long, long time.

There is a close community of freethinkers in Dyvers where I presented—in 574cy—a letter of introduction allowing me to room and board among them for seven months while I researched my dissertation thesis. And, please, no gossipping among you, my class of snickering Snearwells and Snakes at my private school for scandal, about the cankerworm of freethought having infected my brain at that time. The sweet species had eaten its way into me years earlier, as you know, during my undergraduate days at Grey even before I applied to study with Prof Daesnar Braden, the infamous skeptical philosopher and my dinner companion (you may recall) in Luekish one night with also George Byron, Lord Gordyn, the poet of Missolonghi. Prof Braden had provided me the recommendation letter I mentioned above, so, you will understand that I was thinking pretty freely well before I arrived in the City of Sails.

Besides, my research is far too dry for catching and spreading the infection of licentious academia. My area of expertise . . .

Whoa, Professor. Go back to that bit about Raoan ritualism and commercialism being “liberal religion.” You didn’t cite any evidence, so, how do you know?

Because, as I was saying, I study the history of commercial shipping on the Nyr Dvy and tributary and distributary rivers as far back in time as I can manage. I may assure you that, although there is much to be learned by raising sunken ships and decyphering decayed bills of lading, it isn’t going to free shackled minds if it wanted to. What it may do is affirm facts that lie sunk under volumes of wishy-washy misconceptions. So it is that I possess evidence that specific sixth-century shipping practices that are usually presumed to be the natural consequence of Furyondian trade actually began with the importation of Raoan ritualist apurtanences from Veluna into Furyondy. So it was that when I was shown the Belickling Hall journal of Sir Porrish Poundlace I recognized at once the significance of the litigation it describes taking place in Kissail.

Sir Porrish’s journal is, in fact, a rich store of historical significances, so, perhaps I ought to tell you how I came to read it.

⚜

One day, when the acari in the crypts of the Mouseion Library had pervaded me with particularly injurious abandon, and I (having no hands clean of the infection) was sanitizing my eyes lacrymositously and encouraging my recovery through pitiful sobs while seated, head between knees, on the steps to the library floors, I felt a comforting parental hand on my shoulder and heard what was, in the circumstances, the kindliest voice imaginable to me.

“My poor fellow, can I help?”

“It’s nothing,” I cried, “only the dust. I’m not emotional.”

“Of course not, and I have just the thing,” affirmed the good Samaritan, producing a stopped bottle that he displayed to me. “Eye drops,” he said, “of my own concoction. They do wonders against mites.”

“Really?” said I, weeping like a hopeful child.

“Really and truly.” The old man seated himself beside me with an easy dexterity that made him familiar at once. “I explore the crypts myself, you know, and always bring this with me. Look to the ceiling!”

I watched the dropper emerge at the corners of my eyes, the liquid bead as clear as water. What could go wrong?

Plop. Plop.

I was relieved! I betokened my thanks through better tears while reaching for my handkerchief.

“Oh, no, wipe not with that infested rag. I have a clean one. Tell me, what errand took you below?”

I told him of my research and so was introduced to Professor Authenticrates Minerva, the Divergent Undergound’s Doctor Authentic. Of course, I would not know him by that sobriquet until after he had introduced me to the Quiblers, the informal society from which the DU soon emerged. Prof Minerva had fled from Greyhawk College to Dyvers in advance of the growing scandal over his Tranquility bifolium and the consequent antagonism of his employer, the Historical Conservancy. I knew about it from him even before I met the Quiblers. Mutual suspicion was rife among them because the authorities were constantly pursuing the professor at the behest of the Conservancy. The police were being informed of Minerva’s actions and whereabouts, and the Divergent Underground was formed out of the need for a reliable subset of Quiblers to privately aid him. I was a founding DU member not because they trusted me on short acquaintance but because Minerva had given me the first and last sheets of the autograph Belickling Hall journal as evidence of the journal’s existence should it ever be impounded. The professor had obtained the journal autograph by virtue of being Sir Porrish Poundlace’s nephew, and because I was marginally connected to the Quiblers and came recommended by Prof Braden, Minera trusted me on a two-month acquaintance, believing that the pages would be safer with me than any other.

And so it is that straight from the horse’s autograph I know the tale: “liberal religion” was originally a term for the ritualist and commercial innovations introduced into Furyondy through the connection of the Raoan Churches and the Church of Rao. The term had been coined earlier by lawyers at Canon’s College for whom “liberal” had been a reference to policies instituted by the Archclericy of Veluna after the Eademer Concordat had “liberated” the archclericy from greedy Furyondian heretics. Liberal religion was uniquely unwelcome in Dyvers but spread easily to other cities with well established Raoan churches. It moved inland from Baranford on the Royal Highway to Worlende and Fountainspring, where canonical law became important not only to commercial legislation but to all aspects of Furyondian civil trial and litigation. In Fountainspring, a lawsuit brought by the Baron of Littleberg against Lord Plimpson, Duke of the Reach, opened a public controversy over Old Furyondian versus the new canonical law, and the long time affair of Plimpson’s estranged wife and King Thrommel Ⅱ lifted the proceedings to a national scandal.

Overnight, the Duchess of the Reach was demeaned to “the notorious Mrs Plimpson,” and more details of her half decade of love with the king were exposed every day or week. The scandal forced the king to quietly and gradually allow independence for Dyvers, where opposition to liberal religion and to the Plimpsons had been strongest. But the scandal’s original impetus had been the civil trial in Fountainspring, so, “liberalism” soon lost the association with religion that it had in Dyvers in favor of an only political and economic connotation. In the end, Old Furyondian law was largely reaffirmed, although social, political, and economic liberalism retain a place in civic debate that persists today. Mrs Plimpson was remade a lady when the king bought and transferred to her her husband’s entitlement, the Barony of Broile, which was his from before he became Duke of the Reach. Mrs Plimpson then assumed the name of her barony, and today, Lady Liberta Broile’s descendents own lovely Belickling Hall on the beautiful Temton Water.

This was the first (although now less remembered) occasion when a Velunar mistress and a Furyondian prince nearly upset the establishment. I leave it to you to decide whether you like the one or the other better.

I like Mrs Plimpson!

I like Jolene!

I don’t see much difference between them.

Really?

What the hell do you mean by that?

One was a princess, the other was a slut!

One had a love life, the other gave up.

Princess . . . duchess . . . who gives a f– . . .

. . . you see, because liberalism quickly lost its association with religion, the significant roles played by the Church of Rao, by the Raoan Churches, and by canonical law in the Mrs Plimpson affair were publicly suppressible—and it suited the authorities on all sides to see them suppressed. Professor Minerva reached a silent, uneasy agreement with the Historical Conservancy to keep a secret and returned to Greyhawk to resume his academic career. The secret is kept today by the Democratic Underground, probably. After Doctor Authentic’s death nine years ago, I do not know what became of Sir Porrish Poundlace’s Belickling Hall journal apart from the two sheets in my possession.

For a while, the true but strange history (as I told it) was more widely known. By 526cy, public recognition of the informal and ancient alliance of Furyondy and Veluna had reached a low ebb; especially in the kingdom the esteem of it had soured. But when King Thrommel allowed the independence of Dyvers, he brought cryptic references to the Mrs Plimpson affair back into currency. Furyondians referred to the scandal by way of the cryptic symbol the “obscure D.”

By using the "D" journals, newspapers, and public jesters mooted jocund, even farcical allusions to the kings infamous (d)alliance with his Raoan Churches friends, a pun played just as well on (d)allying with his (d)ally. You may refer to the nearest excerpted blockquote from above to see how it was done.

§

Interlude: High Moon Inn encore, the Red Monk’s tale

Although it is not always the way in Grimwood-under-Sky, the forest sleeps tonight. The innkeeper was looking conspiratorial—he wanted that book—but if he had friends to call on, they had not appeared. Although our heroes were prepared for a fraught departure if that were how it came, the guests of the High Moon Inn were content when the storyteller began the second tale of Prince Thrommel’s last words.

Adjacent the pond in the forecourt of the temple, witnessed by no one and drunk on our feet, we addressed the red-clad assailants. We outnumbered them (so hopelessly) two to one. Where to go? They were unnerving, uncanny. Where to look? They moved in perpetual gyration, proffering no weakness and ceding no advantage. Two of us had fallen, although we had touched none, when an enemy took an (unaccountable) arrow to his back—hence they kept to their rounds until another of them departed the same way. At a signal, in unison, the comprehensive whirlwind then vaulted to the temple steps, turned to face the hidden archer (where he might seem to be) and caught us confounded between.

Thrommel came from the shadows, and dropping his bow, he pulled his dagger and cried, “Our turn, boys!” We charged with a will, but from the temple’s roof there leapt a red fear, a javelin streak, a scarlet banner, flung and unfurling across the night sky. The flyer landed beyond us (the paving stones easing to cushion its fall) and Thrommel turned to face it alone.

Our fascination lasted a moment too long. A shuriken surged through a fellow’s ear, lodging in his skull. We returned to the fight. The enemy came at us, cycling our ranks, scything us down, until we were outnumbered and they had disarmed us, untroubled to kill.
