They bid us kneel to witness the combat of Thrommel and their cheif. I cannot say how it had been going, but it cannot have been well. The red monk was toying, silent, evasive, strong, and more graceful than the scarlet silk it wore while eluding and soaring impossibly high.

When Thrommel saw us made captive he yielded, placing his dagger’s point on his heart and offering his assailant the hilt. “Set them free,” he said.

“You fight well,” the monk replied.

“You too, girlfriend.”

The red monk laughed, unwinding the silk ribbons that bound her face and hair. She was beautiful, unoerthly, a heavenly sigh and, oh, so sweetly so! The liquefaction of her clothes jostled the lilles of the pond as she bid the prince go before her out of the temple.

We captains were set free. I live to tell the tale, and tonight, I, Captain Lorenzo D'Amico, bid you—farewell!

The adventurers did not stop to acknowledge the applause as they exited the High Moon Inn, but the storyteller flourished The Veil of Lunacy defiantly at the innkeeper on their way, getting a chiding from the others for the trouble.

The innkeeper bore them ill will, of course. The forest took them deep into the night and on to Doraka’a.

A story well told, although—we may ask wheter the book knew anything more concerning the abduction of Prince Thrommel. Had it more to say than what was contained in the two tales told?

§

Chapter 25: Prince Thrommel’s disappearance

About Prince Thrommel’s death, Mistress and Prince had said nothing beyond alluding to fate and grief. Even so, the prince was surely not abducted by red monks, which is a tale of recent invention. Yet it is the story most often told today and, to me, a lost opportunity: I want to have asked Sir Edmore Wunsay whether, when I wrote to him, he knew the red monk’s tale? If so, he might have had something so urgent to tell me that it might have resigned him to an interview with me had I thought to mention it. Wunsay, after all, had led an investigation into Thrommel’s disappearance shortly after the event in 570cy. The investigation had been his last (and unofficial) public service before his retirement to Castle Elfride.

Three investigations in fact were conducted at the time. One was commissioned by the King of Furondy, purposed to locate and save the prince; another was commissioned by the Archclericy of Veluna, purposed to identify the prince’s abductors; the third was privately sponsored by the Celestial Order of the Moons and (fabulously!) by Lady Nancy Crewe, third Baroness of Broile, purposed to discover, save, and publish evidences of the incident, whatever they were. Lady Crewe often and infamously honored her grandmother by sponsoring investigations into hushed up royal scandals, and although the chief suspect in this case, the Canon of Veluna, was not a royal, he was close enough so that an improper exposure could (in theory) have toppled his stall.

Lady Crewe’s investigation was led by Countess Sulda Lorrish (on behalf of her sister, Jolene, Supreme Mistress of the Celestial Order) and Wunsay (on behalf of “every Furondian’s right to know”). There was in Furyondy a considerable appetite for discovering what the authorites were dismissing as a conspiracy theory. Lady Crewe believed it worth pressing the issue.

What the public suspected was obvious. Who had more to gain by Thrommel’s disappearance than the Canon of Veluna? Who, more reason to hide his involvement? Who, more resources to succeed in such a deception? No one thrice over. And when no ransom request followed the prince’s abduction (a kidnapping was the official expectation), the difference between disappearance and assassination narrowed.

But despite public doubt, King Belvor did not want his son’s tragedy to bring political strife with Veluna, and the royal court, too, considered it disruptive to peace and prosperity. Three months after they began, both official investigations concluded in a joint statement identifying the most likely perpetrators to be a remnant of the Temple of Elemental Evil, and the most likely outcome, the execution of a prince. Records, notes, and evidences were never publicly shared.

Lorrish and Wunsay took four months longer to close their investigation but had little more to say. Evidence was nonexistent, sketchy, or misleading; Lorrish returned to council her sister, and Wunsay escaped to his Castle Efride hermitage. But whatever details were to be known about Trommel’s abduction were known to the two romantic recluses, Jolene and Wunsay, and either might speak capably today to the possibility of red monks.

In 573cy, when rumors had begun linking the suddenly rampant Scarlet Brotherhood to the Sea Princes’ slave trade out of the Amedio Jungle, the Celestial Order conceived a connection to Thrommel’s abduction. The prince when he was captured had been campaigning against the Sea Princes in support of Keoland’s King Skotti, and although the piratical slavers had seemingly nothing to gain by abducting Thrommel and inviting international notice and condemnation, connecting them to the red monks might change that logic. But Veluna’s theocrats decried a revivification of public grief on flimsy evidence, Furyondy’s royal court showed no interest, either, and the Celestial Order—presumably at Jolene’s order or with her consent—immediately quelled all suspicion.

Eleven years later, at the end of the Greyhawk Wars, incitement came again. This is from a report made in the city of Greyhawk at the time:

The existence of the highly secretive and paranoiac Scarlet Brotherhood was first confirmed by returning travelers in 573cy. It seems incredible now that this monastic sect of religious militarists could have escaped notice for so long, but although the secretive nature of the monks became widely known, the existence of a veritable army of spies and assassins in the imperial courts of the Flanaess did not. At one time, a decade ago, the marriage of the Prince of Furyondy to the daughter of the highest-ranking noble of Veluna had promised to unite the two states and help resolve Furyondy’s internal squabbling. But the prince’s abduction, surely at the hands of Scarlet Brotherhood agents, destroyed those noble hopes. No one suspected the red monks at the time.

The excerpt is from a speech given in 584cy by Cobb Darg, mayor of the Free City of Irongate, against recognizing the Scarlet Brotherhood as a signatory to the Pact of Greyhawk ending the Greyhawk Wars. Irongate was under siege by the red monks at the time, which was being overlooked by other nations rushing to peace. In raising it to attention, Darg pointed out that his objection to the red monks was shared by Veluna.

Velunar diplomacy is the major hand at work in maintaining the cohesion of all the non-evil central Flanaess states, so far as such cohesion exists. Velunar agents have taken a strong role in unmasking Scarlet Brotherhood agents since the kidnapping of the Prince of Furyondy, while themselves acting as eyes and ears for the rulers of Veluna. We would do well to heed their warning.

Darg’s speech was largely responsible for a gathering conviction, widely held today, that Veluna’s diplomats and spies had long worked for the security and unity of the Flanaess. There is little evidence supporting it, though.

Let’s consider. History informs us that the Eademer Concordat left few kindnesses shared by Veluna and Furyondy, and that Raoan liberal religion, the Mrs. Plimpson affair, and the controversy over canonical law deepened mistrust. The Six Nation Alliance against the Temple of Elemental Evil was short-term and provisional, and although victory by the Six Nation Army raised the hope of a Unified Kingdom founded on the distinction of a temporal kingdom and a spiritual church, the Unified Kingdom's abortion ended opportunity to “unite the states and help solve” what was not, as Darg had said, merely “Furyondy’s internal squabbling” but “the cohesion of all the non-evil states, so far as such cohesion exists.” Cohesion's limitations were evident during the negotiations for the Pact of Greyhawk, as they had been fifteen years earlier when Iuz escaped his prison beneath the city and started plotting his revenge through a devasting attack into the heart of nations that Darg had telling described as "non-evil," not good.

If Veluna had been working for unity all this while it had failed, and anyone might see it. Yet the archclericy was not only unscathed but plainly more influential than before. Darg's plea for a just peace was an appeal to Veluna, yet the Scarlet Brotherhood would sign the Pact of Greyhaw despite it. Was that the Archclericy's fault? Had Keoland’s occupation been the archclericy’s fault? Had liturgical reform been bad? Is canonical law inappropriate? Was the archclericy responsible for Furyondian civil law? Ought Veluna to have shunned the Six Nations? Hadn’t Canon Hazen agreed to the Unified Kingdom on spiritual terms? Are you saying that Veluna stands for evil?

Well, my hero adventurers, is that what we are saying?

Mayor Darg may be forgiven for casting Veluna in a favorable light. Irongate was under siege, and in spite of it his enemy, the Scarlet Brotherhood, was bargaining for peace in Greyhawk. Improving the situation depended on Veluna’s support at the negotiating table, where the archclericy was the only participant sitting wealthier and mightier than before the wars. A universal need to placate the archclericy was restraining any expressed resentment; it went unremarked that the “Velunar agents unmasking the Scarlet Brotherhood” in 573cy had not been government spies but courtiers of the Celestial Order that suspected Canon Hazen of abducting Thrommel, failing to discover the culprits, refusing to investigate reports of red monks in the Amedio Jungle, and blaming the monks ten years later for sewing divisions among non-evil nations that were negotiating for peace with Iuz.

Have you ever heard a tale more fabulous?

§

~Conspiracy and theory

You, my historical newbies, will be suspecting that my history seems, at times, in its methods and conduct, to be a vast conspiracy theory comprehending centuries, overturning everything, and written to suit myself. Is it so? Is everyone else in error and only Bifurcati correct?

Apart from their application to me, your doubts go to the heart of the historiographical arts. How far ought we to rely on our reasoning? When ought we to accede to the authority of others? How should we account for our biases? How far should we depend on experience? What do we really know? What methods are adequate to an appreciation of the past? Do we make it all up?

I, more than anyone?

Here there is so much to say, and this is hardly the time. Your months in my tutelage draw to a close. Your thoughts turn from me to the darkness ahead. Doraka’a! The terrible god Iuz! And although your doom is relentless, mine is relenting. We—you and I—have arrived at the Greyhawk Wars. Only five years remain to the end of my monograph on canonical infamy. And although my judgement awaits per the terms of my contract (I must be honest and withhold nothing evident), so much has been written that by now things are likely to be finally settled in the mind(s?) of my unnatural judge. I have done my best. But who may be assured of their personal integrity? What punishments justly await those that . . .

Oh, come on, Professor.

Yeah. It’s not that bad.

Cheer up. It’s been fun!

I don’t know what you’re talking about.

You don't, for real? How about that. It won’t, I suppose, be on your final exam when proctored by the demons of the abyss and graded by their lords and masters. Yet, should I be worried? Are you really as free from doubt as you profess? How . . . wonderful. I commend you to my point of view, of course, in good conscience. Where else would you look? But even so, doubts are to be expected. Yet, I would not plague you with them. Yet, ought I to have had so much influence on you?

Oh, well, you’ll figure it out. Only this much will I say: imagination, intuition, veracity, and fidelity are greater powers than reason, but we must never break our engagement with the sovereign Queen of All Veritable Things, who will never admit that something is right or wrong, true or false, good or evil, on the ground of a private conviction. You cannot reason by private conviction. Our categories of thought are unstable, our definitions equivocal, and when they are not persuasive to Reason she makes the absolute claim to withhold her consent.

It is not exceptional for a church, a nation, a government, a war, a great venture, an institution, a corporation, a company, an investment, a bank account, a reputation, a cause, a hope, an expectation, a belief, a savior, a love, a fear, a faith, a promise, or a romance to exist in half-life, in a state of active decay, where our convictions soon underweigh their lost radiation, their actual diminishment. Consider, in the end, that radiation wins out; doubt and decay are inevitable.

That is what it means to stand in the light of reason. Reason is not our answer, but she endures over time, and in the end, she measures our decay and reaches for new knowledge. Whether we ever reach it seems impossible, but that is the reason for historiography: the differential quest that explores change over time.

Despite all existing opinion, then, it is not impossible that the Canon of Veluna has fabricated history, not I. The allowance for it equals my point of departure.

§

Chapter 26: War, evil, annexation, liberalism, and a maxim of my own

The Greyhawk Wars are inaptly named. Other than bandwagon opportunism (and perhaps the concept titles for a movie franchise) there was little in common among the machinations of Iuz, the attack of the Ketites, the return of the hobgoblins, Ahlissa's insanity, the Scarlet Brotherdood's intrigue, the revenge of the Pomarj, and the march of the western giants. These several conflicts were bundled into the Greyhawk Wars in the widespread conviction that “evil was on the rise everywhere,” but the shibboleth meant nothing when it was taken as the general cause of wars whose specific causes were sufficient. Iuz entered the alliance with Ket one full year after his second invasion of the Shield Lands; it barely affected the war east of Thornward and arose from the long history of hostility between Ket and Bissel, not from the spontaneous procreation of evil. The dogmatic and racial supremacism of the Scarlet Brotherhood was unlike the chaotic and appetitive depravity of Iuz. The ill and servile nature of the hobgoblins (as it was supposed to be) was superfluous to their reasons for warring against the enemies at their border. Insanity accounts for the proclivities of Ahlissa, not vice-versa. The orcs invaded the Lortmil Mountains attempting to reclaim their loveliest stronghold, whether or not the evil of the red-eyes is eternal. And the giants' invasion of Sterich was related to Iuz only by rumors of an “unknown agent” at work in the west. The Greyhawk Wars each followed opportunity and coincidence, not destiny; their explanations are historical, not supernatural.

The matter is not whether evil caused the wars but how the good nations came to see it that way. Although—it is risky to say so. When mortals moot the nominal or ontological existence of evil they dare irking the gods, and although the ontic powers are confined to their heavens, hells, abysses, and other supernatural regions, yet the oerth is yet a mixture of good and evil, and what is unnoticeable to the gods is frequently taboo here, where humans see things diffrerently.

Nonetheless, the renuciation of immortal good and evil must not daunt us. On the contrary, nothing is more necessary, and as I have said, humans are the only historians capable of doing so. The commensurate races are unconcerned to know, and the gods are so nearly omniscient that they barely recollect the past. Nonetheless, historians are far from fair recorders of precedent years. We see the blemishes on good nations—distrust and unresponsiveness among allies, inequitable shares in the costs and benefits of war, King Belvor’s cynical abrogation of the Pact of Greyhawk, the berserk massacre of hobgoblins at Crockport, etc.—but apology is basic to our way of thinking: we are not evil; they are. Furyondians momentarily doubted this after Crockport, but their misgivings were eased by (you may remember) royal decree: hobgoblins are “Paragons of War” that must be defeated at all cost. This forceful reiteration of malice returned the kingdom to its headlong rush into a forever war against Iuz. When evil is absolute, pretty good is absolutely good enough.

I differ with my historical colleagues right there: evil is not absolute. Even reckoning with Iuz, the problem is not evil per se—there are other evil gods—but that Iuz is the only resident evil on oerth, which obliges us to deal with him.

But there is doubt whether we are doing it right, and a resolution must be historical because our doubt has emerged and extended over time. Happily enough, the subject of my monograph is historical, too: the life and works of the Canon of Veluna, good shepherd, mortal man, and eternal saint embodied at present by Hazen, most gracious of the living sons of men. Yet, when shorn of his claim to being immortal evil's due opponent, the canon's life likens to a trajectory aimed wide of grace’s bullseye. So I at least maintain.

History is always on trajectory, never at a point or place in time, and consequently (take heed) the canon’s works are unfinished. Hazen is today an agent for good (purportedly) replete with further purposes and intentions. The purport (to my mind) is out of character, but the man has worked one miracle already in wielding the Crook of Rao to bansih from the Flanaess an infestation of fiends. Does a change of character exceed his grasp?

Historians must grant him time; hero adventurers (take heed) need not. You, my children of wondrous and dire portent, will continue your adventure when my monograph reaches the end. Hazen's history will be yours to realign, if you make it to Doraka'a in time.

Before then I must inform you of a current event: the Annexation Crisis in Verbobonc. You will expect me to see it differently from most people, of course, especially if you absent my Divergent Underground friends, who agree with me. But this time the reason will not be my discontent in the galaxy of my fellows. The last hour for such preliminaries has passed.

(Adjusts his jacket and tie)

The annexation crisis is happening now. My understanding of history informs my view of it, but strictly speaking an historian is inadequate to the occasion. Other artists more suited to the present and future are needed. Deprived of my historiographical privilege, I differ from others over how things are going, not how they came and went.

(Straightens his tie)

I do not see today as others do, and my view of the past is in part the reason. If my view is an improvement, so, (all else being equal) I see the present day better, too, because history’s trajectories reach the future; they do not stop in the past.

(Loosens his tie)

It is commonly said of the past and the future that only the present is real. I disagree. The past, whether remembered or forgotten, reaches the future and the future, whether follwoed or foresaken, reached our past. When we focus on the present, all reality edges away.

(Unbuttons his collar)

The vast difficulty of looking at time's direction lies in the biases that provoke our vision and get in—way, way, way in—to our mind’s deep reaches, like looking through a tinted glass, like a color blindness, like a skewed optic nerve conducting everything that reaches within. The biases are less necessary than essential, a trap set by our affection and like it excessively persistent.

(Mops his brow with the tie’s long end)

I am addressing the problem of objectivity and subjectivity, which, in a lost age, did not mean that subjects are objectified when looked at objectively. No. (Voice rising) The problem then (hands chop the air) was that subjects will determine whatever they see; identity is what we see and not what we are—baffling, cheating, deceiving! Erroneous, positively! Foolproof, apparently! The fools of ourselves, the mistakes of others. (Calms down, straightens tie) So, I have formulated a maxim to cautions against this. A maxim of my own. This is it:

“You might never see what you are obviously looking at.”

¿Que, el profesor?

Pardon?

Is that a maxim?

Its circular reasoning.

Its a false dichotomy.

No—a tautology.

Hmmm . . . tautology? I don’t think so. It solves more conundrums, I think, than only “Why do race horses wear blinkers?”

Why?

So that, when a horse is winning, it won’t see a horse’s behind.

Oh.

You see, the maxim has many useful applications. For another: When reading something that's meaning is obvious, don’t be too sure. Look around. Something might be missing you.

Missing me?

What's missing?

What’s happening?

Where are we?

I think I get it!

Of course, you do. My maxim is applicable to what we’re talking about, which is the annexation crisis in Verbobonc.

Is it?

It is. I have right here the authoritative account of the crisis, clipped from the viscounty’s newspaper of record, The New Verbobonc Times, and taken from an editorial published five months ago wwitten by Bishop Huafren of Verbobonc, who supports the new viscount, Langard, in these troubled times, when citizens in the town and the provinces alike are in an uproar, and no one even knows what to do with the gnomes. So, while we read it, remember my maxim.

Verbobonc was not an official participant in the Greyhawk Wars, but dozens of volunteer companies from the viscounty had bolstered the allied armies of Furyondy and Verbobonc in the fight against Iuz. Upon their return, they found their homeland embroiled in a desperate political struggle with the nations they had left to assist. In 585cy, the Furyondian Knights of the Hart called for the annexation of Verbobonc. Though representatives from Veluna sniffed at such talk, the emergence of the Great Northern Crusade, in which Veluna and Furyondy acted as a single political unit, frightened many in the town who had long preferred the reason (and liberal tax laws) of Mitrik to the zeal (and active monitoring of the finances of the aristocracy) of Chendl. The situation came to a head when old Viscount Wilfrick died in his sleep, in Harvester 587cy, and left Castle Grayfist to his eldest known son, the Right Honorable Sir Fenward Lefthanded. Though Viscount Fenward publicly denounced all talk of annexation, he also enacted a number of rash policies that harmed the city and its friends. Fenward withdrew costly patrols from the forests and hills, and demihuman communities that depended on those patrols to protect them from real and still present threats exploded in uproar. A series of slanderous dispatches between Viscount Fenward and the Kron Assembly followed that left many city gnomes unsure of their allegiance. This dangerous development ended only when papers implicating the viscount as an agent of the Scarlet Brotherhood were discovered in Fenward's chambers. The papers were later revealed to be forgeries, a fact that helped Fenward little, as he had been slain by the captain of his guard when he resisted imprisonment for treason. Thereafter, rulership of Verbobonc fell to Langard of the Gnarley Border, a half-elven, half-forgotten bastard son of Viscount Wilfrick. The new viscount was surprised to find himself in charge of the town and is a cautious although naively open ruler (hoping that his past affairs as a minor smuggler do not come to public attention). In a land so controlled by fear (of monsters, evil cults, and annexation), many look upon Langard's "discovery" with the suspicion that he is a Scarlet Brotherhood agent and no relation to the former viscount.

Right. Who can summarize what we read? How about you, young lady.

Me? Well, ok. It says, obviously, that Verbobonc didn’t participate in the Greyhawk Wars except as volunteers that fought for Furyondy and Veluna. After the wars, Furyondy tried to annex Verbobonc (I don’t know why, or who the Knights of the Hart are either) but Veluna wouldn’t allow it. Later, Furyondy and Veluna were allies once again in the Great Northern Crusade, and Verbobonc worried that this time Veluna would agree to an annexation, which would mean higher taxes in Verbobonc, and things must have gotten pretty ugly with the gnomes, because somebody assassinated Fenward, and Langard was chosen to be the viscount, which he is now, although things really aren’t any better because of the Scarlet Brotherhood. Right?

That was lovely. Adorable. Simply irresistible. You really hit the high notes.

(Dawdling idly)

Did you do your hair differently today?

No.

It’s pretty. I will tell you about the Knights of the Hart. They got started in the third century after the Great Kingdom and the Viceroyalty of Furyondy had broken up. They have branches in Furyondy, Veluna, and High Folk, each pledged to watch the borders of their respective nations and to mutual defense when called on. In Furyondy, they are beholden to the northern nobility; in High Folk, to the elven aristocracy; in Veluna, to the Celestial Order of the Moons; and together, they were the vanguard against Iuz on the northern front.

So, the knights in Veluna supported the annexation of Verbobonc?

A charming question. Very sweet. What made you ask?

The Furyondian branch called for it, and the king and the royal court apparently agreed, even though Verbobonc was Veluna's vassal. Veluna rejected annexation out of hand, but the Celestial Order was part of the archclericy, the branch of the knights in Veluna is beholden to the Celestial Order, and the knights pretty much side with Furyondy all the time, or anyway, pretty often.

Pretty often. Very pretty often. Did the Times tell you that?

No. You did. (Fidgeting) You say it all the time. It’s in your history. Come on!

The Times didn’t mention it, but it’s in my history, and you remembered it. How engaging! What else didn’t the Times say?

How should I know what it didn’t say?

Because you’re so sweet when you’re not saying it.

(Banging the desk)

Stop it. Leave her alone. You lech.

Lech, my boy?

That’s right. Don’t you see? You’re embarrassing yourself.

(Others chime in)

Yeah, Professor. You’re out of line.

What does he think he’s doing?

I didn’t . . . I’m not . . .

Maybe you should apologize to me, Professor Bifurcati.

I do. I will. I promise. I vow. It won’t happen again. Have I ever thought that you were pretty before?

Oh, Professor! What would the answer be to that?

What a clown.

Do you believe this? He’s fifty years old.

Forty-four!

He’s just some old guy.

A joke!

A pantaloon!

Although, something is a little off about that editorial.

Is it? (Glancing again) It seems pretty clear to me.

Don’t say “pretty.” It will set him off.

It won’t! I don’t!

I’m bothered by the bit that says, Verbobonc “long preferred the reason (and liberal tax laws) of Mitrik.” It doesn’t make sense.

Doesn’t it!

Verbobonc and the archclericy have been at odds since before Voll became Veluna. The viscounty was never a willing vassal, it was made one by the overking, and it didn’t worked out too well. When the archclericy declared Veluna’s independence from Furyondy, Verbobonc stayed neutral. During the trade wars, the viscounty sided with the Celestial Order, with Veluna City, and with the counties and dioceses against Mitrik. Keoland’s occupation strengthened ties between the viscounty and the occupied southern provinces. After liberation, Verbobonc sided with the Celestial Order and Furyondy in attempting to replace the archclericy with a secular government. Prior to the Eademer Concordat, the viscounty broke from the Church of Rao and from the archclericy to establish the Diocese of St Cuthbert while continuing as a member of the Celestial Order. For the next one hundred years, the archclericy was mistrusted because of canon law and the Temporalites, and when the Temple of Elemental Evil arose, it was Furyondy (once again) that rescued Verbobonc in the Six Nation Alliance. So, what exactly is this “long preference for the reason of Mitrik?” It’s unlikely, I say.

Delightful.

But you’ve forgotten about Mrs Plimpson and liberal religion. The Mrs Plimpson affair marked the beginning of liberalism, and Verbobonc has become a liberal state. That ties it to Veluna, definitely.

Cute.

No, because explicitly it was not Mitrik’s liberal tax policies alone but also its reasonability that appealed to Verbobonc in contrast to the zealotry of Furyondy. Reason is theological in Veluna, so, that's a tie to the Church of Rao.

Saucy.

What zealotry was that? When was Furyondy ever zealous? It was always Veluna that was zealous. That report is false.

Pert.

Your wires are crossed. It was the Furyondian branch of the Knights of the Hart that was zealous, as knights usually are.

’At a girl.

The knights could not have annexed Verbobonc, only the king could do that.

Sweetheart!

But they had political power, and if you are going to have chivalry in government, better it were rational than zealous.

She’s a keeper!!!

(Silence and astonishment)

She? Who? (Pointing) Do you mean him?

It, I meant. I meant, “It’s a keeper.” I was referring to my aphorism.

Professor, he’s a boy.

No, my dear, he’s an aphorism. I mean, it is.

Right.

Really.

You are employing my aphorism to see what you aren’t really looking at, all of you! Lordy, lordy, it does this tutor’s heart a great deal of good. I am so proud of you and her. I mean, it.

That’s weird.

No it's not. You are debating Verbobonc's liberal religion, politics, and economy. That’s the point of contention. The whole question entirely. You have arrived where my history left us: at Mrs Plimpson and the obscure D, Prince Thrommel’s abduction, rumors about the Scarlet Brotherhood, and the Archclericy caught meddling in international affairs. So beautiful!

That’s not what’s weird.

But it is. So many obscurities are discovered when we stop believing what we are just reading. Oh, lovely! Oh, excellent! Oh, adoration! Join me, join me, join me in extolling the virtues of my maxim.

Professor?

Yes, my boy. You have a question?

Not exactly. I mean to say, it’s personal.

Personal? I see. To you or me?

You, sir.

I see. Go on.

It’s just that you seem a little distracted and you’re blushing. So, I was wondering. Are you in love with your maxim?

In love with her? Ah, it? I wouldn’t say that. It’s just that I have hopes for it. I hope it meets with your approval.

Why wouldn’t it?

Well, I’ve never introduced it to anyone. It’s a shy and modest little maxim, almost my child. I have no idea how my debutante will be received. Suppose she is scorned. Suppose she is unlovely.

Well, the best remedy, I suppose, is to get to know her . . . it . . . a little better.

My intention exactly. I want to introduce it to you. And, Lo! My maxim is descending the high, baronial stair to its debutante ball wearing its enchanting white gown, purer, more fetching than snow on snow. It is smiling differently this evening. Not the same playful grin that I have ever known but more—captivating? conquering? inviting? My goodness! Can it be? Is my mind changed? Do I wish it go back upstairs to its room, where it will remain my little maxim forever?

Not gonna happen. Its out now, wearing its magical and nonrefundable gown of alluring, which cost only ten or twenty times what a modestly prosperous professor can afford on his stipend. And I notice that you, too, my amazed pupils, have turned your attention away from me. All eyes are on it! Well, that’s what I wanted. It’s not so bad. My maxim thinks for itself now and is applicable on its own. It was conceived for this day!

Waist high, it holds a white, handwritten card. When I introduce it, it shows it to you. Having anticipated the turn of your attention to itself, it prepared the card and now places it in a silver holder to leave when the clock chimes twelve and my maxim disappears. Which, it does. You read the card, and it says:

My new friends—what does reason have to do with liberalism?

Then it smiles—captivating or conquering?— and vanishes like a dream in a fairytale. And perhaps your heart breaks a little, too, like its dad’s.

Here, Professor. Dry your eyes.

Thank you, my girl. I must say, I have never had finer students. I hope you all get back alive.

So do we, Professor. I think we owe you that, since you introduced us to your maxim and all.

It’s a precious, useful child, isn’t it?

Truly.

So, now. Let us recollect ourselves. Who can tell me, which lines in the blockquoted text has my maxim referred to?

I can, Professor.

Though representatives from Veluna sniffed at talk of annexation, the emergence of the Great Northern Crusade, in which Veluna and Furyondy acted as a single political unit, frightened many in the town who had long preferred the reason (and liberal tax laws) of Mitrik to the zeal (and active monitoring of the finances of the aristocracy) of Chendl.

Yes, that’s the one. When you actually read it, the plain passage apparently begs many questions. What is this preference for Mitrik? (That’s your question.) Why is Verbobonc’s fate up to Veluna and Furyondy to decide? Why is the union of Veluna and Furyondy so frighten people now, when a decade earlier the Unified Kingdom had been the best hope of the six nations?

Professor, we also have a question.

Go on.

Since the Archclericy of Veluna and the Knights of the Hart are connected to the Celestial Order, the Celestial Order's supreme mistress, Jolene of Samprastadar, is implicated too. What’s she up to? That is, if she really exists, because you said, she’s romantic.

No, I said Mistress and Prince was a romance.

No, you said she was a romantic too.

What Jolene is doing nowadays few know, only that she is still supreme mistress and that the Celestial Order speaks occasionally in her name. Not often publicly but more often in private. Don’t ask me, How often is more often than not often? because I don’t know. I only know, through Wilna Pummenford, that members of the Celestial Order and of the Velunar branch of the Knights of the Hart speak in her name sometimes, as it were, for emphasis.

Which reminds me of a book that makes a reference to something that would be useful right now. Give me a minute, will you, to consult my PISS?

(Twenty-five minutes later)

Ah, yes. Here it is.

Viscount Wilfrick of Verbobonc grows old, and a city that once maintained a powerful militia and a neverending watch against evil, especially over the Gnarley Forest and the dread Temple of Elemental Evil, has grown tired along with him. It is entirely plausible that Scarlet Brotherhood agents and "advisers" have counseled the Viscount to sit tight in troubled times. If there is still vigilance and strength in Verbobonc, it resides in a handful of rulers of local towns and fortifications, several of whom are known to have meetings with Furyondian representatives and members of the Knights of the Hart. It may well be that determined efforts will be made by these people to formally align Verbobonc with Furyondy and Veluna, states that gratefully received volunteer Verbobonc warriors during the Wars.

This excerpt is from The Viscounty and Town of Verbobonc, by Carl Sargent, published in Greyhawk, in 585cy, only a few months after the end of the Greyhawk Wars. As you see, it fits very well with the longer blockquote given ahead of it: both feature volunteer soldiers from Verbobonc, unnamed political “representatives,” Knights of the Hart, and a possible formal alliance (or a union or realignment) of Veluna with Furyondy, which is somehow threatening Verbobonc’s stability and independence.

Sargent’s book was written prior to (although published after) the call for annexation had been given by the Knights of the Hart, and as you see, many aspects of the crisis were already known at that time. But questions and ambiguities plague his early assessment of Verbobonc’s political situation.

For example, has Sargent implied a connection between the Temple of Elemental Evil and the Scarlet Brotherhood in Verbobonc? If so, he reached enormously beyond Veluna’s initial speculation about red monks abducting Prince Thrommel in the Sea Princes fifteen years earlier and seven hundred miles away.

Were the “Furyondian representatives and members of the Knights of the Hart” all Furyondian, or, might the knights have been from the branch in Veluna? The referent in the text is grammatically ambiguous. Yet five years later for no expressed reason The New Verbobonc Times designated “Furyondian Knights” while ommitting a mention of representatives.

Sargent wrote that “a handful of rulers of local towns” in Verbobonc was preparing a “determined effort to formally align Verbobonc with Furyondy and Veluna.” Those nations were already informally aligned although at odds at the moment over annexation. So, we may ask, what had the annexation crisis done within an alliance that had served well enough for three hundred years by avoiding whether Verbobonc had remained a vassal of Veluna's after Veluna had broken its feudal troth by declaring independence from Furyondy and the Great Kingdom?

Why was a “vigilant handful” of rulers quietly contacting Furyondian representatives about a new, formal alliance? Was this an effort to bring new government to Verbobonc by ending vassalage to Veluna? If so, we may ask whether the politics of these few, not the controversy between Furyondy and Veluna, had frightened the liberals in Verbobonc Town. After all, there was no way Furyondy could force annexation on an unwilling viscounty. Annexation was ultimately the viscounty’s choice. No matter what the Knights of the Hart may threaten, Verbobonc’s domestic politics would be the crux of the controversy. Moreover, when considering the viscounty’s domestic quarrels, were gnomes any more likely resort to assassins than were vigilant rulers, liberals, and aristocrats? What about the Scarlet Brotherhood? Only a few years after Veluna's diplomats and Irongate's Lord Mayor Cobb Darg had recalled them to attention in Greyhawk, here we see them rumored again. Was any of it real?

Given the complexity, to summarize the viscounty’s political turmoil by the declarative sentence that “many people in Verbobonc prefer Mitrik and liberalism to Chendl and zealotry” will both beg and beggar belief. Who would write such a thing? Why would the editorial board of the Times tilt so far to the liberal side of the controversy and throw shade on the others? I and you, my adventuring few, would be beggared to buy what the editors monger: Mitrik is so reasonable! Rao is reasonable! The archclericy is reasonable, the canon is reasonable. For one thousand years, the editors exhort us to believe, Veluna and the Church of Rao have been our light in dark places; in our current crises, we must depend on the good shepherd all the more. At this time, when good nations are impoverished by war and must pledge themselves to a war forever, The Times begs an answer to one question: Will you abandon Mitrik now because you doubt the perfect purity of its benevolence?

The Times wants us to believe that Verbobonc prefers liberalism and reasonability. Does it? Are liberal taxes better (and lower) than zealous ones? May the quest to lower an aristocrat’s taxes be zealous, or only the need to raise them? Are liberals too free in their possession of things? Are people that claim to be liberal and equal so free with each other? Is it right when liberals yet again exceed their grasp?

Why must reason be liberal? Why kisses she the assets of the wealthy? Why stands she reduced to a predicate of Mitrik? Oh, why, why, why? My prisoners freed from a true prison, I have many times asked Our Lady by Necessity these questions, but she only pouts and frowns. “Am not! Do not!” cries She Who Must Be. So, that’s settled.

Don’t panic. We need not risk Her Permissible Indignation by trying Her Limited Patience with such queries. The reason at stake in Verbobonc is not the Measure of Justifiable Cognition but merely the reason of Rao. At stake is the teaching, the dogma, the authority, and the multiplicate biases of the Archclericy of Rao, whose canon preaches casuistry in Mitrik.

As for Jolene of Samprastadar: you have asked how the annexation crisis implicates her. It is well that you ask. Every node in annexation’s political nexus has an immediate connection to her. She is Supreme Mistress of the Celestial Order, the archclerical house of congress affiliated with the Knights of the Hart. She knows the leaders of the Hart from their negotiations at Castle Estival (for the Six Nation Alliance) and Reymend Town (for the Unified Kingdom). The knights are in contact with Verbobonc’s vigilant rulers, and therefore, so is Jolene. She knows the Viscount of Verbobonc (a member of the Celestial Order) and the Canon of Veluna (who receives her political advice). She is beloved as nearly-the-Queen of Furyondy, as nearly-the-daughter of King Belvor, and as the true princess of the people, their hope and delight.

She is also the inveterate adversary of the Archclericy of Veluna and the most comprehensive schemer of her time, when the alliance of Furyondy and Veluna is more fiercely contested than ever since the Extraordinary and Episcopal Conclave in the Eademer Battistero. Is it all a coincidence?

Many people “plausibly” believe that the Scarlet Brotherhood is behind the annexation crisis. But are the red monks more plausible than Jolene? Or is she the more likely agent of our discontent?

§

Interlude: Class Dismissed

(The next morning)

You, the esteemed subscribers to my magical tome of learning, met prior to our assembly this morning and voted a collective action against me. You insisted on asking me a question. How bold! Which of you will speak this portentous doubt? Which has the gravity to raise a voice before me? The temerity to interrogate the obscure Bifurcati in his temple? Is it you, young man? Are you the messenger? You will deliver the lines well enough, no doubt, but it will matter what they say, won't it?

Well boasted, Your Worshipful Mightiness! I bow until I'm backwards in front of you. To propitiate the omnipotence of your derogation we bring a sacrifice, a bun, left over from breakfast.

A bun? Well, bring it here. Mmm. And the question?

The scholar raising it wishes to remain anonymous, and because we agree with the question we put it collectively. It arises because you love your maxim. There are many things in your manuscript that you confess loving. Reviewing the text, you love your bookseller in Molag, the poet Lord Gordyn, a waitress serving beer in Bay’s Stop, the Veracious Queen of Veritableness, hobgoblins, Molag, language, Luna, the tale of Thrommel and Jolene, romance, and other things too. You didn't have to confess them but you did. You said you were blessed twice by thrice-kissed Myrhiss and won’t tell tell us the second one. So, we’d like to ask, What do you think about love?

Gasp! Startle! You want me to speak of love? What on oerth would I say? You ask too much. What is love? What does it do? Some say, love is what death becomes, that life and love are one. Others say, Love's flower will forever bloom, no faded evening or wilted noon. We lullaby our children to sleep at night singing, “The sun will rise for love of you.” But what do I sing? What do I say? . . .

Professor? Are you alright?

O! my companions in misadventure, your question comprehends the world. It gives me pause. Wait a moment, I'm going to write it down . . . What . . . is . . .

We didn’t mean to . . .

But you did. You put me in mind of something, of someone, of a place where I have not been for a score of months and would always go if I ever could. And it occurs to me that this is the way to end our book. What is love?

Class dismissed. A field trip, the scholar's vacation, awaits you tomorrow to Verbobonc Town, the most fortunate of history’s preserves, where you will see elves, gnomes, humans, knights, chivalry, halflings, and dwarves as they once were, ought to—and may yet—be.

Our adventure has moved on. You have passed Lake Aqal, traversed Fellreev Forest, and reached the barren plains of the far north. You sleep tonight in the unlovely mud of the Opicm River, under the sunless skies of awful Doraka’a. One hundred miles down the icy river’s stream Iuz awaits you.

At this point, at this time, when my grievance against Hazen has been mooted and my historical work is complete, you slake your thirst and hunger on the meager yield of bleakness and are to hear this said:

I, Annalo Bifurcati, am stipulated within and bound by contract to inform you that from henceforth you shall own or, as it is written,have power of attorney to disseminate in any manner you choose the contents of this book. It is yours, not mine, from now on, no matter what more may be written within. Soon, soon, soon, I hope to escape entirely from my contractual obligations and from most of my oerthly ties. I regret very little (although possibly very much) other than leaving you, my scholars of hope and peril, when I am gone. I would not willingly abandon you even now to the gloom and the darkness and the mud were it not for what requires my departure tonight.

You should rest, then, my hero adventurers, since gloom is not without solace and occasionally leads to morning. Prepare for what tomorrow may bring. The sky here is sunless but not moonless; may you dream of the consolation of life.

Seek your repose below lighted, diffuse Luna, who soothes the bubbled blisters of day. The sun demurs to th'enticements of gloaming and delineates his sister's auguries. Sweet deviser and bearer of tremorous dreams—you will be gone when (unwantedly) we wake in the morning—and miss you!

I have work to do by candlelight.

§

SCENARIO SEVEN—VELUNA

§

Chapter 27: The history and the Knights of Verbobonc

The sun falsely dawns—no, he falsely declames! that his dawning means more than Luna's loss to us. Whatever. Let's just agree with him.

This morning I salute you, my sleep-dispelling dedicates to learning in the pre-dawn. Although, some of our group—oblivion’s laggards—still nod in their places in our coach. We should give them pillows. May their dreams tarry under auspice of night while we start our journey to Luna’s vale, three-quarters of a thousand miles onward. The driver snaps his whip, and we’re off!

We journey to the most ancient artifactual land in the Flanaess. Nothing historical in my story, excepting Lake Aqal, is older than the origin of Verbobonc Town. The eldest ipt treehouses are nearly as ancient as Boboncan elves, and like the latter they, too, are primordial. The town rests in a garden so timeless it may testify to an earlier Oerth, where the ipt trees are twice as tall as anywhere else, the river runs clearer than it arrives from upstream, and the breezes go where they will, dispersing the prevailing winds.

The road to Verbobonc is scarcely less wondrous. It goes west through Great Belly Valley, where silt anciently dissolved out of the karstic Cairn Hills was carried by the undermining rivers and deposited to fathomless depths. The fertile soil of the Belly begat the upland Cairns civilization, forgotten to time but so wondrous that its hill tombs survive and entice us to their witness—had we but world enough, and time!

§

~The Nyr Dyv

Professor! It's the Nyr Dyv!

Hmm? Yes, dear, so it is.

It's magnificent!

It's water.

Aghh! How can you be so dull!

Dull? That seems uncall . . . ah. It is your first time seeing the lake. How dull of me not to have realized.

Does it go on forever? Is it always perfect?

Pretty near. A wee bit short, and dull.

Those sails, like floating ivory towers! Those birds, like soaring ivory ships!

They ferry a lot of rats, though.

Rats? How can you be so unenthused?

I live in Nyrstran. My rooms are ten minutes from the lake and the rats are everywhere. They are, of course, very dull rats and very dull rooms.

Professor . . .

I've been on the lake, in the lake, under the lake, over the lake, along the lake, across the lake . . . It's probably very dull to think of what I've done with the lake.

Are somebody's feelings hurt?

If so, I can't say whose. I can only say that it was dull of me not to take you there sooner.

Oh, dear. My good Professor. Your history is a bit unnerving at times, but if you let me sit beside you and link your arm, I will tell you that you were dull about the lake, not in your character. It matters very much that you took me to see it. I would else be in the shadow of Iuz, which is no fun.

Iuz? Shadow? Oh, my dear . . .

Did you say shadow? My friends! I had forgotten it for a moment. Sometimes words run me round like legs a little child lost in fun. But it is reprehensible to have forgotten where you really are while we seem cozy by the lake. Did you eat today while you travail in the fruitless Lands of Iuz? Are you well and safe? Do morbid pestilences plague you? Perhaps you believe that I forget what you do and where you are, but I don't for long, because much the same is on my mind.

We have only one question among us: Does a devil or something better run our little show? Who sends you to Doraka’a? What contracted me to write this history of sketchy things? Have you, have I or have we all together been fooled by false saviors and left for damned? What awful blind man’s buff is this?

For me, the game is already played. I have committed my version of events to parchment, and my judgment—whatever way it skews—awaits. But you still read. Your game is still on. You could call it quits, abandon your quest, return to Law’s Forge, and be part of the fate of the thorpe once again. It could happen.

I cannot recommend it. In my experience, the devil you know is no worse than the angel you don’t. A reputation for good will hide a wealth of ills; a reputation for ill may go either way.

§

~Fog bound

Bay's Stop gathers fog from the Nyr Dyv, brought by onshore winds that blow through the town, rebound off the mountain cliffs, and envelop the place again. The fogs off the lake are stirred by rivals that drift off the slow Selintan River, and local folk can tell which sort—river or lake—of fog beclouds them, although outsiders bide an undifferentiated soak, beseeching the afternoon sun to disperse the fog of the morning before the evening fog is in. And other than the fog there is nothing here. No prospects, no aspects, no features. Bay’s Stop is stolidly built to resist the seep and decries architectural interest.

It is my favorite place on Oerth. It sees me regretful, sad, hopeful, and lovely. (There are more feelings—but those may represent the rest.) We have only five minutes before the coach wheels past the Stop, a village so small to be at the heart of the world.

Of course, I am not really here. This, my fantastical friends, is a half way house between Nyrstran and Verbobonc, between where I instruct you from my rooms at Olde Maurian and where we go searching for Jolene of Samprastadar and her phantasmal plot against the Archclericy of Veluna. Of course, my instruction may be phantasmal, too, a fictional distraction from your deceitful trek through a healthless empire. Are any of us sure?

The coach swifts us past a familiar place having a public sign. Who is it, there, just the other side of that door? I hesitate, the chance is lost, the coach carries on. That’s fine, because I am no longer here. I never was, perhaps, although—between yesterday's phantasms and those of tomorrow there is a difference that keeps sorrow at Bay and hope alive to be dashed, perhaps, another day.

§

~Verbobonc Town in summer

Why are we hacking through this thorny thicket? The girls will tear their summer dresses or scratch their arms left bare in the sun.

That, my boy, is why we go first. Be gallant and clear a path. Thwack!

Right, Professor. Chivalry is not dead. Although, the absurdity of our situation seems undiminished. Thwack!

Absurdity? Soon you will be wondering how a place without access could be known to me, just wait and—see!

By the gods! What a sight!

Yes, but my boy, the ladies are in peril. Turn your back to the scene and put it to work. Thwack!

Pardon. Thwack! Ladies, after you.

Ladies, observe!

(Ladies cheering collectively) Verbobonc! It must be Verbobonc! Let us see!

Yes, its Verbobonc. Or, more properly, Verbobonc Town, which is older than the viscounty.

Professor? Did you bring any bandages? I've pricked myself awfully while hacking the thorns.

No, my boy. Girls, within the walls you see, the town is substantially unchanged for five hundred years. Many of its elements—the high, fluted, wooden towers, the ipt treehouses, and the odd stone lintels built into the hillsides and leading into dwellings that the gnomes call “rents” (although they own them—are one thousand years old and almost as pretty as you.

One thousand? (Big eyes) We were told about elvish things that old in the Fellreev Forest, but I laughed at it! (Giggles becomingly)

No, no. At Lake Aqal there are elves . . .

Uh, Professor? This particular stab right here in my wrist may have popped a vein. I can't bind it with only my other hand. Would you . . .

Not now, boy. As I was saying, girls, the elder elves at Lake Aqal may themselves be two or more thousand years old.

But Professor, how do you know this place? (Quizzical smiles, enraptured poses)

Well, ladies, that's a tale. Or a long sentence. This panorama is figured by a second century van Valckenborch landscape that happens to hang in the Museum of Nyr Dyv Antiquities, which I happen to curate, and so, it was only a matter of . . .

I've removed the thorn, Professor. At least, I think I got it all. But it's made the bleeding worse.

Uggg. Ahhh. Ouuu. Ladies, if I may trouble you to loosen your arms from mine. Delightful. Now, son, let me wrap that for you.

Sally's mine.

She is?

I've liked her since we were kids.

Oh. Have you told her?

Grrr. Bark! I think she knows.

“I think she knows”—the four most dangerous words a man may speak. I'm sure she likes you. Stay alive, get out of Doraka’a, and tell her. Understand?

Yes, sir. Oww. Hey. Owww!

Don't make me come after you about it.

§

~Verbobonc Town and the Cathedral of the Holy Cudgel

The problem with Saint Cuthbert is that common sense—which he is the god of—is too self-congratulatory and lacks self-awareness. Cuthbertines believe they are right and are ready to discipline us over it. Their faith is a horrible mix of well-sounding phrases and deplorable practices. Here is a catechism they recently published and that speaks for itself:

The words of St. Cuthbert are wise, practical, and sensible. The word of the Cudgel is law, and the word must be spread so that all may benefit from his wisdom. Weakness in faith and acting against the Saints [sic] teachings are intolerable in believers. Unceasing effort should be made to bring unbelievers into the fold. Honesty, truthfulness, practicality, and reasonability are the highest virtues.

The Cuthbertines believe that their god is common sense, so, they see no difficulty in declaring that the Cudgel should be spread to everyone and that, after it has been spread to you, independent thinking is intolerable. Their zeal seems sensible, practical, and reasonable to them. No use remonstrating—many have tried—because they have common sense, which outfoxes reason without having to explain how.

Professor, are you sure you've got that right? Back in Law's Forge, we used to smelt the armor of dead Cuthbertines the demons dragged in. I know the corpses were Cudgelites by that symbol over there, which they wore. The demons believed the Cuthbertines were good knights, which is why they ate them alive—slowly.

Well, lad, zeal for good and for ill are arbitrary things. If you go around saying, “I'm good,” and wearing a white tunic, then demons tend to believe you. Spotting that symbol was keen, though. What do you suppose the building is that bears it?

A Cuthbertine armory?

Hoot! Your answer is better than the truth. This inauspicious construction is the Cathedral of the Holy Cudgel, looking like a warehouse dropped among the horse carts at the bottom of a hill rather than set aloft in the usual way.

The location is instructive. In Verbobonc, the Diocese of Saint Cuthbert was established to aid the anticipated abolition of the Archclericy of Veluna one hundred fifty years ago. The basic functions of the diocese were to place a Cuthbertine episcopate within the Raoan College of Bishops and to replace Raoan clerics with Cudgelites in governmental positions. But the viscount was wary of disposing of Raoan troublemakers by creating Cuthbertine ones and of the cudgel’s dogmatic insistence on interfering in peoples' lives. Consequently, the civil authority of the new diocese was restricted to the government postings, to a small militia of about two hundred clerics patroling the forests and hills, and to the new, twinned orders of civil servants, the Bishop’s Ministers and the Knight-protectors, which we read about in Lights and Shadows: “Marvelous agreement! I am proud to be a Verboboncan, where at least I have the Cudgel.”

The civil diocese and its cudgel are still helpful to the viscounty. Verbobonc's troubles with monsters and evil cults are as primordial as the ipt trees and elves. The viscounty worries especially about spies, because its remaining connection to Veluna and the Church of Rao is promoted jealously by the insidious factions. Cuthbertine dogma —with its emphasis on laws, cudgels, and unceasing application—serves to keep other troubles at bay, because St Cuthbert’s zeal for religious conversion is now equivalently dedicated to service as the viscount’s lawful civil deputy.

Converting religion to nationalism is not that difficult; it may even happen spontaneously, as with the subject of this monograph. As a rule, faith will convert by believing that it is a civil authority’s sacred accoutrement. Believing that they wield St Cuthbert’s cudgel, many of the militant’s saints zealously transform themselves into a national security service: vigilant, honest, truthful, and opposed to anything that distresses civil order, such as evil cults, rumours of spies, monsters in civilized places, and outsiders generally speaking.

This explains the depression and architecture of the cathedral. The seemingly functional structure and its location on a low-lying thoroughfare represent the dependability, accessibility, and inevitability of St Cuthbert's service to the diocese. There is no escaping the Cudgel, so, you may as well accept it.

Most citizens believe that Verbobonc’s has a tempering influence that softens the force of the cudgel by comparison to the damage it dealt elsewhere in the Flanaess by that blunt instrument, and they are partly correct. But even so, nationalism is never an innocuous thing; it can turn virulent at any moment. It remains necessary to watch the vigilant, and the viscount keeps an eye on the cudgel.

Nonetheless, the humble cudgel is not without grandeur. If you direct your gaze to the top of the hill that rises behind the cathedral, you will see a kind of villa or chateau made of mullioned glass and—judging by the tower on this side that can be seen straight through—vast rooms and impressive spaces. The vines creeping up the villa’s walls are in harmony with the park that encircles it, and althat make an architectural unity with it. Behind the houses there are walls enclosing gardens that reach up the hill to the park and that delineate what is, comprehended in its entirety, a luxurious compound finely displayed on a landscaped high pedestal.

It is Billets Palace, the residence of the Bishop of Verbobonc, the chief of St Cuthbert’s diocese. The Billets is reached from the cathedral by the long street with houses and gardens; the gates to the compound are barred at the low entrance adjacent to the cathedral.

The supremacy of The Billets over the cathedral communicates an idea: in Verbobonc, the glory of the diocese is the bishop, not the church. This unusual ecclesiology reflects the diocese's role in the social and political world here. The palace and its cathedral were built following the establishment of the diocese by the viscount. Although the viscount’s lineage is not Cuthbertine, the accord of viscount and bishop is foundational to Verbobonc’s exemption from vassalage to Veluna. There had never been a bishop of Verbobonc before the installation of Cornelius Speiknhammer, in 446cy, which ironically led not to the abolition of the archclericy but to its restoration. Verbobonc’s bid to become a part of Veluna had failed, and from that time, the viscount has looked to the plar of the Celestial Order rather than to the Canon of Veluna as his representative in the theocracy.

St Cuthbert’s faith in Verbobonc, as we know, is not an established religion; it is an established civil diocese, marking a clear distinction of the cudgel’s civil and religious aspects. Viscount Langard will not condone an overlap lest he be accused of a two-fisted assault on his citizens. The current occupant of Billets Palace, Bishop Haufren, is a religious reformer that may be seeking to reduce the role of the civil diocese and return to cudgelite values of faith. He supports Langard’s proposal of a Verboboncan branch of the Knights of the Hart, because the knights could relieve the viscounty's dependence on the civil knight-protectors and bishop's ministers. The idea is making headway, and his continued support could be crucial.

The wonders of Verbobonc’s architecture are equalled by its politics, which resemble a brainless nervous system where everything does on.

§

~Reymend Town and the Romantics

I know where we are!

Hey, now?

I know where we are.

Is that so?

I do too.

So do I!

That's Concordance Stack!

That's the Velverbridge's Old Lane, Viscounty Park, and Leeward House. It's Reymend Town, from Mistress and Prince!

Oh, I don't think so. The growing darkness deceives you.

Stop it. May we go across?

That’s a collective decision, but we are headed to dinner, which awaits on this side of the river.

(Crossing over)

There's a fire in the Stack.

A new one is laid every night in homage to the missing prince. He may still live, and this light would guide him home to his lost Unified Kingdom.

Could that be construed as anti-Raoan sentiment?

Could be, generally isn't.

So, there's really nothing left of what happened at Reymend Town? At Leeward House? In Viscounty Park? Even here, in Leeward’s ballroom?

Tomorrow we will see what is left.

The ballroom is grand and brilliant, with dancers and an orchestra. It's fabulous and terrible. They were here and are swept away!

At Leeward, the Romantics were happy sometimes. They thought they'd won.

May we see the garden where Ferrica and Edmore waited for their friends after the smoke signal from the Stack?

It's out here.

It's beautiful!

Not as it was, though. It's been relandscaped.

Now there's a metaphor.

Class, I am pleased that you chose to cross to Reymend. It was in my heart, but I did not want to drag you along. The attendance is voluntary and warm or it is nothing. And now, spiritually fed, we may attend other fare.

Actually, Professor, there's a pub right there, and the customers seem to relish the food.

Maybe. But the braised lamb my stomach craves is served over that bridge.

Can this be a collective decision?

Oh, I don't think so. The college pays for our trip, and I am the college.

Autocrat!

Don't walk so fast. I can't keep up!

Don't stress, my dear. We have passed the point of no return and may go at our leisure now. Here we are! Let me get the door.

That’s very considerate for a tyrannical old man.

I heard that. Doesn't this look nice?

I'm having the lamb and it had better be worth it.

No lamb yet. Drinks? Shall we say, five bottles of wine to share before dinner?

(Eyebrows raised)

As you know, young padawans, a war of propaganda was waged by Edmore Wunsay and Ferrica Aposnos in the taverns of these towns on behalf of Prince Thrommel and his princess, Jolene of Samprastadar.

They rock.

They do. And for all we know, this identical vintage was consumed by them in the course of their conspiracies. There is no greater utility to a literary man and his sister than a bit of inebriation before song.

Say it loud!

Who may gainsay?

I'm switching to ale!

Mostly, these spontaneous songs and recitations concerned the prince and princess, whose love for one another gave hope to the desperate in the way this refilled goblet gives hope to me. The joy of the people was especially Jolene, who remained their princess while bearing the burdens of birthing their new world.

Go Jolene!! (Megaphone hands) Rrriot Grrrrrl!!

One of Wunsay's most famous compositions was not his own. Right here, in this tavern where we lose our inhibitions, he heard a song sung and declared it “the new national anthem.” It was published the following day.

Wunsay! Wunsay! Wunsay!

The anthem is not sung anymore and its sheet music is treasurably rare. But even so, if you possess one copy you might make others, and I have a sheet each for you. The song sums up the spirit of the times—if you are crocked when you sing it.

. . . two, three, four:

(All)

I AM AN ATHEIST!

I AM A SECULARIST!

That’s bitchin'!

That’s bestest!

It’s off the chain!

Why does it sound like Anarchy in the UK?

I'm hungry. Can we order?

I second that.

§

~Verbobonc Town, the Meanders

(Upon the morrow)

May we enter?

Of course. The owner is an old friend of mine, and so a new friend of yours, as humans generally are to elves. We call them “evenses,” but that's a stretch. We entertain them a short while, then we vanish. Although, some of the elves take to us. “Whether you row the lake or barrel the falls,” as they say.

There's more beauty in this house than in a thousand iterations of Law's Forge.

Please, more Law’s Forges only augment the ugly.

They constantly craft their houses while the ipt tree grows. The ipts in town grow vastly taller than anywhere else, even higher than deep in the Gnarley Forest. No one knows why. The trees are inhabited long before they mature, making continuous reconstruction necessary and allowing the ipts to adopt the dwellings. They are pruned and shaped according to the plans of the architects that inhabit them. We say that the treehouses are thousands of years old, and in parts they are, but the dwellings always evolve according to the growth of the trees and the designs of the elves. An ipt tree will share three or four dwellings that are in common at the top. The ipts over there, with bridges that link them, are public spaces for whatever occasion.

This isn’t a treehouse, it's a sculpture! Curves, lines, angles, tones, textures, tracery. The rooms, doors, windows, and stairs are parts of it.

Uh oh. The door is locked. Professor, we have no key!

It's an arcane lock, my love.

Don't call me that. How does it work?

You speak a password, and the door opens magically.

Cool! May I speak it?

You don't know it.

An ignorace you could rectify, I'm guessing.

The password is private, silly.

“Private!”

No, no. To elves, friendship is kin, and kin know the password. The elf living here is my friend, you are my closest relations (with a prospective exception), and so, the password may be spoken by this pretty young la . . . mmm . . . sweethea . . . mmmm . . . woman!

Professor! It worked!

Ooou. Paintings and carvings! Walls, ceiling, floor, vines, flowers, rivulets, and creatures. The entry isn’t painted, it’s a painting! A mannerly garden.

Is that a word woven into it?

μαίανδροι. “Meanders,” in Common. The noun, not the verb. The dwelling’s name.

These stairs look a bit shaky.

Not stairs, an escalator, going thirty feet up to the inhabited branches. Walking down the steps depresses the plates that load a weight chained to the outside that lifts your ascent. Unfortunately, the escalator can lift no more than it took down, so, only one of us may use the device to see how it works. The others must climb on our own.

Weeee! Beat you to it!

Damn girl is quicker than a fly.

Weee! Weeee! (Running away into the upper reaches)

If you don't come back, wait for us in the library!

(In the library, lounging on a sofa, waving a book) Look what I found. It’s Osgold’s Epitome. Remember?

Meanders’ inhabitant is an amateur associate in the Divergent Underground, although unlike humans, he does not need to hide the book or risk the consequences. There are very few libraries where the countess’ treatise is shelved openly. This is one of them.

(From a room opposite the library, beside a window open to the world)

Hey! Why is this book displayed on a reading stand next to a spyglass pointed out the window? Are we meant to read it? It’s handwritten in elvish, maybe a journal or a diary?

§

~The elf’s journal

As you may remember from an earlier context, elves enjoy espying by spyglass out their ipt treehouse’s windows. This particular casement has a fine view to the east, where the hills of Verbobonc Town drop to the river. You will notice that, just there, the scar of a wooden palisade mars an otherwise pretty rural district half a mile from town. Beyond the pallisade is a voluminous white canvas tent held high by great poles that obstruct our view of what is within and beyond. Seven months ago there was nothing on the plot but grass, mown occasionally for the benefit of picnickers.

Meanders’ inhabitant, my elf friend, has been watching this alteration to the town’s landscape and documenting his discoveries in this journal. The entries are presented in full for our perusal, although, for our benefit, he has glossed their contents in a half dozen additional pages. His meager obervations are of no consequence to anyone and draw no one’s attention, and he cannot imagine why we take the time to inquire after them.

⚜

The gloss:

Moon’sday, 10th Snowflowers. While preparing my evening oblations to Celene, I noticed the viscount’s coach stopping at the picnic ground on Asters Lane, just below town. Langard disembarked with a gentleman and a lady, each forcefully striding (especially the lady) to reach the top of an undulation that rises to where, on the far side, picnickers often compare their baskets of delectables and the valley’s visual delights.

But no picnic had been brought by this trio, perhaps because the spring whether was chilly. The servants remained with the coach and horses while the viscount’s party went walking from side to side, looking out widely, gesturing broadly, and conferring intermittently. Langard, in his unmannered way, stood to the left, the gentleman to the right, and the lady—the locus of attention—was allowed the central place. Their manners were businesslike, unleisurely, and the woman, whose initial credit as a lady was my mistake, had a crude, almost professional manner that complemented, as I saw through my glass, her rough dress and hard features.

The men deferred to her. She carried a telescope that she used to survey the terrain before parading off, men in tow, to stomp down selected spots of mud and grass with the thick heels of her (I swear) boots, pointing and waving all the while and occasionally driving—by a hammer that she wore fastened to her belt—into the ground a metal rod that she otherwise wielded as a walking stick. Langard offered to assist her by his greater strength, but she dismissed him as redundent.

The scene was so intriquing that I forgot to greet Celene when she appeared. It was quite dark when I saw her at last in her aquamarine gown, patiently awaiting my lapsing meditation.

oerthday, 13th Snowflowers. This week’s Nosey Neighbor has announced that Baron DePloyer, from the Viscounty of the March, in Furyondy, will purchase the aforementioned picnic area with the intention to construct a chateau there.

Moon’sday, 17th Snowflowers. The dubitable lady has reappeared several times the past two days, at different hours, to stand on the higher ground and stomp down the meadow’s undulations while taking notes and making sketches. She took an abrupt and dismissive tone with me, however, in responding to my friendly inquiries and attempts to initiate conversation. I was obliged to retreat and watch from my window. I did learn that, as I suspected, she is an architect from Furyondy and from Dyvers particularly.

Starday, 22nd Goldfields. Today cartloads of timber stakes arrived at Asters Lane and were offloaded at the picnic ground. Their lengths appeared regular, at first, but through my glass I could tell that they were only approximately uniform, and later, when I inspected up close, I found them rough and splintered. Whatever they will make—a palisade, most likely—will be ugly. My neighbors are depending on my vigilance and vantage to keep them informed.

⚜

(Confused) Professor—didn’t you say that this was a gloss?

Yes, in a manner.

⚜

oerthday, 27th Goldfields. The palisade took only two days to set up, a row of spears staked through the innocent side of poor, gentle Asters. The lane’s beauty bleeds like mud from the wounds. Why a baron would buy and spear our picnic area seems unreasonable to me. The palisade is deplorably tall and sits high on the undulation. Our view of the valley is ruined and obscured. A huge canvas curtain—like a circus tent—has been raised on the sloping meadow even higher than the palisade, fifty feet up, I estimate, in a rectangle that blocks all view of what is going on. The baron may want to unveil his erection all at once rather than one stone at a time. A riverboater from Rhynehurst told me that the first stones have shipped from Luskan and are barging their way here.

Sun’sday, 9th Sunflowers. The stones have arrived. They are simple limestone bricks and none too many, probably intended for the foundation, not the edifice. More lumber has been arriving, too, mostly at night pulled by teamsters bearing torches to light their way. How much stones and lumber there are is difficult to say, since I do not count well in trance. The wagons pass through a high gate excavated through the undulation and at the level of the lane, leaving empty the next day. Within the tent there isn’t much going on. A little digging, cutting, and hammering. If progress is being made, it’s difficult to say toward what.

Waterday, 12th Sunflowers. She reappeared today looking womanlier than ever in her shiny, well worn, corderoy pants. She rode as one of the teamsters at the head of three heavy wagons from Dyvers. Cannily, she feigned not to remember me but ostentatiously recalled me to mind and inquired, “whether Master Elf strolls just as frequently in Asters Lane when I am not in it.” After acknowledging my admiration of a woman that sits a good wagon, I walked to the rear and, finding a spot where the tarp was only loosely tied, peeked into the bed. Then turning and leaping with the ungainly yet hazardous speed of a sow bear, Miss Bompton (that is her name) raised a great, booted rear paw and brought it down on me with a force likely to mangle head or hand were they not withdrawn in time. I was so shocked that I looked into her eyes, finding them to be a dim brown that through malice was bright with mendacious wit.

“Since boncky elves live in trees,” she said, “perhaps they are leafed out of noticing that the weather is clear, it is unlikely to rain, and under such skies there are tarps on carts to shelter them from inspection, not the elements.”

Oh.

⚜

oerthday, 13th Sunflowers. Bompton’s unexpected mixture of transfixing speech and artillery fire shocked me out of a verbal reply, but I hinted a retort by glancing at her wagon with the satisfied suspicion that things had not gone entirely her way. Peeking in the bed had revealed wooden and iron assemblies whose familiarity I am still pondering. Moreover, the term “boncky elves” is heard barely more than never, is used exclusively in reference to Verbobonc’s ipt tree dwellers, and is peculiar to the northeastern meadows of the Diocese of Kempton, in Veluna, which is horse country for the Knights of the Hart. Evidently, Miss Bompton has not been in Dyvers long enough (if she lives there at all) to shed her provincial manners.

Freeday, 14th Sunflowers. Bompton’s crew of workers—five, I think—is taking a day of rest, but she is diligent. Over the past few days, windstorms have parted the sheets of the canvas tent far enough to disclose a wooden frame that is being built in a farther portion of the meadow. But the curtain, the palisade, the lay of the land, and the intervening trees obscure it from my view. Apparently, Bompton is inspecting the frame’s construction. She is in sight at times, at other times screened from view, while occasionally her head alone appears over the pallisade, where the breeze dries the sweat in her hair and forms clumps like straw in manure. Her 'do looks especially stylish today. She must have lopped it herself this morning.

I thought I would inspect the wooden frame to determine its purpose. The day was warm, the sun was high, and Miss Bompton had neglected to bring a lunch. Remebering the fond, former use of Astor’s Lane, I packed an ironical basket and carried it to Baron DePloyer’s estate. When she answered the bell at the gate, I stepped inside.

She intervened. “Pardon, master elf. You weren’t invited, and it says right there, No Entry.”

“But there’s no other place to picnic for miles and miles, and I’ve gone to all this trouble out of kindness and concern.”

She hiccupped and burped, a sort of grimace or grin propped her mouth open, her head turned askew, and her eyes rolled up in bafflement and dismay. She changed her attitude five seconds later, bowed to me in a mockery of welcome, swept the air with one strong arm, and stood aside.

“Under the new management,” I went on, “the best picnicking seems to be over here,” and I walked to a spot near the construction.

“Oh, goody. My favorite, too,” said Miss Bompton, whipping the blanket from under my arm and spreading fully it with an emphatic shake.

She looked at me while we sat, turning her head as though it changed the perspective. “Is the view good,” I asked, “or does the construction that surrounds us spoil the whole prospect. You might look into the basket. There may be something more to your taste.”

“OK, darling.”

I finished my inspection, came to my conclusion, and gave my explanation.

“The daub is drying nicely. Judging by the spacing of these posts, there will be room for twenty stalls—six box, fourteen standing. The hayloft will be well placed above the entrance when it’s up. You have fastened a hitching ring —chosen from those I had seen by peeking in your wagon—to a brick column to test their strength.”

“Fascinating.”

“The stable seems large for the baron’s needs. The chateau won’t be that large if it is proportionate to the tent. How many guests will it accomodate? Does the baron keep horses for hunting? Will he run them in his meadow?”

“It is the viscount’s meadow and the baron’s chateaux.”

“Will the baron run horses in the viscount’s meadow?”

“He will be welcome, I suppose.”

“Indeed, the visccount does seem welcoming. Was the land for the chateaux sold to the Knights of the Hart? Was it gifted to them? Or is it let for free?”

“Hold on. The Knights?”
